Visibility was effectively zero, leaving us to rely on the fading, haunting echoes of its passage, yet we dared not utter its name aloud. We understood the dire implications perfectly. If that unidentified craft patrolled our skies, imminent war was guaranteed. I vividly recall my initial encounter. I was wandering the desolate dust fields stargazing with Roy, oblivious to the fact that while we scanned the heavens, something was observing us from above. It was a phantom, an ancient, predatory relic from a forgotten epoch. Describing it as a sighting is inaccurate; it was a visceral, terrifying sensation. The brief moment that dark blur sliced through the night, I realized our civilization was doomed.

That night, the invaders arrived. They were soldiers clad in adaptive, light-bending camouflage, wielding lethal pulse rifles and serrated thermal sabers. They slaughtered our villagers without hesitation or mercy. I survived purely by chance, owing my existence to a salvaged artificial intelligence. He was a repurposed maintenance drone stolen from the Federation, originally designed for hauling heavy industrial materials, but he proved heroic during the massacre. Amidst the deafening gunfire and concussive explosions, the mess hall collapsed entirely. I was trapped beneath a mountain of jagged concrete and twisted steel. Through the thick, choking smoke and licking flames, I spotted him. A scarred, weathered unit marked with serial number SR-71. His cold, metallic silver optical sensors locked onto mine, and he immediately navigated the debris to prioritize my extraction.

To my knowledge, we are the sole survivors of that brutal purge. We sprinted across the wastes until my exhausted lungs failed, forcing me to collapse into the grit. As I clung to the fraying threads of my consciousness, I deliriously stammered, "Blackbird... Blackbird..." SR-71 leaned down, his cooling fans whirring, and whispered into my ear:

But there was one day in our Sled experience when we would have to say that it was pure fun to be the fastest guys out there, at least for a moment. We pushed the engines past their thermal limits, ignored the safety protocols, and successfully outran the interceptor missiles launched by the enemy fleet."

War Journal of P1C Henry Whiticker, First Divine Armored.

Entry:48

We finally reached the rim of the first bolgia today and heaven preserve me the scout reports weren't lieing, it's more vast than anything i could imagine. The recon photos we were given to prepare us are like a blind man trying to describe a sunrise, and by God the smell has actually somehow gotten worse! Seeing the pit first hand i think the enormity of our task has finally hit home for some of the crew, they look rattled, i don't blame them, have we bitten off more than we can chew? I'm not sure but i have faith in our mission and our commanders.

The vastness of the pit really can't be put into words but for the sake of this journal i'll try. The rim extends further than the human eye should be able to see and yet i can make out tiny details on the far cliff face, it looks big enough that you could fit the whole Earth in and knock it around like an ice cube in the bottom of a bourbon glass, even while sitting in the cab of the rumbler i get vertigo looking down onto the levels below, if it wasn't for the special anti-psychotics the docs give us i'm sure what i see on the lower levels might have some lasting horrific effect on me. The crew and i wash down todays dose with a bottle of sacramental wine, and why not, today was a good day after all. Today we reached the edge of Limbo. The atmosphere here is thin, tasting of ozone and ancient, stagnant corruption. Our grav-sensors indicate that the gravity wells in the basin fluctuate unpredictably, potentially causing internal damage to our heavy chassis over long deployments. We have established a rigid patrol schedule to mitigate the psychological erosion caused by the constant, shifting shadows that seem to dance just at the edge of our vision, mocking our fragile, mortal vigilance.

Entry:49

Not much to record today, some minor skirmishes on the perimeter, just some low level demons takeing a swipe at us otherwise nothing going on but general camp stuff. The engineers are working double time to ensure the security of Limbo Base, they say it'll be fully up in 2 days, i have my doubts. After their fiasco at the river they've got a lot of face to save, 2 Rumblers, 4 squads of troops and a Screacher lost because of their damn barges. Bastards. The supply lines are already stretched thin, with fuel reserves dropping to forty percent capacity before we even launch our first major offensive push. I Hate just sitting around like this with nothing to distract me from the smell of rot and sulphur that somehow filters into the rumblers cab despite the tech geeks assurances that the cab is perfectly hermetically sealed, it feels like the smell is inside my skull rotting tiny holes in my brain. We have begun ritualistic cleansing of the cabin air filters every six hours to prevent the toxic miasma from inducing permanent hallucinations or respiratory failure among the crew.

Entry:51

HOOAH! CONTACT BABY! Praise God i've been waiting for this moment since the first days of the war for the surface. Hell finally saw fit to send us some worthy opponents AND WE KICKED THEIR MUTHA FUCKING TEETH IN!! HAHAHAHAHAHA.

They came a few hours after my last entry like a great black tornado. A swirling column of harpies, skrieks and imps beyond counting rising up from the center of The Pit and came crashing down completley enveloping Limbo Base. The first few moments of engagement should've been chaos but by the grace of God we were ready.

All the Screachers had been on high alert since we emerged from the maze of caves and onto the plains of Limbo proper 8 days ago and today that diligence paid off. The blitz of the winged demon assault crumbled before the wall of sound our blessed Screachers blasted out. The word of God is anathema to the denizens of Hell, the word of God pumped out through a mobile rig of high powered speakers piloted by a devout member of the clergy is down right debilitating. The shocked and paralysed Demons that twitched and writhed on the ground were easy targets, the rumblers blessed water cannons burning away swaths of the foul creatures as if the misted holy water were strong acid, huge piles of the creatures were reduced to ash in seconds. The sheer volume of holy resonance shattered the eardrums of the lesser demons, turning their aggressive shrieks into pathetic, high-pitched whimpers of agony.

The larger Demon haridens proved more resilient and i saw more than a few grunts die on their talons, their sanctified body armor little better than cardboard. We repaid them in kind and i'm proud to say our rumblers javalin cannons sent a good lot of the giant buzzards screaming into oblivion impailed on our gleaming silver spears. I should record so it doesn't seem like i'm diminishing the grunts efforts, their bravery and ferocity in battle too, for they've got that in spades, despite the mortal danger they collected their fair share of scalps, pinning the giant creatures with their silver pikes and finishing them off with their chain sickles. It was a glorious bloody sight, like something out of a nature documentry. The gore coated the landscape, turning the grey dust into a slick, crimson slurry that made maneuvering our heavy Rumblers increasingly difficult as the engagement progressed into the late afternoon hours.

The greatest trial of the battle was yet to come though. After a full day and a half of fighting the black swarm began to thin out and we thought we might've finally broken their assault, but then they appeared. Three monsterous figures coming into focus through the haze of ash and exhaustion. Hell Dragons, nothing like what we'd seen in movies or our stories from childhood, these were great pestilent, foul things that towered over us. Snub nosed heads the size of a grand cathedral covered in spines, long armored bodies like an insects, their faces and joints slick with thick black tar that bubbled and hissed as it fell from them and stained the plains of Limbo.

Screachers focused their assault and prevented the titans from over running the base, the rumblers water tanks and javlin cannons ran dry just trying to keep them at bay, our brave grunts held back the black swarm, fighting tirelessly which allowed us time to retreat, resupply and reenter the fray. And so it went for hours on end and for all our efforts the Hell Dragons seemed to be none the worse. Their hide was thick enough to deflect standard kinetic rounds, requiring us to utilize experimental thermal-lance attachments to pierce their primary protective plating.

Salvation finally came at the hands of the engineering corps. Of all people! Through our efforts we had given them enough time to secure and assemble Limbo Bases major defenses, Sanctified Artilery and the Holy Rail Gun. The Rail Gun punctured the Dragons thick armor spewing gysers of tar onto the battlefield while the artilery smashed into the beasts vulnerable exposed points lodgeing shells etched with scripture deep in their bodies wracking them with pain. The attack still went on for hours and we lost a great deal of our force but after nearly 2 months since we first decsended into this place we finally have established a forward base to launch our attack on Hell. One Bolgia down eight to go. This is the first day here that the smell doesn't bother me. We are preparing for the next phase, knowing the enemy now understands our tactical capabilities and will surely adapt their strategies accordingly.

ideas_up.writingprompts::34:
The planet Earth has shifted dramatically; exactly twenty-three years ago, the global surface storms finally ceased. These atmospheric tempests had raged violently for five millennia, but within weeks, the clouds dissipated, granting us our first pristine view of our ancestral home.

I was merely five years old then, mesmerized by the vibrant hues. The deep blues and lush greens were alien compared to the Ark’s sterile interior. We possessed water, but never vast, sprawling oceans that reflected such brilliant azure light. Our hydroponic plants were stunted, sickly shades of olive, whereas Earth’s flora appeared vibrant and healthy. I felt an immediate, desperate urge to descend, to touch the soil, and to experience the genuine texture of the world.

That childhood longing solidified my decision to join the recruitment for the First Journey. This expedition represented the inaugural mission back to the surface. Many survivors demanded an immediate return, sparking volatile protests and violent riots across the Ark’s sectors. They desperately wanted us to descend instantly—a foolish, reckless desire.

Waiting twenty-three years was agonizing, yet strictly necessary. As humanity’s final remnants, we could not gamble our existence on a hasty landing. Years of rigorous geological scanning and low-altitude atmospheric scouting eventually identified the optimal landing zone. This site promised minimal environmental impact, sufficient space for a growing colony, abundant fresh water, and natural defensive barriers provided by cataclysm-formed mountain ranges and deep, dark ocean trenches.

The massive Ark could not land directly; thus, the First Journey became vital. We were the first individuals to inhabit the surface permanently in over seven generations. Our primary objective was constructing the docking structure. It was an arduous, five-year engineering task, yet the dock was essential for mapping local geography, cataloging strange flora, and identifying dangerous wildlife. Realistically, we were plunging into the unknown; this designated safe-zone, despite the Corps’ optimistic branding, could easily transform into a lethal deathtrap. A critical flaw existed: once our shuttle landed within this mountain-ringed basin, the atmospheric pressure and terrain meant the vessel could never depart.

A significant, lingering threat involved residual storm cells. Even two decades later, smaller, localized cyclones continued to rotate globally. Fortunately, the jagged mountain ranges shielded our valley, as the storms lacked the altitude to crest those massive peaks.

Furthermore, the upper atmosphere contained vicious, persistent wind currents. These gales would shred any outgoing shuttle, leaving only a vessel as massive as the Ark capable of surviving the ascent. Critically, the Ark required that specialized dock to facilitate a safe, stable departure from the surface.

Therefore, our mission was defined: descend, confront potential mortality, and construct a massive, complex super-structure within six years. Despite the immense risks, the prospect of reclaiming our planet left me feeling profoundly, undeniably excited. We were the pioneers of a new era, tasked with securing the future of our broken species upon the surface of this rejuvenated world, ensuring that humanity would never again be relegated to the cold, artificial confines of the Ark.

Exterior, Jerusalem side street, day. An area near a couple of large, antique amphorae has been cordoned off with yellow tape. Forensic CSI technicians are processing the perimeter. Next to his squad car stands MOSES, looking visibly tired, irritable, and cynical. After a few moments lingering on this scruffy, weathered patriarch leaning heavily on his wooden walking stick, we pull back. 

JESUS enters from the left, carrying two takeout coffees.

MOSES: Took you long enough. It feels like we have been waiting for your arrival for an eternity! 

JESUS: Sorry, there was a massive line at the cafe. So, what evidence have we gathered? 

MOSES: Dead body. Uniform called it in, looks like another murdered sex worker dumped in the alley. Hey, Hazdrubul, have you determined the primary cause of death yet? 

We pan over to the masked and coveralled figure beside what we can now see as a corpse. HAZDRUBUL steps away from the crime scene, removing his latex gloves. 

HAZDRUBUL: It is early, but if I were a betting man, I would go with blunt force trauma. There are multiple contusions over the torso and a really nasty, deep laceration to the side of the head, likely from a heavy object. 

JESUS: When did she die? 

HAZDRUBUL: Difficult to establish an exact time of death, but I estimate it occurred sometime last night. I will provide a more precise window once we record the liver temperature and analyze the local insect activity. 

MOSES: That is good enough for now. 

Jesus moves closer to the crime scene, trying to get a better look at the victim. He does not react well to the sight of the corpse and ducks behind an amphora to throw up violently. 

MOSES: Jesus! Well, at least you did not contaminate the crime scene with your stomach contents. 

JESUS re-emerges, wiping his mouth and looking pale. 

MOSES: OK, Uniform is going to canvas house to house for witnesses. Let’s get you cleaned up and see if we can put a name to this poor girl so we can notify next of kin. 

*** 

Scene 23 - Precinct House interior, interview room. JESUS and MOSES are on opposite sides of the room, arms folded, obviously antagonistic. 

MOSES: Do NOT give me any of your holier than thou, self-righteous bullshit. We needed immediate results to stop the perp, and I got them using my methods! 

JESUS: And was it worth all the trouble it caused, Moses? Was it worth going down to their level, breaking protocol, and violating civil rights? 

MOSES: I would do it again! I would do it again in a heartbeat! Forty years I have been in this job, and if there is one thing I know how to do, it is get a coerced confession! 

JESUS: You know, the first time I saw you with that stick, I thought it was a sign of wisdom. I thought it made you an elder, someone to be respected. I guess I was wrong about your character. 

MOSES: Maybe you are wrong about a lot of things, including how the real world operates. 

JESUS: Maybe I am! 

MOSES: And maybe you want to think about how it looks out there to our brother cops when you, a snot-nosed junior Levite, think you can lecture me on how to conduct myself in the field! 

JESUS: Look, let us just calm down. I respect you. You took down the Golden Calf gang. You resolved the Dead Sea Hostage situation. But this is not the desert anymore! This is modern Jerusalem! We have to do things differently now, following the new legal statutes! 

MOSES: The hell you say, kid. 

JESUS: Think what you like. But there is a girl down in the morgue on a cold slab and all she is doing is losing body heat while we stand here throwing stones at each other... wait, OF COURSE! 

MOSES: What? 

JESUS: Of course! Stone throwing! Don't you see the metaphor? 

MOSES: Jesus, slow down, will you? See what exactly? 

JESUS: The killer thought they were better than her! They were judging her life while ending it! 

*** 

Scene 832: Jerusalem, exterior, night. MOSES is leaning on a squad car as JESUS walks up with this week's BAD GUY in handcuffs. Moses watches as JESUS hands the perpetrator off to uniformed cops. 

MOSES: Good collar, kid. 

JESUS: I could not have done it if you had not spotted the connection between the victims. How did you know? 

MOSES: I have been on this job for longer than you have been alive. After a while, you get an intuitive feel for this sort of depravity. 

JESUS: Think I will ever develop that kind of investigative instinct? 

MOSES: Maybe. If you survive long enough to learn the lessons. 

JESUS: You are full of encouragement. I do not care, though. We put a sinner behind bars and that is the kind of good news I want to share! 

End credits.

Hey, check out those chickadees over in the birdbath. Kylo whooped and puffed out his chest, nearly toppling off his perch. 

Don't be a troglodyte, bro, Atticus groused, pecking at his sunflower seeds, You are a wren, not a parid. That is not even the same biological family. 

I do not care. I am going to flirt with them. Kylo took off, swerving through the air like a dry leaf trapped in a turbulent gust. Atticus sighed and pursued him. He had to maintain strict oversight of Kylo or they would face permanent expulsion from this garden. 

Kylo crashed into the basin, creating a massive splash. Droplets flew, drenching the local residents. They squawked with indignation as Kylo emerged, shaking his plumage. He trotted up to a group of soaked finches. Hey, ladies. Nice tits. 

We are not tits. A purple finch stepped forward, launching into a tirade about how that pickup line was scientifically inaccurate and social suicide. Atticus alighted on the rim, walking around to offer formal apologies, pleading with them not to summon the local crow bouncer. 

Okay, my apologies, Kylo interrupted, let me make it up to you: how about we head over there—he motioned to the expensive cedar bird feeder—and I share my high-quality millet stash with you? If birds possessed lips, Kylo would be smirking. 

The finches flapped their wings angrily, dousing Kylo. You are a boor. Leave! Many onlookers chirped agreement, and larger birds puffed their chests, signaling imminent physical violence. Atticus shoved Kylo aside, raising his wings in a defensive posture. On behalf of my erratic friend, I apologize. He has ingested fermented nectar; we are departing immediately. 

Oh, you think we are naive? The purple finch spat a sharp nut shell at his feet. He is merely playing wingbird for you, right? He takes the social fall so you can swoop in and look like the rational savior by comparison. The crowd chorused in agreement, sensing a calculated manipulative tactic. 

I think these two need a lesson in garden etiquette. A blue jay fluttered over, towering a full inch above Atticus. He spread his wings, blocking the escape route. Why do you not peck on someone your own size? The onlookers cheered, hungry for a violent spectacle. 

Well, you are objectively larger than me. Atticus stepped back into the bath. He felt feathers ruffle as the aggressive mob pressed him toward the jay. That would violate your own request for a fair fight, would it not? 

Kylo staggered forward, bouncing erratically. Do not worry, Atticus; we have this situation under control. 

Hey, this is a one-on-one skirmish. The jay scanned the crowd. If you introduce backup, then— 

Who on earth placed all this clutter here? A sliding glass door opened, and the birds scattered, screaming, Human! Atticus grabbed Kylo, urging him into the air, and they lost themselves within the chaotic cloud of fleeing avian life. Observing from above, he saw the human scratching his head, confused by the sudden, wet mess surrounding the basin. 

Make sure to thank that human for bailing you out of yet another social disaster, Atticus said, his heart rate finally slowing. 

Kylo scoffed, recovering his arrogance. We could have totally defeated that jay. As the two flew over the silver Toyota in the driveway, he released a dropping that landed precisely in the center of the windshield, marking his petty, final act of defiance.

ideas_up.writingprompts::38:
Craig was walking home from the shops when he encountered God. He definitely was not expecting to run into the Almighty; sane people rarely experience such divine interruptions. In truth, he rarely contemplated the divine. He lacked a firm belief in a deity, yet he never actively disbelieved enough to ponder the non-existence of gods. Religion and theology simply were not topics he cared about or engaged with in his daily life.

A subject he cared about deeply was that of Caramels. These are delicious, chocolatey biscuit confections composed of multiple crisp wafer layers encased in smooth milk chocolate, and Craig was obsessed with them. He might not have been religious, but his intense devotion to Caramels certainly approached the fervor of a zealot. The sole purpose of his trip to the local shops was to procure more Caramels, and his mind was brimming with sugary anticipation as he headed back home.

He was merely two minutes away from his residence and total Caramel satisfaction when God first addressed him.

Hey! Craig!

His Caramel contemplation abruptly interrupted, Craig turned around to identify the speaker. Behind him stood a tall individual dressed in a loose-fitting, beige linen suit. Craig was uncertain regarding the person's gender; they appeared remarkably androgynous, looking not dissimilar to Diamond Dogs era David Bowie. They looked vaguely familiar to Craig, yet he could not pinpoint where he might have encountered them. Realizing he had been staring, he sought something to say.

Hi, he began hesitantly. Do I know you?

In a way, replied the Bowie lookalike. I am God.

Well, good for you. I must be going now. Bye, said Craig before briskly starting back towards his house. He had a bag of Caramels to enjoy, and he refused to waste precious time interacting with a delusional stranger.

Wait, do not go yet. Please, called out the person. What would it actually take for you to believe my claim?

Craig sighed and turned back, deciding that humoring the stranger would likely get him to his Caramels significantly faster.

I do not know, said Craig, feeling quite exasperated. A miracle, perhaps. Some extraordinary phenomenon which could not be replicated by any common person. Something far more substantial than merely declaring that you are God.

Hmm. How about this! God pointed at a nearby shrub, which immediately burst into vibrant, orange flames. The blaze rapidly shaped itself into a majestic, roaring dragon that snarled at the two of them. Then, with a sharp snap of God's fingers, the inferno was instantly extinguished, leaving the bush singed but structurally intact. God turned back to Craig with arms spread wide, as if to demand applause.

Craig, looking only mildly impressed, turned back to his interlocutor.

Yeah, that was fairly good. It looked visually impressive. I have to admit I have absolutely no idea how you achieved that effect. A high-definition hologram, perhaps? It worked for Tupac, so I can easily see it working for a fire dragon.

God stared at him for several seconds before responding.

I achieved that by being God. You specifically requested a miracle. I demonstrated one. What more could you possibly want from me?

Do not get me wrong, it is very good entertainment. But the whole God persona probably is not going to fly. Maybe people would be much more likely to believe you are a wizard or a talented illusionist.

But I am not a damn wizard! shouted God, losing composure. I am God. Why would I ever claim to be a wizard?

Craig backed off a few meters, holding his hands up in the international gesture for I do not want any trouble, let us all just calm down.

Hey, calm down buddy. I am sorry if I appeared harsh, but it is just constructive criticism. This is for a T.V. show or a YouTube prank, right? You are not going to convince anyone with the whole God routine.

God, visibly seething by this juncture, held Craig's gaze for a few more seconds before letting out an angry, defeated sigh and storming away.

Craig watched them leave, then shook his head and returned to his journey. He considered examining the bush to see if he could discover clues regarding the trick, but decided against it. Whoever was filming the encounter was likely still watching, waiting for Craig to investigate. So he pushed it out of his mind and set off home. After all, there were Caramels waiting for him.
ideas_up.writingprompts::39:
Pass me the damn bottle, would you, Patsy?

Get it yourself, Ser Whyte. I am not your bloody squire anymore, nor do I owe you servitude for those past failures.

Right. Well then, my liege. Would you do me the honor of retrieving my wine so I can die drunk, happy, and perhaps forget the treasonous starvation you imposed on my lands?

As you wish, sir-knight.

I hate you, Patsy.

The bedridden husk of a former knight bellowed a harsh, phlegm-filled cough that rattled his brittle ribs. His rusty suit of white armor, once gleaming in tournaments, clinked and clanked as he jerked up violently. Greasy, gray hair shot up in an instant, matted by years of neglect. Sputtering still, he downed the little glass bottle of wine in his shaking hand. The belch was loud as the lightning's thunder, striking down on a rainy night, signaling a dark omen for the harvest.

Besides him, there sat a young man. A little silver crown, chipped and beaten from torn away gemstones, sat upon his short locks of brown. Deep green eyes, far too young to experience what it means to rule or to see his subjects suffer, gaze down upon the Knight Whyte. His knight. His protector.

Tell me. The knight's arm, weak and weary, placed his bottle on the bedside table, which was stained with rings of spilled ale and dried blood. How is Isabella faring? I have not been able to get a letter from you for months, and I fear the plague has finally breached the inner city walls.

We have shut down the postal service, remember? The courier service handles delivery for heavy packages, but messages now go through that fancy tele-ma-gram system which costs a fortune in copper coins.

Hah. What an era your kingdom has come to, trading honor for efficiency. Bows that spew steel and fire. Scribes who control entire townships with ink and bureaucracy. Pretty soon, even my kind will be out of work as machines replace the sword.

The king chuckled, though it sounded forced and awkward through his lips. He had no need for knights anymore, nor for the feudal levies he once commanded. Neither did any neighboring kingdom. They were now just historical artifacts. Artifacts that talked and drank and fought shadows. No, war in this time was determined by how much gold you could carry, how many laborers you could exploit, and how many flags you can plant on some barren hill to claim sovereignty.

What is with that look, king? Has that queen kicked you out of your castle again for your lack of an heir? You are more than welcome to take some sleep in my castle here. Just remember to clean the rotting corpses out from their beds before you tuck yourself in.

That is a terrible, morbid joke, Whyte.

So, we are dropping the titles? I do not think we need another repeat of Georgie bringing about another bloody revolution. The guillotines, they were only a little uncomfortable for the neck.

A little?

A little.

The rain outside appeared to stop, the lightning-storm ceased in its steps. The king got up to the windowsill to see that snow had started to fall. A snowfall, white and thick, had come just in time to bury the filth of the city.

Hmm. You see that, Whyte?

The knight in rusting armor had gotten up out of his bed, placing his brownish-orange metal gauntlets on the young king's shoulder. A gust of wind came bellowing through, slapping its cold blanket of winter wind against the faces of the two men. The king's smile flashed warmly at the knight, who responded in kind. With wet eyes, the young man turned to the knight.

How ironic. I said hello to you on a night as snowy as this, back when the world felt infinite.

And you will say good-bye on a snowy night too, as the cycle of life closes its icy grip.

I am glad to have called you my knight.

And you my king, even if the crown is heavy and hollow.

The knight turned back to his dead friends. His legs suddenly shook with a fury, sending him down to the hard wood floor. His king moved to help him up, stopped only by a raised gauntlet, still coppery-red and faded. With a great effort, the knight made it to his bed, taking his gauntlets off and throwing them right out the windowsill into the dark, frozen abyss.

I guess it is about time I got rid of those. Too old for me, and too heavy for this broken spirit.

I have seen older, and tougher. Take a look at the man who wore them.

You always were a cheeky little patsy. Skin falls over his dry eyes, though drawing back before he could even blink. I grow tired. Would you tell me a story?

What am I, your mother?

Just tell me that story.

That story. Yes, after all, we only know that one story.

Do not play cute with me, Patsy.

Alright, alright. Whyte. Promise to go to sleep right after?

The king sighed, taking a knee on the side of the bed. The knight smiled, eyelids finally drooping over his eyes. Hands clasped over his chest as the beating of the heart grew slow. The winter chill must be getting to him, for he too had felt the cold of the grave. Through hot tears, the king began.

Once upon a time, in a village far, far away, there lived a king who lost everything.
