One metre high and as wide across, the blackened and dusty car roared down the desert road. Ahead ran the troupe with their tank of pressurized helium, the motorized unicycle blazing as they tried in vain to stay ahead of Kinko. The fifteen clowns inside readied their jagged weapons as they closed fast upon their rivals on the unicycle ahead, their engines leaking oil. 

Boffo, Luffy, Bobo, grated Kinko, fucking clowns fucked with us for the last fucking time. When we catch up to those assholes, I want you to fucking whitewash their asses. Fuck them up so bad that they can honk their noses from the inside. They nodded, and gripped their sharpened slapsticks all the tighter while checking their heavy, grease-stained pockets for extra confetti grenades.

With a roar, the car pulled ahead of the clowns in front and slid to a halt. The doors opened in unison and the fifteen of them tumbled out and rolled to their feet. Two of them grabbed the weaponized ladder from the roof, knocking over another three as they stood readying their semiautomatic pielaunchers - and the same three again as the original two turned to see what they hit. Two others ran into each other and fell to the ground, outstretched and immobile. To one side, Bobo and Kinko hefted their heavy, sticky pails of industrial custard, and started towards the unicycle with grim, painted smiles.

Bastards! screamed a whitefaced warrior as she fell from the shoulders of the topmost clown. Rolling as she landed, she sprayed a stream of pressurized water from the flower on her lapel, knocking Kinko to the ground with a highly amusing parp!. Grabbing a stiff rubber chicken from the driver, she waded into the fray, knocking Kinko's clowns over like bowling pins. That helium is ours, she declared while brandishing a sharp squeaky hammer.

The hell it is! roared Luffy, pulling the pin on his volatile rubber nose before tossing it at the jesters falling from the unicycle seat. That helium is ours, for our massive balloon displays! Balloon zoos are ours, you hear? Ours! Grabbing the back of her pants, Bobo upended the bucket of rancid custard into them before pushing her to the ground. As she bounced up and started running in circles, he grabbed the cylinder from the unicycle and tossed it in the car. Our troupe! he cheered, as the rest of the clowns piled into the car. One cranked the front handle to life, and with a cheery melody, they drove off down the road, to their big top in the desolate, irradiated wasteland. As they disappeared in the horizon, the whitefaced warrior sadly blew her horn, and watched the dust cloud fade in the distance.
ideas_up.writingprompts::41:
The air remains unseasonably cool here, carrying a crisp bite that signals the coming frost. A thick, opaque fog rises off the manicured gardens, and the atmosphere is saturated with the cloying, heavy perfume of night-blooming flowers. A sudden, piercing shout echoes from the high stone tower. A stranger is seen approaching from the barren south.

There is nothing to the south, logically speaking. It is merely a void of shifting sand, abrasive dust, and perhaps, if the ancient superstitions of the local barbarians are to be believed, the bleached bones of long-dead monsters.

He is a tattered, wretched man. Along the grueling march, he lost his sandals to the jagged rocks. The soles of his feet are raw and bloodied, leaving crimson tracks across the courtyard. Rags hang loosely off the protruding bones of his shoulders and hips, exposing his frail frame to the wind. He remains alive only through the inexplicable grace of the gods.

Before he can be presented to the commander, he must be thoroughly cleaned. He must be fed nutritious broth and dressed in clean linens as well. A reward is premature; it is not yet known if he deserted his post or was the sole survivor of a catastrophe.

The initial contact with water nearly kills him. He screams like a terrified babe, thrashing violently in the stone pool and sobbing uncontrollably for his mother, his father, and his lost commander. He begs for the mercy of death.

It is not granted. Soon he falls into a catatonic silence. The slaves scrub him until his skin is clean of grime. His wounds are surprisingly not grievous, merely superficial lacerations. As he is being dressed, a cynical sentry mutters that he is not yet a man, suggesting the fine armor he wears must be stolen property.

When food is brought to him, he initially refuses to eat, his throat tight with trauma. Stale bread eventually agrees with him, though he is strictly forbidden from gorging himself lest his stomach rupture from sudden intake.

The commander demands details about the others. A hundred thousand strong, it had been whispered, a host of the strongest, most loyal soldiers. The men who purportedly feared absolutely nothing.

They are all dead now. The boy looked stunted, his growth arrested by starvation. Fear had stolen his nerve and his iron will, but it had not touched his sense of honor.

They had walked thousands of leagues into the unknown. When they entered a shadowed valley, the sun and stars were permanently lost to them. There were monstrous things inhabiting the gloom—half-men with sloping, malformed torsos and razor-sharp teeth, cats twice the size of a war horse composed of fire and smoke, and beasts with writhing snakes for noses and tusks like a boar that roared with the volume of a thousand war trumpets.

Deeper they must have marched. The jungle was essentially Pluto's garden, a place where every leaf and vine brought swift death.

They did not actually possess a hundred thousand men, only five thousand at the start. By the time they found the true objective—that thing of nightmares, a titan's aborted fetus—they numbered in the mere hundreds.

It arrived in the dead of night, drawn by the scent of woodsmoke and the heat of their fires.

It was here the boy stopped. He trembled violently. His teeth ground together with such force they might have shattered in his mouth. But he possessed honor, and he spoke of what he had witnessed in the darkness.

It must have been drawn by the flickering fires. Perhaps it remembered the hell it had originally come from, or in the flames it saw a reflection of its own malevolent strength.

The appearance was sudden and violent. It fell near the fire pit, stirring the coals and sending sparks into the air. It had small, hooked claws and was armored like a shimmering fish. It was not large, but it was dense. The boy gestured to his waist. He was missing half his hand, the flesh jagged. It was about the size of a large war dog. It possessed wings like a monstrous bat.

It drank the fire. The gods gave it terrible power, and it rose up to slaughter a hundred men the first night.

The host fled back through the hell garden. Some were felled by the sentient plants or the predatory beasts. One man awoke screaming in the darkness. Insects had eaten away at his flesh during his slumber. They swarmed through his open mouth, his nose, and the empty, wet sockets of his eyes.

After that incident, no one dared sleep.

Was that how the boy lost his hand? No. That injury occurred on the fifth day of the retreat.

The men had begun to succumb to madness. Every twisted tree looked the same. Every rock, every stagnant puddle, and every patch of red dirt blurred into a singular, agonizing memory.

They came to a sheer cliff. They must climb it, someone suggested, so they did.

The boy was quick. Some men were quicker and stood along the top of the world, helping the others up. When the boy pulled himself over the ledge, he saw the piles of bodies and called down. There is death above, wearing the faces of our brothers. One of the men tried to kill him in a delirious rage. Instead, he lost half of his hand to a jagged rock. It was crushed and mangled beyond repair. The boy hauled himself up and scrambled away.

He left the men and headed north. The host was scattered. The boy walked north. He could see the sky again. His hand felt tight and hot. His fingers turned white, then red. On the fifth day, he gnawed them off to stop the pain.

On the seventh, he lost one sandal. He threw the other away, and in a fit of madness, stripped off his clothes. The forest became thinner. He was burnt by the sun. There was no water, no food. Once he saw a golden eagle and followed it, but there was no eagle. On the ninth day, he found a man hung from a tree.

The boy stripped the body of clothes and dressed himself in the dead man's rags.

As he walked north, his hand leaked blood and his feet cramped. One night he built a fire. It started a great fear in him. He was brave enough to put his hand inside the flames and stop the rot from spreading. Afterwards, he crawled away and cried until the sun rose.

As he walked, he left the grasslands. He wanted to see water. He wanted to die.

On the tenth day, he saw the beast again. Or it may have been a different one. It had the body of a dog, upright. It had long claws and chattered like a bird. It was the size of a man's leg, from the ground to his knee. There was a flock of them. They called to each other. The boy followed them.

The creatures took down a beast—the one with a snake for a nose. It had leather for skin and wailed as it died. After the dog-beasts left, the boy ate what he could.

The boy stopped there. What else? There was nothing else. He had come to the sand and walked. His voice was quiet. Tired. His body told the toll his voice could not.

Could he die now? No. Not yet. More would want to hear of this.
ideas_up.writingprompts::42:
The subway stopped abruptly. Laurentius awoke with a sharp gasp, his lungs burning from the sudden jolt of deceleration. He struggled to take in his surroundings: It was cold, that was certain, and the air smelled of ozone and stale electricity. He examined his armour: His hands were covered with gloves that appeared to be made of sturdy cow hide, stitched with precision. His boots were black, fur-lined and surprisingly warm against the drafty floor. Underneath a thick black wool coat was a soft white shirt, with complex metal clasps holding it together in the front. A red strip of silk fabric reached around his neck and made its way to just past his stomach, perhaps a sign of rank or mourning. "What is this," he thought, his pulse quickening. "Is that how I died? Do we wear tokens of our death in this purgatory?" His eyes met those of a rotund, darker-skinned woman, who was intently reading a curious layered-parchment device on her lap, swiping it with her thumb. He looked around her neck: a silver cross hung there. He looked at her sympathetically, interpreting the symbol as a marker of her faith or her end. "I suppose so," he whispered to the empty air.

Tubes of flickering light illuminated the metal chamber he was in. A smooth, melodic ding announced itself, and the sliding doors closed shut with a hiss. To Laurentius' surprise, the metal chamber began to move again, accelerating with an unnatural, jarring force. He stood, his legs shaky, and made his way to a man he assumed was in charge of this vessel. The man was covered in what seemed to be traditional dress for the era, with the exception of a large, ridiculous silver wig, and plastic glasses that read "2015" across the front in bold, garish letters.

"Salve," Laurentius began, his voice echoing against the sterile walls.

The man returned a confused look, his brow furrowed, then returned to gazing out the window at the dark tunnel walls. He smelled of fermented wine and desperation.

"Aut ubi sum? Quis hic locus?"

The metal chamber shook once again, slightly, disrupting Laurentius' balance as the wheels screeched against iron rails. A voice rang out over the loudspeaker, distorted and alien, but Laurentius couldn't make out what it had said. The metal chamber made another stop, but Laurentius wasn't prepared for the sudden halt. He fell onto the floor below as a wave of people exited, their faces blank and unmoving. He got up and followed the crowd, which weaved through narrow, tiled tunnels. He struggled to take everything in: Musicians lined the enclosed street, playing strange, vibrating strings. Few vendors were present, selling bags of synthetic food, from what he understood. He continued until he reached a flight of stairs. He ascended, and was astounded by what he saw.

Bright lights flashed around him, in all directions, blinding him momentarily. What was the steady hum of voices, interrupted occasionally by an outburst, had now turned into an onslaught of voices and chaotic action. To his left and right, the streets were lined with people all moving towards a central location, where a large, illuminated spire reached into the heavens. Atop this spire was a metallic sphere that pulsed with rhythmic energy. He looked into the sky.

No stars?

No stars. He pondered the cosmic implications. Suddenly, a realization came to him, and with it, a wave of happiness and relief. There were no stars, for he was above them all: Might these be the plains of Asphodel? They were more beautiful, and more terrifying, than he'd ever imagined.

Suddenly, a man in a similar outfit – a black coat, black pants, white shirt – ran up to him. Black metal covered his eyes, masking his gaze, and frost came out of his mouth when he spoke.

"Dick!" he said, grabbing Laurentius by the arm with a firm, urgent grip. So overwhelmed, Laurentius had no expectation of arguing; he was a captive of this new, strange reality. He followed this man through the sea of bodies.

"Dick, where have you been? We've been looking all over – the crowd's waiting, and they ain't happy. Kathy's been doing what she can, but..."

Laurentius paused. Clearly, he must learn the language of the afterlife to survive. He noticed some of the crowd had begun to direct their attention towards him, whispering and pointing. He returned the same greeting he was offered, hoping to appease them.

"Dick," he said, nodding his head at the passers-by as he was carried off by the man he had met.
"Dick," he said once more, this time at a young girl. Her ears were covered immediately by her mother, who left a scathing glare in her wake.

A few minutes of navigating the bustling streets passed, and Laurentius passed by other similarly-dressed gentlemen who padded him down, feeling for weapons. After greeting both of them formally, he was ushered up steep metal stairs, and onto a platform which overlooked the massive crowd below. The platform held a woman, red-haired, who was holding a microphone. "Dick!" she said, "Where have you been? We're on in 2."

"Dick," Laurentius smiled, mimicking her tone.

"Well, you know what I like," she quipped, adjusting her earpiece.

Someone handed Laurentius a plastic cord with a bud on the end. He looked at the woman, who had it placed in her ear, and did the same. Perhaps this was part of the welcoming ceremony, a ritual of connection.

He heard the woman speak with the man behind a larger metal contraption, one with a folded glass mirror in the centre.

"Live in 30."

"Alright. You ready?" she said, looking directly at Laurentius. He nodded. She handed him another metal stick with fur at the end, much like the one she was holding. She stared into the contraption. Her lips formed a smile, and Laurentius couldn't help but smile himself.

A small red light went on in the corner of the metal-glass contraption. There was a brief pause. The woman nudged Laurentius expectantly, her eyes wide.

Laurentius smiled and inhaled deeply. "Dick," he said, and looked expectantly once again at the woman to his right, awaiting his fate.
ideas_up.writingprompts::43:
Locating a pizza company willing to service my isolated residence proved immensely difficult. Predictably, delivery drivers returned disoriented, noticeably pallid, and visibly emaciated, clutching their untouched thin-crust orders. Naturally, a vampire requires sustenance, yet my terrifying reputation hindered basic procurement.

I once believed myself exceptionally cunning millennia ago. Rome offered sanctuary, serving as the epicenter for every faith except the one that truly mattered, far removed from those wretched wooden crosses appearing on every Jerusalem doorway. I assumed Italy would remain safe, mistakenly convinced Christianity would never infiltrate the greatest nation the world had ever witnessed.

How profoundly erroneous that assessment was. Missionaries arrived almost instantly, and within a century, a cross adorned every threshold while a church occupied every block. I became trapped, facing certain destruction if I dared expose myself beyond my ornate wooden door.

Presently, I sensed three children giggling while shoving each other upon my doorstep. Eventually, one leaped up to strike the bell, then sprinted away, thrilled by the audacity of tormenting the local recluse. How remarkably tedious.

I despise humanity, I muttered to the empty foyer. Flipping through the eight-hundredth phone book jammed into my mail slot this year, I searched for a restaurant that had not yet heard the local folklore regarding the feared Pale Master of The Takeout. Every establishment seemingly shared my dark history through neighborhood gossip, creating a culinary blockade. I scanned the glossy pages, desperate for a new, ignorant vendor. Surely, one naive business owner remained nearby who valued profit over preserving their soul from a hungry, ancient, and immortal predator. One could hope.
ideas_up.writingprompts::44:
The wizard held the small garden slug in his palm. He was Marvolio IV, a man who had summoned demons the size of castles, diverted mighty rivers, and invented a charm preventing nose itches during intense spellcasting. Surely he would not mistakenly summon a common gastropod when seeking the Creator? He placed the mollusk down, wondering if it was perhaps God’s favorite pet or a divine avatar. He spent hours cross-referencing his arcane notes, measuring the geometric precision of his sacred summoning circles, and teasing element distillations for minute impurities. A calculation error had to exist somewhere. The slug nibbled the corner of his leather-bound workbook.

After the moon began falling toward the ground and the sun started peeking over the horizon, God finally spoke.

LETTUCE.

Wh-what, Marvolio whispered. The voice manifested directly inside his cranium, vibrating against his consciousness. Though his mostly sane mind struggled, he recognized that tone; it was the ancient source from which all existence sprang and was sustained. He knew this voice predated time itself. He knew this voice emanated from the three-inch slug resting upon his workbench.

BRING ME LETTUCE. IT IS NOT WISE TO REFUSE ME.

Marvolio walked in a daze into his kitchens and found a basket of greens. He examined it. The leaves were wilted and fuzzy blue mold crept around the edges, as wizards rarely consumed vegetables. Though the slug remained in another room, its voice sprang again, unwelcome, into Marvolio's brain.

YES, THAT WILL DO NICELY.

Surely not, Lord? I could run to the market and fetch fresh black Italian cabbage that—

NO, I LIKE IT LIKE THAT. NICE AND SOFT.

Marvolio gibbered quietly while transporting the rotting vegetable to the one true lord of life. God enjoyed the snack thoroughly as Marvolio sat trembling.

WELL.

Well what? Um, yes, Lord.

YOU WANTED TO KNOW SOMETHING? YOU PUT SIGNIFICANT EFFORT INTO BRINGING ME HERE, SO YOU SHOULD PROBABLY ASK.

Oh. Why did you create everything? I mean, there is so much suffering, and—

LETTUCE.

I do not think I have any more.

NO, I CREATED THIS WORLD SPECIFICALLY TO PRODUCE THE CORRECT KIND OF LETTUCE. THIS IS THE MOST LETTUCY OF ALL POSSIBLE WORLDS.

That actually explains a lot.

If God could shrug, he would have; instead, he stared at Marvolio impassively with his divine, slimy stalks.

Should I try to send you back?

NO, JUST POP ME OUT IN THE BACK GARDEN, THAT IS A GOOD LAD.

Marvolio never spoke of his experience, nor did he practice wizardry again. However, he took up professional gardening and became famous nationwide for his impressive variety of award-winning lettuce and cabbages. He found peace in the soil, knowing the ultimate purpose of the entire universe was simply to cultivate the perfect crisp leaf for a slug. His life was forever altered by the divine mandate of the garden.
ideas_up.writingprompts::45:
I don't know Sharon, I am just exhausted by this monotonous existence, Markond sighed, leaning back into his jagged, high-backed throne constructed from the bleached, calcified bones of countless fallen heroes. I sit in this damp lair every single day and night, waiting for some poor, unsuspecting group of wide-eyed, foolish adventurers to stumble blindly into my traps. I am feeling deeply unfulfilled professionally and spiritually.

Well honey, perhaps it is time for a drastic change, a fresh start?

But we have an excellent financial situation, a beautiful cavern perfect for raising some undead minions, and I have absolute job security, he argued.

Marky, it means nothing if you are not truly happy. You always dreamed of opening that cozy inn, remember? She strolled over and lightly massaged his tense shoulders. We talked about it on those long, cold nights before your dark ascension; we would buy a rustic barnhouse, renovate the structure, rent out rooms, brew potent craft beer, cook hearty meals, and hire a talented bard or two.

I remember, but that was a stupid dream; a Lich cannot run a tavern, it is simply not the done thing.

Who cares about social norms? Let us do it! There is that nasty little tavern down the road where you send minions to spread rumors of your hidden treasure, but that is our only competition. We have the market cornered!

You are right, you are always right, Sharon. Let us do this, he agreed.

Six months later, Markond cleaned a wooden mug with his rag, smiling. The tavern was bustling, the fire pit roared, and the minstrel sang ancient songs. Sharon served rowdy dwarves, looking more beautiful than the day he kidnapped her. Everything was perfect; the ale flowed, the profits soared, and the patrons were finally happy.
ideas_up.writingprompts::46:
I knew I would not achieve immediate clarity. The process demanded immense labor, and experts warned that sensory overload might prove debilitating. I held vague, fractured memories of visual reality. A catastrophic car accident had rendered me completely blind in both eyes at age three. I suspect those early years proved advantageous; processing light and color before the trauma likely allowed my neural pathways to recall visual data rather than learning entirely anew. My brain possessed a dormant framework that facilitated this arduous sensory recovery.

James provided essential support. Sometimes I would intentionally close my eyes to navigate using familiar tactile habits. He would suddenly intercept my path, teasingly blocking my progress. It was never malicious; if I protested, he would extend his arms to impede my movement, eventually closing them around me in a firm, protective embrace. He would whisper, I won't let go until you open your eyes. No one had ever expressed such profound devotion. I detected deep affection in his cadence and felt it physically during every intimate hug.

I practiced constantly. Frequent, throbbing headaches resulted from the strain of interpreting visual stimuli. Dark, ink-like blotches smeared across the kitchen table as I attempted to eat breakfast. James explained they were merely shadows cast by the oak tree outside. That tree had never bothered me before; now, it disrupted my morning, complicating the simple task of eating cereal. I still used my hands to verify visual input, ensuring I could trust my new perception. It felt profoundly strange to witness my own hands, appearing as two misshapen, ghostly blurs fumbling with every object I touched. I had once cherished the tactile sensation of my hands, but seeing them felt alien.

Eventually, the dark smears resolved into defined shadows, and James's features crystallized. I believe that remained the happiest moment of my life. I awoke one morning, he turned toward me, and I finally perceived his eyes. They shone with an internal radiance, seemingly housing their own light source. He was truly beautiful. I had never understood the extent of his aesthetic appeal.

The blotches no longer obscured his face, but my personal crisis began when I realized my own reflection remained distorted. The dark marks on my skin were not optical illusions. I discovered a collection of deep acne scars clustered along my jawline. My skin had always felt smooth to my touch, yet I remained ignorant of these visible blemishes. I possessed minor wrinkles, which I expected, but the sickly, greenish circles beneath my eyes contrasted poorly with my dark irises. My eyes lacked the luminous quality of James's; they appeared dull, weary, and profoundly sad.

I hesitated to query James. I never realized I was so unattractive. If I was unsightly, I assumed James must share those flaws. Why would a handsome man choose an ugly, formerly blind partner? I finally witnessed how other women stared at him. Nobody ever gazed at me with such desire. Grocery trips, once enjoyable, became agonizing opportunities to observe every attractive woman—those he could easily possess—stealing furtive glances at him or smiling when he caught their eye.

My internal confusion grew. Sometimes I suspected he reciprocated their interest. I caught him observing two women walking past us at a restaurant, triggering immediate, agonizing knots in my stomach. I remained silent, staring at my pasta, struggling to suppress my nausea. Is something wrong? James asked. No, why? I replied, forcing my pockmarked face into a rigid, artificial smile. Just asking, he said. I love you, he added, his expression radiating warmth. I desperately wish I could believe his words.
ideas_up.writingprompts::48:
The Author

I cannot shake the feeling. You know, that sensation creeping along your spine waiting to take up residence in the base of your skull like some kind of parasite. It is an indeterminable feeling that you are being watched by an unseen entity. I cannot shake it off. I am sure I know what it is, but I am not ready to admit I know. The... author, let us call him that. He is watching, waiting, and building a narrative. Even as I think this, he is scratching it down in his chicken-scratch scrawl, touching the pen against his teeth in deep, calculated thought. I can feel his intent; I can see it in my mind's eye. He is trying to figure out exactly how to kill me.

I suppose it is my own fault. I kept asking, I needed to understand the mechanics of existence. I had to find out if there was some directing hand to life. If mankind had a purpose, a reason, I needed to appreciate what purpose we worked toward. There is a moment, one of particular realization, which caught me and held fast. Like my apprehension regarding an observer; only, this feeling was deeper, more primal. I knew, I mean really understood; all of it is a narrative. Life is a story written by a cruel hand. Which inevitably led me to the conclusion—there needs to be an architect, an author.

The car narrowly missed me. I had an inkling of a pressing against my chest verging on the edge of panic. I did not cross when the green man displayed on the crossing signal; instead, I took a step back. My spidey-sense tingled. The taxi-cab driver never saw me, and I had not seen him either. His drunken, sprawling vehicle slammed into the same traffic signal post I had been, until recently, standing by. Can I tell you how incredibly fucked up that is? I have this realization, followed by a sudden, sharp sensation of fear. If I had not heeded my gutless compulsion, I might have been splattered between the cabbie’s car and the hard place which was the traffic signal pole. I turned my gaze upward, burning eyes and clenching jaw notwithstanding, and decried whoever worked at compiling this narrative.

What the actual fuck was that? I said.

Okay, so I realize my choice of words probably did not fall into the definition of circumspect, but hell, we are talking about some kind of god-figure deciding on my time to die. Is this a test of agency or merely a sadistic exercise in irony?

Are you sure? My logical brain asked.

I pondered my position, both in the physical and meta-physical sense, weighing the odds of my own encroaching madness versus the reality of my observations.

Yeah, I am fucking sure, I replied to myself internally. How else do you explain the sudden epiphany and subsequently my almost immediate death? There is an author and he does not want to be known. He hides in the syntax and the subtext, pulling strings like a puppeteer who hates his puppets.

I am not sure how I knew the author did not want to be known, or the fact he was a man, but I figured it was something in my general make-up granting me the knowledge. Oh, do not get all high and mighty and preach at me now; I am not talking religion or spirituality, I want to live, damnit. I stood, still staring up at the sky, trying to impart my utter disgust and frustration when the signal pole creaked, unnaturally so. I adjusted my head so my eyes were level with the pole.

The metal appeared warped, and I realized that the car had burst into flames. When had that happened? Nevermind, run, stupid.

My internal dialog is not always the most kind; I am a blunt sort. So, I ran. What I was running from, if Mr. Omniscient author was already in my head, he could follow me anywhere. Hell, I could have an inopportune flashback, and he could hit me with a mack truck. If this author decided I was going to die, why did he not do it already?

Fuck me, I thought. It is about the drama; the story. He feeds on the suspense. He needs the slow build-up to justify the eventual climax of my expiration.

Sick fuck, I said. I knew he would hear me, or he would write that in his juvenile scrawl, knowing I intended it for him. He is probably laughing at my struggle, savoring the narrative tension he manufactured.

What if I stop? What if I refuse to play the game?

I looked up again, and said, What are you going to do with a character who will not cooperate, huh?

Naturally, he did not respond. It was not like I expected a voice from the sky, but I figured he might strike me down with lightning or something. I mean, it is potentially within his ability, right? He might decide my knowledge of the plan labeled me as a liability.

What the hell is the plan anyway?

I do not know, I guess the plan is for me to die. Perhaps he is not into the mundane. Maybe, just maybe, he wants my death to be something significant, something of a show. I bet that is it. I got the sense again; a gut punch to my stomach making my insides roil like they were leaking to the outside, and the rumbling in my stomach suggested I take a step back. I did. Something pierced the skin in my back. It was a fluid, smooth motion that parted the skin. I felt the warm blood mixing with my sweat as it soaked the back of my flannel shirt.

A quiet voice whispered in my ear. Hello protagonist, she said. I am your antagonist, the author says hello.

That was all she said. She did not have a scent, like you would expect. She was a ghost from the shadows. I do not know who she was, or why her, but she had made it clear... I was right. Take that, fucker. I did not have the strength to say it, but I know he heard me.
ideas_up.writingprompts::49:
Will life improve? What will the weather be tomorrow? Suddenly, she is staring directly at me, likely harboring intense disdain. Am I perspiring? My palms are damp, dripping with nervous anxiety. Waiting in this sluggish coffee queue is agonizing. The surrounding patrons gaze intently, magnifying my internal panic. My hands are definitely slick, perhaps even visibly wet.

I am next. "I will have twenty!" I bellowed uncontrollably. Why did I shout that? I should depart immediately. Everyone observed my outburst; it was a catastrophic social failure. Why did I even leave my bed today? "Sorry," I whispered, "I will have a Venti Matcha Green." The barista appeared visibly rattled, trembling as violently as I was. I caused this tension; I must accept responsibility. "Apologies for shouting; I was distracted," I explained. "It is fine," she replied, "this is my first day working here."

"Oh," I muttered, avoiding direct eye contact while my heart hammered against my ribs. She possesses such a melodic, endearing voice. I handed over the cash and fled outside. I collapsed onto the curb, feeling immense relief. The customers intimidated me; their judgmental stares nearly triggered a cardiac arrest. Yet, she was undeniably charming. When did I last converse with a woman? First grade? It is irrelevant; she surely views me as a complete freak after my shouting. I buried my face in my hands, absorbing the suburban ambience. Birds chirped, distant horns blared, trees swayed, then the door swung open behind me. I turned. It was her.

She sat beside me, soaked in green tea, holding my order. "What occurred?" I inquired. "Well, while preparing your drink, I added too much cream and mistakenly included coffee," she explained. I laughed; she grew more frantic. "That is amusing," I said, grabbing the cup. The tea tasted terrible. "Want to come over?" she asked. It was incredibly abrupt, spiking my anxiety, but her own visible trembling comforted me. I agreed. We walked to her nearby home. Eventually, I visited constantly. She brightened my existence daily. I never experienced that paralyzing anxiety again. She transformed my perspective, making me feel like a knight—ever prudent, ever steady, and possessing immense fortitude. Her presence provided a secure anchor in my chaotic, uncertain world. We shared secrets, laughter, and a quiet understanding that silenced my internal critics. I no longer feared the judgment of strangers or the unpredictable nature of tomorrow. With her, the suburbs became a sanctuary, and every interaction felt like a profound, life-affirming victory against my own deep-seated, irrational fears.
ideas_up.writingprompts::50:
A wise man, in a rare attempt at humor, once said "Heaven was eating pâté de foie gras to the sound of trumpets." Page of a journal of a Chef, recently deceased. As a chef, I wholly agree with the foie gras but I have never had much of an ear for brass trumpets or orchestral crescendos. Foie gras, for those who do not know—and do not worry, many remain blissfully ignorant—is a culinary tradition as old as the art of cooking itself. Foie gras, French for fat liver, is the pièce de résistance of any self-respecting chef who values decadence over ethics. Take a duck, preferably a goose for superior flavor, but more often a duck due to availability. Cage it, restrict all movement, as activity ruins the delicate texture. Take it by the neck and pump corn boiled in rendered fat down its gullet. Do this seven times a day, pump it plump until it bloats. Kill the bird, remove the liver, and a good chef pays a wholesome price for it. Serve with mustard, honey, diced onions, and balsamic vinegar. Never has anything been so delectable to the refined palate. See, it is not the taste that repulses people; it is the brutal process. Does the end justify the means? That is a question for the talentless or those lacking a refined palate. Yes, absolutely! Anyone would scream "YES!" if they tried my specific foie gras. My version is distinct, elevated, and objectively superior.

See, they say that beauty is merely skin deep. It is, and taste is far shallower. I am a chef. A good chef, not a moral man, but I reiterate: A GOOD chef. If I had been born a painter and my only source of vivid red pigment was the blood of the innocent, do not doubt that I would paint in crimson. Of course, I was not born a painter; I was born a chef. A GOOD chef. Foie gras, as most chefs prepare it, is illegal in many nations: the UK, Germany, and Italy to name a few. Needless to say, I do not derive my recipes from law books or ethical guidelines. Foie gras as I make it is illegal in every sovereign country. The Pope once denounced foie gras as cruel; that was, of course, before he sampled mine. Mine is different; mine is better.

A cardinal once told me that if God walked the earth again, he would ensure I was the one cooking. Another priest said, "I once denounced your dish, Chef. I am sorry, Chef. I owe you a thousand apologies, Chef. I have now sampled your dish, and I know the bliss from the supple, marinated flesh on my tongue is greater than all the suffering of all the geese and ducks God ever endeavored to create." They were in total awe of me. Anyone I convince to suspend their morals will, at the moment of contact with my foie gras, be in awe of my genius. Mine is different; mine is better.

People would kill for a spoonful, including good, pious, moral people. They would kill for a single bite of my foie gras. Believe me, I could sell out if I charged a million dollars per pound. But I do not. I do not perform this for power or riches; I do it for the pure art. I am a chef, not a good man, but I reiterate: A GOOD chef. My recipe is worth kingdoms; my dish has made kings weak at the knees. So weak that they kneel before me, the Chef.

My legacy will be my recipe. If you are reading this, congratulations, you have inherited it. Here it is: Take a baby, abduct it, buy it, steal it; it makes no difference. Any foundling or orphan will suffice. Boy or girl, race or origin, it makes no difference. Though they must be newborn! They must be innocent; they must be succulent. Cage the child, give it no room, as movement ruins the texture. Take it by the neck and pump corn boiled in fat down its gullet. Do this seven times a day, pump it plump. Two months should suffice for the desired marbling. Add a pinch of sea salt and an ounce of butter per pint of corn. Two pints of fat per pint of corn. Lard is best; the more linoleic acid, the better the liver composition. When slaughtered, remove the liver and prepare it in the way you are most qualified. I would marinate in clover honey and mustard seed, adding toasted sesame seeds, diced red onions, and a thimble full of dark, aged rum.
ideas_up.writingprompts::51:
Kai crept silently up the creaking wooden stairs, avoiding the loose floorboard that always gave him away. Being caught by Mom and Dad meant immediate bedtime, but being discovered with the leftover broccoli intended for tomorrow’s dinner would trigger a lecture on nutrition. Kai felt relieved that he had successfully intercepted the vegetable dish, ensuring he would never have to consume those bitter, steamed florets.

Closing his bedroom door softly, the six-year-old marched toward his closet. He pulled the door open, revealing a bizarre mass of shifting eyes, coarse hair, and slimy, undulating tentacles huddled in the dark corner. 

Here you go, Blergh, Kai whispered. Blergh grasped the stolen Tupperware with one sticky tentacle and dumped the entire contents into a cavernous, dark mouth the size of a basketball hoop, swallowing the food whole without hesitation. Kai still could not discern if the beast possessed teeth, as it never bothered to chew its meals. 

Kai laid a trail of buttery crackers toward the center of the rug. Lured by the salty treats, the monster slithered out of the closet. Kai dumped his toy chest, scattering plastic soldiers across the carpet. 

We are playing army men tonight, Kai commanded. Blergh grunted in agreement. Kai cherished these sessions because Blergh could manipulate dozens of figures simultaneously and performed a spectacular, enthusiastic reaction whenever Kai simulated explosions.

***

Julia used to feel genuine irritation waking up to find her son sleeping on the floor amid jagged plastic men that threatened her feet. After years of this routine, she simply accepted the mess as a harmless quirk of childhood. 

Wake up, sweetie, she said, shaking his shoulder. How is Blergh doing today? 

As they walked toward the kitchen, Julia prepared for a long, imaginative story about how Kai and his imaginary friend had defeated a great evil. Kids are so precious at that age. 

***

Ten years later, Kai no longer needed to hide his midnight snacks. Every teenage boy eats constantly, right? Kai sat before his glowing console, passing a family-sized bag of Doritos and a two-liter bottle of Mountain Dew to his left. 

Here you go, Blergh. The creature grunted in gratitude, swallowing the items whole. The beast still refused to chew. Blergh gestured with his many tentacles, pointing at the television screen, the three controllers held in his grip, and the final gamepad near Kai’s feet. They were ready to dominate at Call of Duty. It was going to be another legendary night.
ideas_up.writingprompts::52:
As the vessel reached the beacon, the pilot nervously activated his directional scanning arrays, fully aware he had expended his final reserves of jump fuel traversing this desolate sector. An inexplicable, freezing chill settled deep within his marrow as he peered through the thick reinforced viewing port. He dismissed the sensation as mere jump jitters, yet he cautiously routed auxiliary power to his primary security drone. Sensors returned no anomalies; he cursed his wasted effort, prioritizing the urgent necessity of locating emergency fuel caches instead.

The directional scanner suddenly pinged, drawing his gaze toward a massive, drifting hull partially shrouded by a dense, toxic cloud of ionizing gas. The derelict craft was completely powered-down, explaining why the initial long-range system sweep failed to register its existence. He engaged the impulse engines, maneuvering toward the wreck while rhythmically hailing the silent ship on every standard frequency.

No response returned. That was suspicious, yet derelict vessels appeared frequently in these lanes. More baffling was the pristine integrity of the exterior plating; it lacked a single dent or structural compromise. He had salvaged abandoned hulls before, but those were always pockmarked with searing laser scorch marks or telltale teleporter radiation—every previous find bore the undeniable scars of violent combat.

He briefly contemplated donning his pressurized EVA suit for a manual inspection. Instead, he retreated to the drone bay, seizing remote control of his heavy security drone. Though designed specifically for boarding defense, the unit functioned capably as an exploratory tool. Moments later, the drone glided through the airlock, a sleek machine bristling with lethal lasers and serrated close-combat blades that had preserved his life repeatedly. He possessed detailed schematics for this specific class of hull, so he navigated the drone directly toward the engineering deck, hoping to siphon residual fuel cells.

The inherent flaw in controlling the drone remotely was the total cognitive saturation it demanded from the pilot. The airlock door failed to cycle shut—had he been alert, he would have noticed the critical malfunction in his door seal integrity. His agonizing screams soon echoed through the silence as he was shredded. The pilot should have realized that giant, predatory alien spiders are no joke.
ideas_up.writingprompts::53:
My day starts like any other. I lack an alarm clock, as human time means nothing here. Cultist screams of rapturous glee usually wake me, though I sometimes sleep through them after late shifts. Time is difficult to calculate here; the sun, stars, and moon behave erratically. You adapt, and Mister Cthulhu ignores my sleep schedule. However, poor performance results in my soul being devoured like an eclair, with my remains tossed into the vile spawning pool. I have worked here three years without a single major error.

I check the back wall of my ice-cold obsidian house, where Mister Cthulhu leaves my daily to-do list. I find a young woman pinned to the wall with a trident, her body writhing in agonizing pleasure. My list is etched into her skin, indicating a short day. Since Mister Cthulhu murdered Death years ago, permanent mortality is obsolete. I free the woman, retrieve the trident, and plan my tasks.

I must scrub the interior of the temple of Yog-Sothoth, regulate the precise salt balance in the Deep One’s spawning pool, and administer antacids to the Hydra. The poor beast has been thrashing for hours, ravaging Earth's distant coasts with massive, destructive tidal waves. I prioritize this task, as Mister Cthulhu dislikes when other entities carelessly destroy his primary food supply. Next, I must polish the altar of R'lyeh, ensure the shoggoths are fed their nightly rations of raw shadow, and repair the dimensional rift leaking ectoplasm into the pantry. Managing these eldritch chores requires extreme caution, as one wrong move invites immediate cosmic erasure. I gather my tools, steeling my nerves against the encroaching madness, and step out into the swirling, violet mists of the abyss to begin my shift.
ideas_up.writingprompts::54:
Elwood and Shara were leaning against a concrete pillar in the dusty courtyard of a high school, watching Elwood's newest charge, an unassuming young man named Dale, who sat listlessly on a nearby wooden bench. 

So how did you get assigned to this one, Elwood? Shara said while examining her jagged, obsidian-hued claws with a sense of practiced, demonic boredom. 

I am fairly certain this is a softball pitch from the management downstairs, Elwood said, arms crossed tightly against his chest, his eyes scanning the perimeter for potential interference. A group of teenage girls walked over to the pillar and leaned against it, occupying the exact same space as the two demons without sensing the sudden drop in temperature. A strong gust of unnatural wind blew the papers and binders out of the hands of the girls, who shrieked in surprise and scrambled frantically after the fluttering sheets. 

Shara, clearly annoyed, said, I will never get used to that. I do not care if we can occupy the same space; it feels intrusive and messy. Turning to the girls, she held her arm out to them, claws held behind her thumb, and flicked them outwards with a sharp, echoing snap, sending the books and papers again flying out of the shrieking girls' hands. Little wretches, she muttered, watching them panic. 

Dale was chewing on his lukewarm bean and cheese burrito, looking at the chaotic scene across the courtyard with the expression of a placid cow chewing on grass, seemingly oblivious to the supernatural forces swirling around him. 

What is with that kid? Shara asked, tilting her head. Does he have a soul, or is he just hollow? 

I do not know. Maybe he is stupid? Maybe he is protected by some divine oversight we cannot detect? Elwood chewed on his thumb for a bit, strategizing. Let us jump time to 6th period. We need to test his cognitive boundaries and see if he reacts to psychic pressure. 

Shara gave Elwood a sideways glance and raised an eyebrow, Sure, if you want to waste your energy on a brick wall. 

With a sound like tearing canvas, they were transported and rested on the ledge under the window in the back of Dale's 6th period classroom, watching the teacher drone on about ancient history. 

So what is your plan, big boy? Shara whispered, eager for some genuine torment. 

Elwood pressed a long-clawed finger to his lips and said, Sssshhhh. As he did that, Dale's head hit the desk with a dull thud; he was out cold, his consciousness suspended in a sudden, artificial slumber. Flinging his arms out wide and then bringing them in together in a grand, theatrical grouping gesture, every student in the class turned to face Dale without a word, their eyes wide and glassy. 

That is cute, Shara said, unimpressed by the theatrics. 

Elwood smiled and said, It is time to wake up, Dale. As he said that, every single student in the class, in a very flat, monotone pitch, said the same thing in unison with Elwood. Dale, face half-slick with drool, sat up and rubbed his eyes, looking around at the class staring blankly back at him. 

Dale, it is time to wake up, all the students and Elwood said again. No one blinked or breathed. Dale glanced from side to side, confused. I am awake, he muttered. Elwood flung his arms apart, and the class resumed as normal, no one but Dale aware of what had transpired. 

That is your plan? Shara asked, clearly disappointed. That is parlor magic at best. 

Dale, noticing he was a little behind in taking notes, began writing in a frantic, illegible hurry. 

You are kidding me, right? That is a daytime creep! It is not even 3 am. That is some creepy shit, I do not care what you say. It leaves a psychic bruise, Elwood insisted. 

Uh huh, Shara said. Look at him. He has no clue that was out of the ordinary. C'mon, let us go. She flexed a claw over her shoulder as she walked away, begging for Elwood to follow into the hallway. 

As they were leaving through the solid wall, Elwood spun around and made a sharp, bitch-slapping motion. Dale grunted and his head jerked forward, loose tangles of hair at the back of his head flying up, his pencil shot out of his hand and bounced off the back of the muscular kid in front of him. The girl next to Dale looked at him with plain disgust and said, You are such a weirdo, shifting in her small desk to be as far away as possible from him. 

Shara laughed, a dry, rasping sound. 

The two demons waited outside the classroom for the end of the period and Dale. You know this would be so much easier in the nighttime, Shara said, bored by the slow pace of human existence. 

Yeah, but that is not my style, Elwood said, adjusting his cloak. You get more genuine results during the day. Anyone can be spooked at night and when the day comes, they are so quick to forget it. No, what really freaks them out is a daytime haunting. It undermines their reality. 

Shara did not say anything, only yawned, showing off rows of needle-like teeth. 

The bell sounded for the end of the period, and Dale was the last one out of the classroom, walking slowly, looking down at his phone. Elwood flapped his wings and dove into the phone. An alert popped up on his screen; Dale clicked on Read, which cued Elwood to jump into full-view on the screen and yell, DAAAAAAAAAAALE, through the phone's tiny speaker. 

Dale hit the power button and put his phone back in his pocket. Just great, he thought, one of my friends has been messing with my alerts again, and continued walking to his next class, utterly dismissing the supernatural event. 

Elwood stretched out of the phone like elastic with a pop and took his place next to Shara leaning against the wall. I do not get this kid, he said, watching Dale walk away. He is an impenetrable fortress of normalcy. 

Still insistent on the daytime? Shara asked him. 

Elwood let out a heavy sigh. Okay, let us try it your way. And they both vanished with a pop and a sizzle of ozone. 

The two demons burst into the space above Dale's bed and stared down at him, gently flapping their wings in the dark. So what do you do now? Elwood asked Shara, who only gave a half smile and extended her index claw out in front of her, slowly curling it back into her palm. The bed sheet covering Dale was pulled off him in sync with the flexing of Shara's finger. Dale only scratched his stomach and rolled over, muttering in his sleep. 

Wow, I am just at a loss for words, Shara. That is some scary stuff, right there, Elwood mocked. 

She narrowed her eyes at him and shot a hand out to grab something in the air, manifesting a psychic grip. Dale screamed in pain as his subconscious was pinched. Shara then yanked her arm back, and Dale flew off the foot of the bed and crashed against the wall, knocking several heavy books off the shelf which fell one after the other onto the top of his head. 

Elwood's jaw dropped as he looked from Shara to Dale and back again. You have no subtlety at all, woman! You are going to wake the neighbors! 

Just watch, she commanded. 

Dale stood up, dazed, and picked up the books, putting them back on the shelf with trembling hands. The door to his room opened and his mom asked him if he was alright. Yeah, just had a really bad leg cramp and fell when I got up, he lied. 

Oh for fuck's sake! Shara said and threw her arms up in total frustration. 

Yeah, the hell with this kid, Elwood said, and they both popped out of the air, defeated by his persistent, mundane denial.
ideas_up.writingprompts::55:
I must possess a mortal host before noon, or Satan shall fly into a blinding, infernal rage. During my previous attempt, I was struck with such immense physical force that I remained grounded, unable to take flight for three consecutive days. Oh, that is it, Oglathor muttered aloud. Oglathor, have you finally calculated a strategy to resolve our mounting financial crisis and successfully crush our primary corporate competitors? his supervisor demanded. No, sir, I was merely contemplating aloud, Oglathor stammered. Very well, the boss retorted, but remember that failure to possess a human and wreak havoc upon His creation before noon results in immediate execution via lethal puppy licks. Meeting adjourned. Oh Satan, I fear your wrath, yet I have not violated the five sacred codes of Hellfire, Chaos, and the definitive manual of possession authored by Iggy Azalea, the omniscient witch-demon who utilizes rhythmic music to ensnare souls. Before departing along the desolate highway of hell, Oglathor purchased a darkblaze hot dog, his preferred snack since 1988.

Oh my Satan, who is that pedestrian? Is she isolated and vulnerable to my influence? I must ascertain her defenses immediately. Oglathor began chanting the lyrics to Fancy by Iggy Azalea, attempting to hijack her physical form to dismantle the terrestrial world. Ew, this human vessel feels peculiar. I experience overwhelming stress and a total lack of telepathic communication. Furthermore, my wings remain dormant; why can I not fly? Regardless, I shall persist. Driven by the mundane urge to walk home from school, Oglathor and his new host prepared to execute a sophisticated, long-term infiltration.

Mommy, I have returned, Oglathor said instinctively. Darling, how are you feeling today? the mother inquired. I am not functioning well, Oglathor admitted, speaking a rare truth; I intend to lie down immediately. Offering assistance, the mother instructed him to shout if he required anything. Why would I shout? Oglathor pondered. He drifted into a deep slumber, but upon waking, he discovered his white tights saturated with blood. Ah, this is the ritualistic essence I awaited. The blood of the child shall dismantle the world, no one would have suspected—Oglathor’s monologue was severed by a cramp so agonizing he assumed it was the apocalypse. Mommy, he shrieked, desperate for aid, what is happening to me? The mother sprinted inside, exclaiming, Sweetheart, you have simply started your first period!
ideas_up.writingprompts::57:
Dr. Kevin Bruin. Log Entry E72. The Moment. To whoever investigates my disappearance: in case I never return. No person knows when their turn arrives. While we quickly discovered methods to track its movement and evade it, stopping it remains impossible. The most disastrous attempts occurred under Martial Law. Those mandatory isolation periods were truly horrific—brief, certainly, but psychologically devastating. One isolated man asked me if universal survival was actually a curse, forcing us to interact with those we selfishly quarantined. Would death have been preferable? He stared deeply into my eyes. While mine reflected sheer panic and profound guilt, his remained entirely peaceful. Why wouldn't they be? The Moment had passed him; it had not yet passed me.

We identified seven specific rules regarding the Moment. First, it exclusively targets men, affecting every male regardless of biological age. Second, its primary intent is not fatal; while deaths occur among the vulnerable, medical intervention prevents most fatalities. Third, it functions on a singular basis; only one man experiences the phenomenon at any given time, with zero reported simultaneous cases. Fourth, its trajectory is proximity-based; closer physical distance to an active subject increases your own probability of being next. Fifth, physical barriers are useless; containment zones failed completely. Once the Moment exhausted the male population within a sector, it inevitably progressed outward. Sixth, it is possible to outrun; it maintains speeds comparable to an average jogging human. Finally, the subjective experience is reported as being incredibly, agonizingly painful.

As to my whereabouts: I was initially asked what the Moment might be. I demanded logical explanations! I conducted observations, formed hypotheses, and designed experiments for months. A virus, a bacterium, a parasite, or perhaps mass hysteria—none fit the data. There was no scientific explanation. When others suggested extraterrestrial origins or divine retribution, I laughed, insisting science would eventually identify the root cause. Eventually, however, I realized no traditional answer was forthcoming. I doubted everything for a while and began considering the extremist theories. Few colleagues know this about me. However, I accept one final rule that others refuse to acknowledge: the Moment is sentient, and human extinction is its ultimate endgame.

As a man of science, I can no longer afford fear; I must test my radical hypothesis. You now understand my disappearance. Men of my advanced age are statistically less likely to survive the encounter, yet we possess the unique perspective to find the truth; science must prevail. I have performed a self-inflicted orchidectomy to test if biological markers dictate targeting. By the time you read this, I will be within the Moment’s current active spread. I wonder how observers will interpret a naked, elderly man walking directly into the fire. Is he insane? A religious fanatic? If I succeed—which I firmly believe I will—you will likely hear legends before I can return. Hence, this log. Stories will circulate about a crazy old man whose faith made him immune. Know that it was indeed faith that triumphed: faith in science. If I do not return, Dan, love always.
ideas_up.writingprompts::59:
A small lamp burned steadily on the polished desk, casting long, flickering shadows against the mahogany grain. The human wore a pair of thin, gold-rimmed spectacles perched precariously on the sharp bridge of his nose. Stacks of yellowed parchment occupied a far corner of the work surface, neatly ordered by date and urgency. He read through pages at a time, occasionally pausing to scribble notes on another crisp sheet with a quill that scratched rhythmically. Empty, stained ink bottles scattered on the floor suggested the man was rather busy with administrative tasks.

From the threshold, Ronn readied his heavy iron flail, letting the cold chains dangle and clatter, their metallic echoes filling the silent room. But the man refused to look up at the intruders. Instead, he held up a single, bony finger and continued reading, his eyes darting across lines of fine script. Ronn and the rest of his ragtag group exchanged nervous glances and shrugged shoulders. For a moment, they stood perfectly still, weapons poised. With a disappointed, sharp smack of the tongue, the man replaced the parchment, pushed his glasses closer to his eyes, and called for his guests to approach. They did, boots clicking on stone.

Apologies, my friends, he said. His voice cracked slightly as though it had gone unpracticed for some time, lacking the cadence of conversation. Come. Come. 

The adventurers stepped forward slowly, wary of the surroundings. Wilm’s head darted around as he scouted for suspicious stones in the floor or another hidden tripwire. The grey cobbles turned to deep green when the tasseled edge of a velvet rug stood before them. The group stopped, unsure if the floor beneath was structural or merely a deceptive illusion designed to swallow them whole.

Come, the man muttered, any impatience defying detection as he adjusted his ledger. 

Firrel’s armored boot tested its weight against the rug. There was solid, unyielding ground beneath. The rest followed suit, creeping forward like thieves in a temple. 

Wait! the man screamed. The group wasted no time assuming a defensive stance, their broadswords and reinforced shields drawn in a defensive arc. I meant the carpet, you idiots. 

The adventurers looked towards their feet. The jade fibers assumed a purplish, sickly hue as the fresh blood from their various wounds dripped freely, staining the expensive fabric. Querth’s face flushed a deep, embarrassed crimson. 

Sorry, the wizard whispered, lowering his staff. 

The man rolled his eyes toward the ceiling. It is already ruined beyond repair. Nothing we can do now to salvage the weave. Let us just get this over with quickly. 

The adventurers were finally within a single pace of the desk when the open palm of the man begged their sudden halt. The hordes of evil creatures had led them to that chamber, believing they were confronting a dark lord. The supposed throne room of unspeakable villainy was little more than a cluttered, dusty study with a librarian. 

Well, then. I suppose congratulations are in order! The man clapped his hands together, the sound sharp like a gunshot. Smashing job. I am Pollock and I will be handling your bureaucratic processing from here. 

Processing? Edmund echoed, his hand tightening on his axe handle. 

Yes, replied Pollock. You are almost done in this dreadful castle and on your way back home to enjoy the spoils. All that is left is to handle the last tedious odds and ends of your intrusion. 

The adventurers nodded in content, but kept their weapons handy just in case of a trap. The legions they had to cut through in order to reach that chamber began to feel concluded, yet the tension remained. 

Excellent! Let us get started. In total you have slaughtered one hundred and fifty three goblins, twenty nine orcs, eighteen kobolds, and two ancient dragons. Impressive carnage, really. 

Edmund smirked and rolled the handle of his axe to catch the light, drawing groans from Ronn and Dismal. They had enjoyed the chaos that had followed as it stopped their fellow warrior from gloating about his combat prowess. 

In addition, you broke down forty one heavy oak doors, set off two fire traps, six jagged spike snares, three crushing boulders, and one acidic spill. Plus, the audit says you freed the dungeons of ten prisoners who now lack proper documentation. 

All in a day's work, Wilm interjected with a smug grin. 

Quite, responded Pollock, not the least impressed by their bravado. And adding up your little adventure, that comes to a total of eight million, eight hundred thirty seven thousand, two hundred and fifty one gold pieces in damage. 

Even Querth’s brilliant mind could not comprehend such a massive, astronomical figure. They were used to generous spoils, but several hundred coins was the most any had ever seen. 

We could not possibly carry that much coin, Dismal remarked. Or spend it in ten lifetimes. 

That is quite expected, Pollock laughed, a dry sound. You can just pay in monthly installments, assuming you survive the next year. 

Pay? shouted Firrel. What do you mean pay? We are the heroes! 

Your fines, your property damages, and your environmental impact fees. You cannot just go around killing things, damaging historical architecture, and setting off traps that require professional recalibration. 

But we were on a quest, pleaded Ronn. We were trying to save the village from certain doom. 

I see, sneered Pollock. Does that mean the village is going to pay the fines, rebuild the castle, reset the magical protections, mop the floors, rehire the guards, retrain the dragons, and inform the families of those lost? The group stood in wide-eyed, horrified silence. I did not think so. 

B-but, it was a quest, Ronn repeated, his voice failing. 

Do you have a license, a Writ of Pacification for this quest of yours? Ronn shook his head slowly. No need to answer, I already know you do not. If you had bothered to apply for one, this castle would have been better protected and I would not have been needed here. Just a little WP at the start would have been enough to save us all the mess of your unauthorized, violent rampage. 

Who was supposed to file our WP? Querth asked the group. They considered the question for a moment before turning to face Dismal. You have ruined us! 

I am sorry, cried Dismal. I did not know! I did not know this would happen! 

The circle closed around him as the group looked to dispatch their greatest foe: the enemy within. The moral is tag your posts or else your friends will murder you.

ideas_down.xsum::9:
The fundamental legal takeaway from the European Court of Human Rights ruling regarding Nadia Eweida and three other Christian applicants is that the right to manifest religious belief in the workplace is severely limited when it conflicts with the established rights of others or the operational requirements of an employer. While Ms. Eweida secured a victory because the court determined that British Airways had failed to strike a fair, proportionate balance between her desire to wear a discreet religious symbol and the company’s desire to project a specific corporate image, this remains a highly narrow exception. The core principle reaffirmed by the Strasbourg court is that employers possess considerable, broad discretion to set reasonable workplace policies and to insist that their employees adhere to those requirements, regardless of the individual worker's personal religious convictions. This central doctrine of workplace deference to employer policy serves as the dominant theme across all four cases, effectively establishing that religious freedom does not grant employees an absolute license to override professional obligations or the rights of their colleagues and service users.

The cases of Shirley Chaplin, Gary McFarlane, and Lillian Ladele illustrate the profound limitations of this religious freedom when it clashes with the rights of other people in a secular professional environment. For instance, the court dismissed the claims of Ms. Ladele and Mr. McFarlane, concluding that their employers acted legitimately when they disciplined the employees for refusing to perform specific professional duties—such as conducting same-sex civil partnership ceremonies or providing counseling to gay couples—that conflicted with their personal religious beliefs. In these instances, the court emphasized that the rights of those receiving services must be protected, and that an employer is entitled to ensure that all clients are treated equally without discrimination. Similarly, the court ruled against nurse Shirley Chaplin, finding that her employer's policy preventing her from wearing a crucifix was a necessary, proportionate measure designed to ensure the health and safety of both nursing staff and patients within the hospital setting. These rulings collectively reinforce the idea that, while individuals are legally entitled to hold and express religious views, that entitlement is strictly constrained within the public sphere of employment where the operational needs of the organization and the rights of third parties take precedence.

The judgment effectively signals that the European Convention on Human Rights does not provide a mandate for religious workers to ignore company policies or professional codes of conduct. Instead, it places the burden on the employee to demonstrate that a policy restriction is unnecessary or unreasonable, a threshold that is exceptionally difficult to cross in most professional environments. Even in Ms. Eweida’s case, the victory was contingent upon the specific observation that a discreet cross would not have caused any genuine, tangible harm to the public image or the commercial interests of British Airways. This specific finding does not elevate religious expression above corporate policy; rather, it suggests that where a minor accommodation can be made without causing significant disruption or infringing upon the rights of others, it should be considered. However, this does not alter the broader reality that the vast majority of conflicts between religious practice and workplace requirements will be resolved in favor of the employer’s right to manage their business and maintain professional standards.

The legal landscape established by this ruling provides clear guidance for both employers and employees across the United Kingdom. Employers are granted a significant margin of appreciation to implement policies that they deem necessary for the proper functioning of their organizations, provided those policies are not inherently discriminatory or disproportionate. Meanwhile, employees who hold traditionalist religious views are faced with the reality that their workplace participation may require them to set aside their personal convictions when those convictions directly interfere with the core requirements of their roles or the fundamental rights of those they serve. The consensus emerging from Strasbourg is that the workplace is a domain of secular cooperation where professional duties and the rights of the collective often must supersede individual expressions of faith. This ensures that the primary focus of the employment relationship remains on the delivery of services and the equality of all persons, rather than on the individual religious preferences of the staff members. 

Consequently, the attempt by traditionalist Christians to defend their specific values against secular institutional standards has met with limited success, as the court prioritized the neutral, inclusive requirements of the workplace. The message remains consistent: while the law protects the right to hold a belief, it provides little protection for the manifestation of that belief when it serves to restrict the rights of others or hinders the objective, non-discriminatory provision of public and private services. By upholding the decisions of the lower courts in the cases of Ladele, McFarlane, and Chaplin, the European Court of Human Rights has affirmed that secular institutions are not obligated to accommodate religious objections that would compromise their commitment to equality or safety. This sets a clear precedent for future litigation, confirming that the balance of power in the workplace remains firmly with the employer’s right to enforce reasonable, universal standards of conduct. Ultimately, the ruling serves as a definitive confirmation that the professional sphere operates under the authority of corporate policy, and personal faith must be balanced against the essential, non-negotiable rights of others in a pluralistic society. This legal framework ensures that the diverse needs of the public are met without being impeded by the individual religious doctrines of those employed to serve them, thereby maintaining the integrity of the professional environment while respecting the limited scope of religious freedom in the modern workplace.

ideas_down.xsum::14: The fundamental legal issue in the case brought against Bideford Town Council by the National Secular Society is that local authorities lack the explicit statutory power to conduct prayers as part of their formal proceedings. Mr Justice Ouseley ruled definitively that the Local Government Act 1972 does not provide any authorization for councils to include religious acts in their official agendas or to summon councillors to attend such rituals. This decision rests entirely upon a narrow interpretation of statutory construction, specifically regarding the limitations placed upon local government bodies. The judge emphasized that even if a council votes by a majority to retain these prayers, such a vote cannot grant an authority the power to perform actions that are otherwise not permitted by law. The court concluded that holding prayers during formal meetings exceeds the legal scope granted to local authorities under existing legislation. This ruling serves as a significant legal constraint, clarifying that public bodies are restricted to the specific powers granted to them by Parliament, and therefore cannot unilaterally incorporate religious practices into their official business. The absence of an express statutory provision for prayer effectively renders the practice unlawful within the strict context of a formal council meeting. This core argument regarding the limitations of local government power remains the singular focus of the legal determination, regardless of the broader societal debates surrounding religion in public life. The court did not base its decision on human rights arguments, but rather on the objective reality that the 1972 Act provides no mandate for such religious activities. Consequently, the legal prohibition is based purely on the lack of legislative authority, creating a clear boundary for all local councils across England and Wales. This interpretation of the law maintains that local authorities must operate strictly within the bounds of their defined statutory roles. Because the law does not explicitly empower councils to facilitate religious worship, the inclusion of prayers during formal business is deemed an overreach of administrative capacity. The judge’s reasoning focuses on the principle that if a power is not explicitly granted in the governing legislation, then a public body has no authority to exercise it. This interpretation highlights a strict separation between the administrative duties of a council and the personal religious expressions of its members. The ruling dictates that while individual councillors may hold their own beliefs, the institution itself cannot codify these beliefs into its formal operating procedures without clear statutory permission. This interpretation ensures that local government remains an entity defined by its legal mandate rather than by the religious preferences of its current members. By clarifying that the 1972 Act does not authorize these religious elements, the court established a precedent that limits the scope of civic activity to purely secular governance. This focus on the limitations of statutory power serves as the primary mechanism for the court’s decision, ensuring that all local authorities adhere to a consistent legal standard. The ruling essentially clarifies the boundaries of municipal authority, reinforcing the idea that administrative bodies must find their legitimacy solely within the text of the statutes that created them. The decision emphasizes that the legal framework for local government is exhaustive and does not contain an implied authorization for religious practices. This interpretation is consistent with the view that public institutions should remain neutral and operate within the specific, limited powers granted by the legislature. By focusing on the lack of statutory authority, the ruling avoids the complexities of human rights discourse and instead relies on a straightforward assessment of what the law permits. This approach provides a clear, objective rule for all local councils to follow, ensuring that their procedures remain compliant with the governing legislation. The emphasis on the absence of power under the 1972 Act is the central pillar of the judgment, providing a definitive answer to the question of whether prayers can be formally integrated into council meetings. This legal constraint is absolute, regardless of the historical context or the personal desires of those involved. The court’s logic dictates that the legislative silence regarding religious activities in the 1972 Act must be interpreted as a prohibition against them. This strict constructionist view ensures that public authorities do not exceed their mandates, thereby preserving the integrity of the legal framework that governs local administration. The ruling clarifies that the structure of local government is purely secular by design, as it is defined exclusively by the statutes that establish its functions. Any practice not specifically listed as a power of the council is thus outside its legitimate scope. This legal clarity is the primary outcome of the case, establishing a firm boundary for the conduct of public business. The decision serves to underscore that the authority of local government is derived entirely from the law, which does not provide for the inclusion of religious rituals. By maintaining this focus on the limitations of the Local Government Act, the court has provided a clear standard for the governance of all local authorities. This decision confirms that the powers of a council are limited to those explicitly stated in the law, reinforcing the principle of legality in public administration. The determination that prayers are unlawful due to the lack of statutory power is the sole, consistent rationale that defines the court’s stance. This ruling establishes that the legal framework for local governance is complete and does not allow for the incorporation of practices that are not explicitly authorized. Therefore, the focus remains on the interpretation of the 1972 Act as a comprehensive limitation on the actions that councils may take in their formal capacity. This perspective ensures that the legal duties of a council are clearly delineated and strictly enforced, preventing any deviation from the statutory requirements. The judgment stands as a testament to the idea that public bodies must operate strictly within the confines of their legal authority, which is the singular and sufficient basis for the court’s decision.
