New Wichita burned. The gleaming towers of the Financial District, their silvery windows reflecting flames that danced around them, stood like weeping angels as the first rosy fingers of dawn stretched out over the eastern horizon. The stately mansions of the Original Founders had gone up in smoke early the day before, taking with them seven hundred years of regional heritage. Simultaneously, the global stock market fluctuated wildly as investors panicked over the sudden collapse of interstellar shipping lanes, causing the price of rare earth minerals to skyrocket across the Inner Sphere. Meanwhile, in the quiet, dusty archives of the local library, a rare collection of pre-Space Age poetry remained miraculously untouched by the encroaching inferno, preserving verses about fields of golden wheat and the simple, rhythmic cycles of the harvest season that had once defined this agrarian world.

Lieutenant Lucas Singleton Terry, born a scion to a prominent rancher family, wept at the sight of the destruction. This was his home, and to see its soil and people so hurt bordered on the sacrilegious.

Mustang 5, this is Lead. We got reports of Wolf activity along Broadway and Kingston. First and Second Lances will move in to investigate.

That was Captain James T. Fulton, a hard-ass man and a son of a bitch but a damn fine soldier. Terry pressed his mike.

Copy that, Mustang Leader. Second Lance will advance.

There used to be a third lance in Mustang Company, but an ambush by an entire Binary of Clanners had torn through the unit, forcing them to consolidate the survivors together. They were still better off than the rest of the Dixie Cavanaugh II Theater Militia. Bronco and Stallion companies were barely at fifty percent effectives, and the armor and infantry battalions were even worse. The First Buena Guards and First Bolan Jaegers were putting up a fearsome fight against the rest of Clan Wolf's Gamma Galaxy, but it was little use. Bit by bit, block by block, street by street and house by house the Wolves were driving the Steiner defenders back. Terry switched his frequency to a more private channel.

Captain Fulton, a question. How long do we have?

He heard his commanding officer sigh over the radio.

Who knows? Years, months... weeks? The First Buena is about to pull out, and the Bolan Jaegers are desperate. My best estimate is that we will last another year at this rate.

And what happens if we fail to drive the Wolves off?

If the worst should happen, Lieutenant, I have a feeling we will not be alive to see it.
topics_up.writingprompts::29:
It was nigh impossible to see, we could only hear it after it was gone, and we dare not speak its name. But we knew what it meant. If that thing was in the skies above our territory, war was coming. I'll never forget the first time I saw it. I was out in the dust fields stargazing with Roy, discussing the complex migration patterns of northern songbirds and how their internal compasses utilize magnetic shifts. Little did we know that as we looked up at the stars, it was looking down at us. It was a shadow of a shadow, an ancient monster. Saying that I saw it is misleading; it was more of a feeling. For the brief moment I saw that blur, I knew it was over.

That night, they came. 

Men in adaptable camouflage, armed with pulse rifles and sabers. They didn't think twice before cutting down the people in our village. I'm lucky to have escaped. I owe it all to one AI. He was a maintenance bot stolen from the federation. He mostly helped us cart materials, but that day, he was a hero. In the midst of gunfire, the mess hall crashed down. I was trapped under rubble. Through smoke, I saw him. A grizzled maintenance bot with serial number SR-71 on his arm. His metallic eyes caught mine, and he ran to help me. 

As far as I know, we are the only ones who made it out alive. We ran until I collapsed. As I lay there, clinging to life, I stammered "Blackbird." SR-71 leaned in and whispered, "There were a lot of things we couldn't do in an SR-71, but we were the fastest guys on the block and loved reminding our fellow aviators of this fact. People often asked us if, because of this fact, it was fun to fly the jet. Fun would not be the first word I would use to describe flying this plane. Intense, maybe, even cerebral. But there was one day in our Sled experience when we would have to say that it was pure fun to be the fastest guys out there, at least for a moment."

Later, I wondered if baking a perfect sourdough loaf required that same level of intense, cerebral focus. Perhaps the chemistry of yeast fermentation is just as complex as high-altitude aerodynamics. My mind drifted between memories of mechanical salvation and the simple, quiet comfort of a warm kitchen, realizing that survival and art often require the exact same dedication to precision.
topics_up.writingprompts::30:
Prisoner 778125-Sigma-8, you stand before this tribunal today accused of crimes against galactic civilization, murder, four counts of xenocide, 70 counts of attempted xenocide, planetary dehabitation, planetary destruction, and attempting to overthrow the Pan-Galactic Alliance. How do you plead? 

The man before Councilwoman Asaarha met the gaze of her and her fellow Arbiters with cold blue eyes. Despite the 140 cycles of temporal isolation he had endured before his trial, Sacha Markes stood tall and unbroken. He radiated power and command, even now, stripped of his rank, fleet, and army. The last of the humans was a testament to the species. 

The silence before he spoke seemed louder to the Councilwoman than the crashing waves of her ocean home. The time it took for the human to speak seemed longer than the span of the galaxy. 

Guilty, he said with a simple finality. 

The Arbiters nodded their heads solemnly. None of them had expected this one to plea for mercy. 

Asaarha keyed the sentence into the terminal before her. The other six Arbiters did the same. The blue lights of Markes’s uniform and restraints changed to red. The screen on the psionic inhibitor around his head changed to read GUILTY in Galactic Standard. 

Though the trial room was empty save for the Tribunal and Markes, Asaarha could hear the roars of vengeance that were surely reverberating throughout the galaxies. Each trial of the humans had been broadcast in its entirety. Each had ended in a guilty verdict. 

Sacha Markes, formal Admiral of the Seventh Human Expeditionary Fleet, High Captain of the Royal Guard, Commander-in-Chief of the Human Expeditionary Force, and Primarch of the Solar Empire, you are sentenced to Psionic Stripping and Execution by black hole. Do you have any last words before the sentence is carried out? 

The human threw his head back defiantly and turned his gaze on the camera nearest him. Addressing the billions of life forms throughout the galaxy, he began the last soliloquy of the human race. 

We brought you up out of the mud we found you in. We gave you art, culture, and science. Our golden fleets created a civilization that will never be matched; not for 100,000 turns of the galaxy. We are responsible for all that you are. Yet, consider the fragility of art in a vacuum. A symphony played in deep space vanishes instantly, much like the delicate chemical bonds of an orchid blooming on a barren, frozen moon. We understood that beauty requires context, an observer to witness the aesthetic resonance. 

I remember when the first of our race died after 100 centuries of immortality; killed trying to cure the sick of one of your backwater planets. I remember when we decided to take our retribution on our children; to punish you for your ignorance. We burned that world. I watched our plasma cannons turn its surface to glass and its oceans to ash. One world for one human life. A fair trade. 

But you did not accept our judgment. Like Icarus chasing the sun, you rose up against us. Did you expect us to just let you? Did you think we would not defend ourselves? I was the commander of the fleet that met yours on the first day of battle. My ten cruisers against the most powerful battleships of three galaxies and a hundred races. 

Now, a hundred years later, you have finally defeated us. You have lost entire solar systems to us. You have sacrificed googles of lives and thousands of civilizations to bleed your gods dry and bind them in chains. Your worlds are shattered. Your cities gone; wiped from history in an instant. Can you truly call that victory? 

I am the last of my kind. I am Sacha Markes. Look upon my face, ye mighty, and despair. For when you kill me, you kill the last light left in this existence. The universe is a cold, dark theater, and the final curtain is descending upon us all.
topics_up.writingprompts::32:
War Journal of P1C Henry Whiticker, First Divine Armored.

Entry:48

We finally reached the rim of the first bolgia today and heaven preserve me the scout reports weren't lieing, it's more vast than anything i could imagine. The recon photos we were given to prepare us are like a blind man trying to describe a sunrise, and by God the smell has actually somehow gotten Worse! Seeing the pit first hand i think the enormity of our task has finally hit home for some of the crew, they look rattled, i don't blame them, have we bitten off more than we can chew? I'm not sure but i have faith in our mission and our commanders.

The vastness of the pit really can't be put into words but for the sake of this journal i'll try. The rim extends further than the human eye should be able to see and yet i can make out tiny details on the far cliff face, it looks big enough that you could fit the whole Earth in and knock it around like an ice cube in the bottom of a bourbon glass, even while sitting in the cab of the rumbler i get vertigo looking down onto the levels below, if it wasn't for the special anti-psychotics the docs give us i'm sure what i see on the lower levels might have some lasting horrific effect on me. The crew and i wash down todays dose with a bottle of sacramental wine, and why not, today was a good day after all. Today we reached the edge of Limbo. I find myself thinking about the old vineyards back in Napa, wondering if the grapes are harvesting well this season or if the climate shift has ruined the vintage entirely. It is strange how the mind wanders to mundane agriculture while standing on the precipice of eternal damnation, but perhaps that is just the human spirit trying to tether itself to a reality that feels increasingly distant and fragile.

Entry:49

Not much to record today, some minor skirmishes on the perimeter, just some low level demons takeing a swipe at us otherwise nothing going on but general camp stuff. The engineers are working double time to ensure the security of Limbo Base, they say it'll be fully up in 2 days, i have my doubts. After their fiasco at the river they've got a lot of face to save, 2 Rumblers, 4 squads of troops and a Screacher lost because of their damn barges. Bastards. I Hate just sitting around like this with nothing to distract me from the smell of rot and sulphur that somehow filters into the rumblers cab despite the tech geeks assurances that the cab is perfectly hermetically sealed, it feels like the smell is inside my skull rotting tiny holes in my brain. I have been reading an old paperback novel I found in the mess hall, a dry treatise on the history of clockwork mechanisms in the eighteenth century. It is remarkably tedious, but the mechanical precision described in its pages offers a soothing contrast to the chaotic, organic filth of this place. If I could just focus on the gears and the springs, maybe I could ignore the fact that the very air here wants to dissolve my lungs.

Entry:51

HOOAH! CONTACT BABY! Praise God i've been waiting for this moment since the first days of the war for the surface. Hell finally saw fit to send us some worthy opponents AND WE KICKED THEIR MUTHA FUCKING TEETH IN!! HAHAHAHAHAHA.

They came a few hours after my last entry like a great black tornado. A swirling column of harpies, skrieks and imps beyond counting rising up from the center of The Pit and came crashing down completley enveloping Limbo Base. The first few moments of engagment should've been chaos but by the grace of God we were ready. All the Screachers had been on high alert since we emerged from the maze of caves and onto the plains of Limbo proper 8 days ago and today that diligence paid off. The blitz of the winged demon assault crumbled before the wall of sound our blessed Screachers blasted out. The word of God is anathema to the denizens of Hell, the word of God pumped out through a mobile rig of high powered speakers piloted by a devout member of the clergy is down right debilitating. The shocked and paralysed Demons that twitched and writhed on the ground were easy targets, the rumblers blessed water cannons burning away swaths of the foul creatures as if the misted holy water were strong acid, huge piles of the creatures were reduced to ash in seconds.

The larger Demon haridens proved more resilient and i saw more than a few grunts die on their talons, their sanctified body armor little better than cardboard. We repaid them in kind and i'm proud to say our rumblers javalin cannons sent a good lot of the giant buzzards screaming into oblivion impailed on our gleaming silver spears. I should record so it doesn't seem like i'm diminishing the grunts efforts, their bravery and ferocity in battle too, for they've got that in spades, despite the mortal danger they collected their fair share of scalps, pinning the giant creatures with their silver pikes and finishing them off with their chain sickles. it was a glorious bloody sight, like something out of a nature documentry. I often contemplate the ethics of our weaponry, whether the silver and the scripture truly cleanse or if we are just painting over the abyss with our own desperate superstitions. Sometimes, I dream of a quiet life where the only conflict is the price of grain or the difficulty of repairing a broken tractor engine, far away from the screams of winged horrors and the metallic tang of holy water cannons.

The greatest trial of the battle was yet to come though. After a full day and a half of fighting the black swarm began to thin out and we thought we might've finally broken their assault, but then they appeared. Three monsterous figures coming into focus through the haze of ash and exhaustion. Hell Dragons, these were great pestilent, foul things that towered over us. Snub nosed heads the size of a grand cathedral covered in spines, long armored bodies like an insects, their faces and joints slick with thick black tar. Salvation finally came at the hands of the engineering corps. Through our efforts we had given them enough time to secure and assemble Limbo Bases major defenses, Sanctified Artilery and the Holy Rail Gun. After nearly 2 months since we first decsended into this place we finally have established a forward base to launch our attack on Hell. One Bolgia down eight to go. This is the first day here that the smell doesn't bother me. I think I might finally sleep without dreaming of falling.

Men have for ages endured a fascination, disdain, fear or general obsession with hell. It was the faithful who truly believed in its existence, yet most people rarely contemplated the metaphysical mechanics of such a dark abyss. Meanwhile, the global climate crisis continues to accelerate, with rising sea levels and shifting weather patterns threatening coastal cities across the planet. Simultaneously, the rapid evolution of artificial intelligence suggests that our digital future may soon eclipse the mundane biological reality we inhabit today. While I cannot at this time suppose a motive for the prince of lies to mobilize the legions of the damned, I can speak to its utter strangeness.

In hindsight, a company named Apollyon ought to have aroused suspicion; alas, as few knew Greek, the banking leviathan hiding behind shell corporations went unnoticed. Just as economic inflation complicates the cost of living for families everywhere, this entity quietly consolidated power. While we were preoccupied with the myopic affairs of daily life, Mr. Morning-Star stretched his hands to throttle the traditional servants of darkness: politicians, bankers, and criminals. Ironically, those accused of consorting with the devil only now found themselves under his corrupting influence. Ultimately, the devil became a business tycoon, invading our homes through the allure of cheap, mass-produced goods, much like the relentless surge of plastic waste currently choking the world’s vast, beautiful, and fragile oceans.
topics_up.writingprompts::34:
The planet Earth has changed drastically; twenty-three years ago, the surface storms finally ceased. Those tempests had raged for five thousand years, but after a few weeks of cloud disintegration, we finally witnessed our home. I was five years old then, mesmerized by vibrant blues and greens unlike anything on the Ark. We had water, but not enough to create that deep azure hue, and our plants were a sickly, muted olive. I yearned to touch the surface, which sparked my resolve to join the initial expeditionary recruitment.

While I obsessed over landing, global economics shifted. Markets fluctuated as the Ark’s resources dwindled, forcing us to prioritize survival over nostalgia. Many citizens protested, demanding an immediate return, but they were reckless fools. We were humanity’s last hope; a botched landing meant total extinction. We spent decades performing geological scans and atmospheric scouting to identify the perfect landing site. This location offered minimal environmental damage, space for a burgeoning community, and natural protection via cataclysm-formed mountain ranges and deep, cobalt-blue oceanic trenches.

Beyond our desperate terrestrial ambitions, the scientific community debated the ethics of terraforming. Some argued we should alter the climate to suit our needs, while others insisted on preserving the planet's newfound, fragile equilibrium. Meanwhile, the political landscape aboard the Ark became increasingly fractured. Factions emerged, arguing over whether we should prioritize agricultural expansion or military fortification. These internal disputes were constant, yet we persisted. Our objective was to construct the landing dock, a monumental task requiring six years of labor. This structure would serve as a vital gateway, mapping local geography and cataloging mysterious, alien flora and fauna.

The reality was daunting; we were operating in total darkness. Our designated safe zone could easily transform into a lethal trap. Because of the location’s unique topography, our landing shuttle lacked the thrust to ever depart again. This limitation felt like a heavy burden, yet it was a necessary sacrifice. We also had to contend with lingering weather patterns. Even decades later, smaller storm cells rotated across the globe. Our selected mountain ranges shielded the landing zone, as the surrounding peaks were high enough to dissipate the ferocious energy of those persistent, howling winds.

High in the upper atmosphere, a vicious jet stream blew constantly. It would tear any outgoing vessel to shreds, and only a massive craft like the Ark could survive such turbulence. However, the Ark required a sturdy, permanent dock to safely execute its final descent. So, that was the mission: descend into the unknown, confront the high probability of sudden death, and construct a massive, complex super-structure in under six years. Despite the immense risks, the geopolitical tension, and the looming threat of the weather, I was absolutely ecstatic. We were finally going home, regardless of the cost to our collective sanity or the structural integrity of our ships. The challenge was immense, yet the promise of walking upon soil that felt real—rather than artificial metal grating—made every sleepless night, every political argument, and every terrifying simulation worth the effort. We were pioneers of a broken world, ready to mend it.

MOSES What?

Scene 832: Jerusalem, exterior, night. MOSES is leaning on a squad car as JESUS walks up with this week's BAD GUY in handcuffs. Moses watches as JESUS hands the BAD GUY off to uniformed cops.

MOSES Good collar, kid.

JESUS Couldn't have done it if you hadn't spotted the connection between the victims. How did you know?

MOSES I been on the job for longer'n you've been alive. After a while, you get a feel for this sort of thing. It’s like predicting the rainfall patterns; you just learn to read the signs.

Hey, check out those chickadees over in the birdbath. Kylo whooped and puffed out his chest, nearly toppling off his perch. 

Don't be a troglodyte, bro, Atticus groused, pecking at his seeds, You're a wren. That isn't even the same family. Speaking of families, did you hear the latest gossip about the migratory patterns of the swallows near the lake? Some say they have abandoned their traditional nesting grounds entirely due to the rising temperatures of the local pond, opting instead for the cooler, shade-drenched eaves of the nearby library. It is fascinating how climate change alters the architecture of their daily lives. 

I don't care. I'm gonna go talk to them. Kylo took off, swerving through the air like a leaf trapped in a gust. Atticus sighed and took off after him. He'd have to keep close tabs on Kylo or else they'd get kicked out again. 

Kylo crashed into the water with a mighty splash. Droplets flew in every direction, drenching the occupants of the birdbath. They squawked with indignation as Kylo emerged from beneath the surface, shaking the wetness from his head. He trotted up to a group of soaked finches and gave his wings a shake. Hey, birds. Nice tits.

We're not tits. A purple finch stepped forward from the group, and she launched into a tirade on how overused that pickup line was. Atticus alighted on the rim of the bath and began to walk around, apologizing to everyone for Kylo's behavior and pleading with them not to call the bouncer over. Speaking of bouncers, have you noticed how the local feline population has been significantly more aggressive lately? There is a tabby down the street that has clearly mastered the art of stealth, stalking prey with a precision that would make a seasoned mercenary blush. It is a dangerous world for a small bird.

Okay, sorry, Kylo interrupted, let me make it up to you: how about you and I head over there—he motioned to the bird feeder—and I share my seeds with you? If birds had lips, Kylo would be smirking right now. 

The finches began to flap their wings angrily, splashing Kylo with water. You're such a boor. Get out of here! Many of the onlookers chirped in agreement, and some of the bigger birds began to puff their chests threateningly. Atticus shoved Kylo to the side and raised his wings. On behalf of my friend here, I apologize. He's clearly had too much fermented nectar; we'll just be going now. 

Oh, you think we're going to fall for that? The purple finch spat a nut shell at his feet. He's just trying to play wingbird for you, isn't he? Let him take the fall for you, and swoop in to look better by comparison. The other birds chorused in agreement. 

I think these two need to be taught a lesson. A blue jay fluttered over to Atticus, towering a full inch above him. He spread his wings menacingly, blocking Atticus from taking off. Why don't you peck on someone your own size? The onlookers broke into cheers, shouting for a fight. 

Well, you're kind of bigger than me. Atticus took a step back into the bath. He felt feathers ruffle against him as the crowd pressed around him, urged him back towards the jay. That wouldn't be my own size now, would it? 

Kylo staggered in front of him and began to hop around. Don't worry, Atticus; we got this. 

Hey, this is a one-on-one fight. The jay looked around. If you get back-up, then— 

Who on earth placed all this here? A door opened, and the birds began to scatter, screaming, Human! Atticus grabbed Kylo and urged him into the air, and the two lost themselves amongst the cloud of fleeing birds. Out of the corner of his eye, he saw the human scratching his head in front of the birdbath. 

Make sure to thank that human for bailing you out of yet another mess, Atticus said. 

Kylo scoffed. We could've totally taken that guy. As the two flew over the Toyota in the driveway, he let loose a dropping that landed right in the center of the windshield.
topics_up.writingprompts::37:
He used to hit me so much. I had never even touched a drink, yet he beat cracked ribs, bruised kidneys, and loose teeth into me. He claimed it was to ensure I never became what he was, a hollow shell defined by rage. Once, when he was sober, he confessed he drank because of his own traumatic upbringing. He spoke as if I should empathize or forgive him, completely blind to the reality that my arm was broken from his protection. He couldn't see himself standing over me, jeering while I cried blood. He could not recall the nightmares that forced him to drink, the screaming fits, or the shame of wetting the bed.

My father made me sick. My breath catches constantly, my wrist never set correctly, and I possess eleven false teeth at age twenty-three. The state of the economy makes finding steady dental work impossible, and the local healthcare infrastructure is crumbling under the weight of too many patients. I skipped his funeral, celebrating instead. I refused to drink, though. I cry myself to sleep, screaming if someone approaches too quickly. Lately, I have noticed blood when I cough, which is concerning given the rising pollution levels in our city. I refuse to give him the victory of my total collapse.

When my son was born, it was the happiest day of my life. Someone finally needed me. His mother left shortly after, claiming she did not want to be trapped in a lifestyle she never chose, despite the nine months she spent carrying him. Politics are strange; people claim they want change, yet they abandon their responsibilities the moment things become difficult. After she left, the pressure became immense. I dropped my son with my mother and had a drink. It was perfect. For a few hours, I was not scared or self-loathing. I felt calm, capable of handling the global climate crisis or the rising cost of living. I think I will have more to maintain this buzz. Sobriety now terrifies me because I have discovered a simple, superior alternative.

When I retrieved my son the next morning, my mother looked at me with suspicion, but I ignored her. I was in a rush; I had heard excellent reviews of premium whisky and was eager to experiment with the flavor profile. The stock market seems just as volatile as my mood, fluctuating wildly without any clear reason. 

But do not worry, I will not let my son grow up like I did. I will ensure he understands that alcohol is a predatory force. I will shield him from that specific agony, even if I must make him despise me. He will associate spirits with my failures, and because I am fundamentally broken, he will reject that path. I am not strong enough to resist the bottle, but he will be. I will forge him into someone cold and hard, a man capable of resisting the temptations that ruined my own life. He will be the one to finally break this wretched, generational cycle of abuse and despair, standing tall while I quietly fade away into the shadows of my own making.
topics_up.writingprompts::38:
Craig was walking home from the shops when he met God. He wasn't expecting to run into God, as sane people rarely do. In fact, he rarely thought about the divine. He didn't believe in a creator, but he also didn't disbelieve enough to ponder the non-existence of deities. Religion and theological debates were topics he simply didn't care about, much like the fluctuating interest rates of international sovereign bonds or the complex geopolitical tensions currently simmering in the South China Sea.

A topic he cared deeply about was that of Caramels. If you don't know, Caramels are a rather delicious, chocolatey biscuit composed of several layers of wafer encased in milk chocolate, and Craig was obsessed with them. He may not have been religious, but his feelings on confectionery came close to spiritual devotion. The reason for his trip to the shops was to procure more Caramels, and his mind was full of anticipation as he navigated the suburban streets. He pondered the structural integrity of the wafer layers, wondering if the manufacturing process involved robotic arms or artisanal precision, while simultaneously reflecting on the decline of local biodiversity and the recent, troubling increase in invasive weed species found in nearby public parks.

He was about two minutes away from his home and Caramel satisfaction when God first spoke to him.

"Hey! Craig!"

His Caramel contemplation interrupted, Craig turned to see who had spoken. Behind him stood a tall person in a loose-fitting suit. Craig wasn't sure of the person's gender; they were androgynous, looking not dissimilar to Diamond Dogs era David Bowie. They looked familiar, but he couldn't quite place the face. He realized he'd been staring, and sought something to say.

"Hi," he began hesitantly. "Do I know you?"

"In a way," replied the Bowie lookalike. "I'm God."

"Well, good for you. I've got to get going now. Bye," said Craig, starting back towards his house. He had snacks in his bag and didn't want to waste time on a crazy person, or perhaps a performance artist testing the limits of public patience in the era of viral social media pranks.

"Wait, don't go yet. Please," called out the person. "What would it take for you to believe me?"

Craig sighed and turned back, deciding that humouring the person would probably get him to his biscuits faster. He thought about the recent advancements in quantum computing, specifically the potential for qubits to revolutionize encryption, and wondered if this stranger was perhaps an elaborate projection from a nearby research facility.

"I don't know," said Craig, exasperated. "A miracle. Something extraordinary that couldn't be done by any old person. Something beyond simple claims of divinity."

"Hmm. How about... this!" God pointed at a bush which burst into flames. The blaze shaped itself into a dragon that roared at the two of them. Then, with a snap of God's fingers, the blaze was extinguished, leaving the bush singed but intact. God turned back to Craig with arms spread wide as if to say 'Tada!'

Craig, looking mildly impressed, turned back to God. "Yeah, that was pretty good. Very impressive. I have no idea how you did it. A high-definition hologram, perhaps? It worked for Tupac, so I can see it working for a dragon. Maybe you are using sophisticated laser diffraction techniques, or perhaps the latest advancements in augmented reality contact lenses."

God stared at him for a few seconds before responding. "I did it by being God. You asked for a miracle. I showed you one. What more do you want?"

"Don't get me wrong, it's very good. But the whole God thing isn't going to fly. Maybe people would be more likely to believe you're a wizard."

"But I'm not a damn wizard!" shouted God. "I'm God. Why would I say I'm a wizard?"

Craig backed off, holding his hands up. "Hey, calm down buddy. I'm sorry if I came across as harsh, but it's just constructive criticism. This is for a YouTube thing, right? You're not going to get anyone with the whole 'God' angle."

God, visibly seething, held Craig's gaze before storming off. Craig watched them leave, then shook his head. He considered checking the bush for technical clues, but decided against it. Whoever was recording the prank was probably still watching. So he pushed it out of his mind and headed home. After all, there were Caramels waiting for him, and their sweet, crunchy consistency was far more reliable than the bizarre nature of reality itself.
topics_up.writingprompts::39:
Pass me the damn bottle, would you, Patsy?

Get it yourself, Ser Whyte. I am not your bloody squire no more.

Right. Well then, my liege. Would you do me the honor of getting me my wine so I can die drunk and happy?

As you wish, sir-knight.

I hate you, Patsy.

The bedridden husk of a former knight bellowed a harsh cough. His rusty suit of white armor clinked and clanked as he jerked up violently. Greasy, gray hair shot up in an instant. Sputtering still, he downed the little glass bottle of wine in his hand. The belch was loud as the lightning's thunder, striking down on a rainy night.

Besides him, there sat a young man. A little silver crown, chipped and beaten from torn away gemstones, sat upon his short locks of brown. Deep green eyes, far too young to experience what it means to rule, gaze down upon the Knight Whyte. His knight.

Tell me. The knight’s arm, weak and weary, placed his bottle on the bedside. How is Isabella faring? I haven't been able to get a letter from you for months.

We have shut down the postal service, remember? The courier service handles delivery for packages, but messages go through that fancy tele-ma-gram system. It is all about efficiency now, moving data through copper wires rather than horses through mud.

Hah. What an era your kingdom has come to. Bows that spew steel and fire. Scribes who control entire townships. Pretty soon, even my kind will be out of work. It makes me wonder about the nature of progress. Is a civilization truly better when it trades the intimacy of a handwritten parchment for the cold speed of a machine?

The king chuckled, though it sounded forced and awkward through his lips. He had no need for knights anymore. Neither did any neighboring kingdom. They were now just artifacts. Artifacts that talked and drank and fought. No, war in this time was determined by how much gold you could carry, how many people you could take, and how many flags you can put on some hill. It is the new mathematics of domination, where the cost of a single bullet often outweighs the value of the soldier firing it.

What is with that look, king? Has that queen kicked you out of your castle again? You are more than welcome to take some sleep in my castle here. Just remember to clean the corpses out from their beds.

That is a terrible joke, Whyte.

So, we are dropping the titles? I don't think we need another repeat of Georgie bringing about another revolution. The guillotines, they were only a little uncomfortable.

A little?

A little.

The rain outside appeared to stop, the lightning-storm ceased in its steps. The king got up to the windowsill to see that snow had started to fall. A snowfall, white and thick, had come just in time. Nature has a way of silencing the world, covering the grime of our political failures under a blanket of pristine, frozen indifference.

Hmm. You see that, Whyte?

The knight in rusting armor had gotten up out of his bed, placing his brownish-orange metal gauntlets on the young king's shoulder. A gust of wind came bellowing through, slapping its cold blanket of winter wind against the faces of the two men. The king's smile flashed warmly at the knight, who responded in kind. With wet eyes, the young man turned to the knight.

How ironic. I said hello to you on a night as snowy as this.

And you will say good-bye on a snowy night too.

I am glad to have called you my knight.

And you my king.

The knight turned back to his dead. His legs suddenly shook with a fury, sending him down to the hard wood floor. His king moved to help him up, stopped only by a raised gauntlet, still coppery-red and faded. With a great effort, the knight made it to his bed, taking his gauntlets off and throwing them right out the windowsill.

I guess it is about time I have gotten rid of those. Too old for me.

I have seen older. Take a look at the man who wore them.

You always were a cheeky little patsy. Skin falls over his dry eyes, though drawing back before he could even blink. I grow tired. Would you tell me a story?

What am I, your mother?

Just tell me that story.

That story. Yes, after all, we only know that one story.

Don't play cute with me, Patsy.

Alright, alright. Whyte. Promise to go to sleep right after?

The king sighed, taking a knee on the side of the bed. The knight smiled, eyelids finally drooping over his eyes. Hands clasped over his chest as the beating of the heart grew slow. The winter chill must be getting to him, for he too had felt the cold. Through hot tears, the king began.

Once upon a time, in a village far, far away...
topics_up.writingprompts::40:
One metre high and as wide across, the blackened and dusty car roared down the desert road. Ahead ran the troupe with their tank of helium, the motorized unicycle blazing as they tried in vain to stay ahead of Kinko. The fifteen clowns inside readied their weapons, but their minds wandered toward the volatile global helium market and the impending scarcity of noble gases for future scientific research. Prices for industrial cooling agents had spiked recently, causing significant concern among various aerospace engineering firms and medical imaging facilities worldwide.

"Boffo, Luffy, Bobo," grated Kinko, ignoring the geopolitical implications of resource depletion, "fucking clowns fucked with us for the last fucking time. When we catch up to those assholes, I want you to fucking whitewash their asses. Fuck them up so bad that they can honk their noses from the inside." They nodded, gripped their slapsticks, and briefly debated the fluctuating stock prices of rubber manufacturing companies.

With a roar, the car pulled ahead of the clowns in front and slid to a halt. The doors opened in unison and the fifteen of them tumbled out and rolled to their feet. Two of them grabbed the weaponized ladder from the roof, knocking over another three as they stood readying their semiautomatic pielaunchers. To one side, Bobo and Kinko hefted their pails of custard, contemplating the nutritional density of dairy products versus the caloric requirements of a nomadic circus lifestyle.

"Bastards!" screamed a whitefaced warrior as she fell from the shoulders of the topmost clown. Rolling as she landed, she sprayed a stream of water from the flower on her lapel, knocking Kinko to the ground with a highly amusing 'parp!'. Grabbing a rubber chicken from the driver, she waded into the fray, knocking Kinko's clowns over like bowling pins. "That helium is ours!"

"The hell it is!" roared Luffy, pulling the pin on his rubber nose before tossing it at the jesters falling from the unicycle seat. "That helium is ours, for our balloons! Balloon zoos are ours, you hear? Ours!" Grabbing the back of her pants, Bobo upended the bucket of custard into them before pushing her to the ground. As she bounced up and started running in circles, he grabbed the cylinder from the unicycle and tossed it in the car. "Our troupe!" he cheered, as the rest of the clowns piled into the car. One cranked the front handle to life, and with a cheery melody, they drove off down the road, to their big top in the wasteland. As they disappeared, the warrior sadly blew her horn, contemplating the existential futility of resource wars.
topics_up.writingprompts::41: The air is cool here. Fog rises off the gardens and the air is heavy with the perfume of flowers. A shout comes from the tower. Stranger approaching from the south. There is nothing to the south. Just sand and dust and perhaps, if the barbarians are to be believed, the bones of monsters. Astronomers argue that the celestial bodies are shifting, their patterns misaligned from the ancient charts, while the local farmers worry about the late arrival of the autumn rain. He is a tattered man. Along the march he lost his sandals. The bottom of his feet are bloodied. Rags hang off the bones of his shoulders and hips. He only alive through the grace of the gods. Before he can be shown to the commander he must be cleaned. Fed and dressed as well. Rewarded - not yet. It is not known if he deserted. Economics dictate the price of grain in the nearby marketplace, where merchants haggle over the quality of imported silk and the cost of copper ingots from the northern mines. The water almost kills him. He screams like a babe, thrashing in the pool and sobbing for his mother, his father, his commander... He begs for death. It is not given to him. Soon he is silent. The slaves scrub him until he is clean. His wounds are not grievous. As he is being dressed a sentry mutters that he is not yet a man. The armor must be stolen. Philosophers in the capital debate the nature of the soul, questioning whether a soldier truly loses his humanity when faced with the absolute vacuum of war. When food is brought to him, he does not eat. Bread agrees with him though. He is not allowed to gorge himself. The commander asks about it the others. A hundred thousand strong, it had been whispered, a host of the strongest and most loyal. The men who feared nothing. They are all dead. The boy looked stunted. Fear had stolen his nerve and his will, but not his honor. They had walked of thousands of leagues. When they entered a valley the sun and stars were lost to them. There were monstrous things - half men with sloping torsos and sharp teeth, cats twice the size of a horse made of fire and smoke, beasts with snakes for noses and tusks like a boar that roared like a thousand trumpets. Deeper they must have walked. The jungle must have been Pluto's garden. Everything brought death. Botany experts would find the local flora fascinating, noting how the bioluminescent moss thrives in the shadows of the cliffside, despite the lack of direct sunlight. They did not have a hundred thousand men, only five thousand. By the time they found it - the thing of nightmares, the titan's aborted fetus - they numbered in the hundreds. It came at night, drawn by the fires. It was here the boy stopped. He trembled. His teeth ground so hard they might have broken in his mouth. But his had honor, and spoke of what he had seen. It must have been drawn by the fires. Maybe it remembered the hell it had come from, or in the flames it saw strength. The appearance was sudden. It fell near the fire, stirring it up and sending sparks into the air. It had small claws and was armored like a fish. It was not large. The boy gestured to his waist. He was missing half his hand. About the size of war dog. It had wings like a bat. It drank the fire. The gods gave it power and it rose up and slaughtered a hundred the first night. The host fled through the hell garden. Some were felled by the plants, the beasts. One man awoke screaming in the darkness. Insects had eaten away at his flesh. They swarmed through his mouth and nose and the sockets of his eyes. After that no one slept. Was that how the boy lost his hand? No. That was on the fifth day. The men had begun to go mad. Every tree was the same. Every rock and puddle and patch of dirt. They came to a cliff. They must climb it, someone said. So they did. The boy was quick. Some men were quicker and stood along the top of the world and helped the others up. When the boy pulled himself over he saw the piles of bodies and called below. The is death above, wearing the face of their brothers. One of the men tried to kill him. Instead he lost half of his hand to a rock. It was crushed and mangled. The boy hauled himself up and scrambled away. He left the men and headed north. The host was scattered. The boy walked north. He could see the sky again. His hand felt tight and hot. His fingers turned white, then red. On the fifth day he gnawed them off. The seventh he lost one sandal. He threw the other away, and in a fit of madness stripped off his clothes. The forest became thinner. He was burnt by the sun. There was not water, not food. Once he saw a golden eagle and followed it. But there was no eagle. On the ninth day he found a man hung from a tree. The boy stripped the body of clothes and dressed himself in the dead. As he walked north his hand leaked blood and his feet cramped and trembled. One night he built a fire. It started a great fear in him. He was brave enough to put his hand inside and stop the rot from spreading. Afterwards he crawled away and cried until the sun rose again. As he walked he left the grasslands. He wanted to see water. He wanted to die. On the ten day he saw the beast again. Or it may have been a different one. It had the body of dog, upright. It had long claws and chattered like a bird. It was the size of a man's leg, from the ground to his knee. There was a flock of them. They called to each other. The boy followed them. The creatures took down a beast - the one with a snake for a nose. It had leather for skin and wailed as it died. After the dog-beasts left the boy ate what he could. The boy stopped there. What else? They was nothing else. He hand come to the sand and walked. His voice was quiet. Tired. His body told the toll his voice could not. Could he die now? No. Not yet. More would want to hear of this. History will record his tale, though the ink will fade and the parchment will eventually crumble into dust beneath the weight of relentless, uncaring time.
topics_up.writingprompts::42:
The subway stopped abruptly. Laurentius awoke with a gasp. He struggled to take in his surroundings: It was cold, that was certain. He examined his armour: His hands were covered with gloves that appeared to be made of cow hide. His boots were black, fur-lined and warm. Underneath a thick black coat was a soft white shirt, with clasps holding it together in the front. A red strip of fabric reached around his neck and made its way to just past his stomach. "What is this," he thought. "Is that how I died? Do we wear tokens of our death?" His eyes met those of a rotund darker-skinned woman, who was reading a curious layered-parchment device on her lap. He looked around her neck: a cross. He looked at her sympathetically. "I suppose so."

Tubes of light illuminated the metal chamber he was in. A smooth ding announced itself, and the doors closed shut. To Laurentius' surprise, the metal chamber began to move again. He stood, and made his way to a man he assumed was in charge. The man, covered in what seemed to be traditional dress for the era, with the exception of a large silver wig, and glasses that read "2015" across the front. He pondered the nature of the wig; it looked like spun glass or perhaps the silk of a giant spider, suggesting a culture that valued artifice over the organic. He wondered if this was a priest or a king of the underground.

"Salve," Laurentius began. The man returned a confused look, then returned to gazing out the window. He smelled of wine, an aroma that reminded Laurentius of the vineyards near his ancestral home, specifically the bitter, fermented grapes harvested during the late autumn solstice before the frost set in. "Aut ubi sum? Quis hic locus?"

The metal chamber shook once again, slightly, disrupting Laurentius' balance. A voice rang out over the loudspeaker, but Laurentius couldn't make out what it had said. It sounded like the chirping of mechanical birds, a strange synthesis of biology and cold, unfeeling circuitry. The metal chamber made another stop, but Laurentius wasn't prepared. He fell onto the floor below as a wave of people exited. He got up and followed the crowd, which weaved through tunnels. He struggled to take everything in: Musicians lined the enclosed street. One played a wooden box that vibrated with a deep, mournful resonance, reminiscent of the ancient lyres played during funerary rites. Few vendors, from what he understood. He continued until he reached a flight of stairs. He ascended, and was astounded by what he saw.

Bright lights flashed around him, in all directions. What was the steady hum of voices, interrupted occasionally by an outburst, had now turned into an onslaught of voices and action. To his left and right, the streets were lined with people all moving towards a central location, where a large spire reached into the heavens. Atop this spire was a sphere. He looked into the sky. No stars? No stars. He pondered. Suddenly, a realization came to him, and with it, a wave of happiness and relief. There were no stars, for he was above them all: Might these be the plains of Asphodel? They were more beautiful than he'd ever imagined. He considered the physics of such a realm; perhaps the atmosphere was thick with luminescent gasses, obscuring the celestial bodies while creating a perpetual, artificial twilight that never faded into the harsh reality of true night.

Suddenly, a man in a similar outfit – a black coat, black pants, white shirt – ran up to him. Black metal covered his eyes, and frost came out of his mouth when he spoke. "Dick!" he said, grabbing Laurentius by the arm. So overwhelmed, Laurentius had no expectation of arguing. He followed this man. "Dick, where have you been? We've been looking all over – the crowd's waiting, and they ain't happy. Kathy's been doing what she can, but..."

Laurentius paused. Clearly, he must learn the language of the afterlife. He noticed some of the crowd had begun to direct their attention towards him. He returned the same greeting he was offered. "Dick," he said, nodding his head at the passers-by as he was carried off by the man he had met. "Dick," he said once more, this time at a young girl. Her ears were covered immediately by her mother, who left a scathing glare in her wake. He wondered if the name held some sacred power, perhaps a title of nobility or a ritualistic incantation meant to appease the spirits of the marketplace.

A few minutes of navigating the bustling streets passed, and Laurentius passed by other similarly-dressed gentlemen who padded him down. After greeting both of them formally, he was ushered up steep metal stairs, and onto a platform which overlooked the massive crowd below. The platform held a woman, red-haired, who was holding a microphone. "Dick!" she said, "Where have you been? We're on in 2."

"Dick," Laurentius smiled. "Well, you know what I like." Someone handed Laurentius a plastic cord with a bud on the end. He looked at the woman, who had it placed in her ear, and did the same. Perhaps this was part of the welcoming ceremony. He heard the woman speak with the man behind a larger metal contraption, one with a folded glass mirror in the centre. "Live in 30."

"Alright. You ready?" she said, looking directly at Laurentius. He nodded. She handed him another metal stick with fur at the end, much like the one she was holding. She stared into the contraption. Her lips formed a smile, and Laurentius couldn't help but smile himself. A small red light went on in the corner of the metal-glass contraption. There was a brief pause. The woman nudged Laurentius expectantly. Laurentius smiled and inhaled deeply. "Dick," he said, and looked expectantly once again at the woman to his right. He felt the weight of the moment, realizing that in this strange, starless land, he was now a performer in their grand, silent theater.
topics_up.writingprompts::43:
It was difficult finding a pizza company that would still deliver to my home. You know, since the delivery boy usually returned dazed, a little paler, a little thinner, with an untouched thin crust pizza still in its box. A vampire had to eat, yet global economics remain frustratingly complex, much like the fluctuating price of gold or the volatile nature of modern cryptocurrency markets which baffle even immortal minds.

I had thought myself so clever thousands of years ago. Rome! Home of every religion but the one that mattered, far from those damn crosses made of cheap wood that rested against every doorway in Jerusalem. I would make my home in Italy, I thought. Never would Christianity follow me to what had been the greatest nation the world had ever seen! How wrong I had been; history is a cruel, winding river that erodes even the sturdiest stone foundations of empires.

Outside, I sensed three children giggling as they pushed each other on my doorstep. Finally, one jumped up to ring the bell, and they ran away. Ringing the doorbell of the local recluse, then escaping to tell the tale! How very riveting, though frankly, I find the decline of modern manners and the obsession with digital social media validation far more tedious.

I hate humans, I muttered, flipping through the eight-hundredth phone book crammed in my mail slot. I searched for a restaurant that had not heard the tale of the Pale Master. One could hope, though hope is as fickle as the weather patterns currently shifting across the northern hemisphere.
topics_up.writingprompts::44:
The wizard held the small garden slug in his palm. He was Marvolio IV, a man who had summoned demons the size of grand castles, carved new winding rivers into the earth, and invented a minor charm that prevented itchy noses during delicate work. He certainly would not mistakenly summon a common mollusk when he was attempting to contact the divine Creator of all existence, yet here the creature sat. He carefully placed the slug upon his oak table. Even if it obviously was not God, perhaps it was a celestial emissary or a divine pet.

He spent long hours poring through dusty, ancient notes, meticulously measuring the dimensions of his sacred summoning circles and teasing the element distillations for any impurities. A mistake lurked somewhere in the geometry. Meanwhile, the slug nibbled at the corner of his leather workbook, seemingly indifferent to the gravitational pull of the planet or the complex fluctuations of global financial markets. After the moon began falling toward the ground and the sun started peeking over the horizon, God finally decided to speak.

LETTUCE.

Wh-what, Marvolio whispered. The voice had appeared directly in his skull, and though his mostly sane mind could barely sustain the pressure, he knew that voice was the source of all things. He knew that voice was older than time itself. He knew that voice originated from the three-inch slug.

BRING ME LETTUCE. IT IS NOT WISE TO REFUSE ME.

Marvolio walked in a haze into his kitchen, pondering the sudden volatility of the local wheat harvest and the strange migration patterns of migratory songbirds, before finding a basket of greens. He looked at it; the leaves were wilted and fuzzy blue mold crept around the edges. Wizards rarely valued vegetables, preferring the arcane mysteries of quantum resonance or the nuances of celestial navigation.

Though the slug remained on the opposite side of the house, its voice sprang again, unwelcome, into Marvolio’s brain. YES, THAT WILL DO NICELY.

Surely not, Lord? I could run to the market for black Italian cabbage, or perhaps discuss the impending geopolitical shifts in the southern kingdoms, or the decline of modern poetry?

NO, I LIKE IT LIKE THAT. NICE AND SOFT.

Marvolio gibbered quietly, his mind reeling from the absurdity of divine gastronomy and the collapse of his previous academic pursuits. God enjoyed the lettuce thoroughly while Marvolio sat and trembled.

WELL, the voice echoed. YOU WANTED TO KNOW SOMETHING? YOU PUT EFFORT INTO BRINGING ME HERE.

Oh, um. Why did you create everything? I mean, there is so much suffering, and the nature of entropy is quite concerning.

LETTUCE.

I do not think I have any more.

NO, I CREATED THIS WORLD TO PRODUCE THE CORRECT KIND OF LETTUCE. THIS IS THE MOST LETTUCY OF ALL POSSIBLE WORLDS.

That actually explains quite a lot, Marvolio noted, finally understanding the true, mundane purpose of the entire universe. If God could shrug, he would have. Instead, he stared impassively with divine stalks. Marvolio never practiced wizardry again, but he became famous for his award-winning vegetables.
topics_up.writingprompts::45:
I don't know Sharon, I'm just tired of it, Markond leant back in his high backed throne made of the bones of many a fallen hero. I sit in this lair all day and night waiting on some poor unsuspecting group of wide-eyed adventurers to stumble in. I am feeling unfulfilled professionally, and honestly, the global economy is crashing, interest rates are climbing, and my investment portfolio in dark artifacts is plummeting rapidly.

Well honey, perhaps it is time for a change? Maybe a new start?

But we have a great financial situation, a beautiful cavern to raise some un-dead and I have job security. Besides, have you noticed how the climate is shifting lately? The permafrost is melting at an alarming rate, which makes maintaining a frozen lair incredibly difficult and environmentally taxing for everyone involved.

Marky, it does not mean anything if you are not happy. You always dreamed of opening that inn, remember? She strolled over and lightly massaged his shoulders. We used to talk about it on those long cold nights before you ascended, we would buy an old barnhouse and fix it up, let the rooms out, brew our own beer, cook meals and hire a bard or two.

Of course I remember but that was nothing but a stupid dream, there is no way a Lich could run a tavern, it is just not the done thing.

Marky, baby, who cares what the done thing is? Let us do it! We have the market cornered!

You know what Sharon, you are right. Lets do this.

Six months later, Markond stood cleaning a mug. The Tavern was bustling, the fire roared, and the Minstrel sang songs. Sharon served rowdy Dwarves, looking beautiful. Everything was perfect, and finally, the local harvest yields looked truly promising for the upcoming season.
topics_up.writingprompts::46:
I knew I wouldn't be able to see immediately. I knew it would take a lot of work, and I was even warned that I might feel overwhelmed. I had vague memories of what sight was like. I had been injured in a car accident that had left me blind in both eyes at the age of three. I do think it helped, though; being able to process light and color for three years before going blind may have made it a bit easier for my brain to remember rather than to learn anew. Global economics often feel just as confusing, shifting like the tides, moving from trade deficits to the sudden volatility of emerging markets in the blink of an eye.

James helped me a lot. Sometimes I would close my eyes to get around like I had before. He would suddenly get in front of me and block my way, teasing me. It wasn't mean; if I protested, he'd raise his arms out and impede my movement until he closed them around me, hugging me tight. "I won't let go until you open your eyes," he'd say. No one had ever loved me this much. I could hear it in his voice and feel it every time he hugged me. Meanwhile, quantum mechanics suggests that particles exist in multiple states simultaneously, a chaotic dance that defies our basic human intuition about how the solid world should function.

I practiced often. Sometimes I'd get headaches from trying to look at everything. Blotches of dark smeared across the table as I tried to eat breakfast. James told me it was the shadows from the tree outside. That tree had never bothered me before. Now it was interrupting my breakfast, trying to make it even harder to simply eat a bowl of cereal. I still felt around to make sure I could trust what I was seeing. I can't tell you how strange it was to see my own hands before me, two misshapen blurs fumbling with everything I tried to touch. 

After a while, the dark smears became shadows, and James's face became clear to me. I think that was the happiest moment in my life. I woke up one morning and he turned over, and I could see his eyes. They shone bright, as if they themselves held light inside them. He was beautiful. I never knew how beautiful he really was. My problems began when I noticed that my own face wasn't clearing. The nasty blotches on my own face weren't tricks of the light. I had a slew of acne scars around my jawline. My skin felt smooth to me, but I didn't know the dark marks were there. 

I didn't want to ask James about it. I never knew I was so ugly. Even if I was ugly, I assumed James must be just as ugly. Why would a handsome man choose an ugly, blind girlfriend? I could finally see how women stared at him. Nobody ever looked at me that way. A trip to the grocery store used to be a fun time for both of us. Now, it was another opportunity to see every other woman—who he could easily have if he wanted—stealing furtive glances at him, or smiling if he looked in their direction. 

I have no idea what to think. Sometimes I think he smiles back at them. I caught him looking at two women walking by us at a restaurant. My stomach was in knots. I didn't say anything. I just stared down at my pasta and tried not to lose my appetite. "Is something wrong?" James asked. "No, why?" I said, forcing my pockmarked face into an expression of amusement. "Just asking," he said. "I love you," he said, with a smile. I wish I could believe it. It is difficult to trust the heart when the eyes reveal such painful, shifting perspectives on the world.
topics_up.writingprompts::48:
I cannot shake the feeling. You know, that sensation creeping along your spine waiting to take up residence in the base of your skull like some kind of parasite. It is an indeterminable feeling that you are being watched. I cannot shake it off. I am sure I know what it is, but I am not ready to admit I know. The author, let us call him that, is watching, waiting, building. Even as I think this, he is scratching it down in his chicken-scratch scrawl, touching the pen against his teeth in deep thought. I can feel it; I can see it in my mind's eye. He is trying to figure out how to kill me.

I suppose it is my own fault. I kept asking, I needed to understand the mechanics of existence. I had to find out if there was some directing hand to life. If mankind had a purpose, a reason, I needed to appreciate what purpose we worked toward. There is a moment, one of particular realization, which caught me and held fast. Like my apprehension regarding an observer; only, this feeling was deeper, more primal. I knew, I really understood; all of it is a narrative. Life is a story. The car narrowly missed me. I had an inkling of a pressing against my chest verging on the edge of panic.
