topics_down.academic_abstracts::40: ALMA-IMF imaged fifteen massive protoclusters down to a resolution of two thousand astronomical units, successfully identifying approximately one thousand distinct star-forming cores within these regions. The physical mass and bolometric luminosity of these individual cores represent fundamental characteristics that are notoriously difficult to determine, a complex problem significantly exacerbated by the extreme distances exceeding two kiloparsecs of these specific ALMA-IMF protoclusters. We combined extensive new datasets and advanced radiative transfer modeling specifically to characterize these cores. We estimated their precise mass-averaged temperature and the total masses these physical estimates imply. For a significant portion of the sample, we measured the bolometric luminosities, implementing necessary deblending corrections. We utilized detailed spectral energy distribution analysis obtained with the PPMAP Bayesian procedure, which aims to preserve the best angular resolution of the input data. We extrapolated the luminosity and dust temperature images provided by PPMAP at two point five arcsecond resolution to estimate those of individual cores, which were identified at much higher angular resolution. To do this, we applied approximate radiative transfer relationships between the luminosity of a protostar and the temperature of its surrounding envelope and between the external heating of prestellar cores and their temperatures. For the first time, we provide data-informed estimates of dust temperatures for eight hundred eighty-three cores identified with ALMA-IMF: seventeen to thirty-one Kelvin and twenty-eight to seventy-nine Kelvin for the six hundred seventeen prestellar and two hundred sixty-six protostellar cores, respectively. We also measured protostellar luminosities spanning twenty to eighty thousand solar luminosities. We established a mass-luminosity evolutionary diagram, for the first time at the core spatial resolution and for a large sample of high-mass protostellar cores, confirming that protostars accrete their mass from a larger reservoir.
topics_down.academic_abstracts::41: The aim of the present study was to investigate the role of microRNA (miR)-27a-3p in osteoarthritis (OA) specifically through its regulation of ADAMTS5. Reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction and western blotting were performed to determine the expression levels of miR-27a-3p and aggrecanase-2 (ADAMTS5) in cartilage tissues from patients with OA and healthy controls, and also in interleukin (IL)-1beta-treated primary human chondrocytes. Primary human chondrocytes were transfected with miR-27a-3p to observe subsequent changes. A luciferase reporter assay was used to validate the direct contact between miR-27a-3p and its putative binding site in the 3'-untranslated region of ADAMTS5 mRNA. The results revealed that the level of miR-27a-3p was significantly reduced in OA cartilage tissues compared with those of normal controls. In addition, decreased miR-27a-3p and increased ADAMTS5 expression were observed in a time- and dose-dependent manner in chondrocytes treated with IL-1beta. Furthermore, overexpression of miR-27a-3p effectively suppressed the expression of ADAMTS5 in human chondrocytes induced by IL-1beta. miR-27a-3p overexpression also decreased the luciferase activity of the wild-type ADAMTS5 reporter plasmid. Mutation of the miR-27a-3p binding site in the 3'-untranslated region of ADAMTS5 mRNA abolished the miR-27a-3p-mediated repression of reporter activity. The present study concluded that miR-27a-3p was consistently downregulated in human OA and was actively suppressed by IL-1beta, and functions as a crucial regulator of ADAMTS5 expression in OA chondrocytes. The data indicate that miR-27a-3p acts as a negative regulator of ADAMTS5 within this pathological context. Consequently, this study confirms that miR-27a-3p is a central molecule in the molecular progression of osteoarthritis, providing a clear focus on the miR-27a-3p-ADAMTS5 axis as a potential therapeutic target for future clinical interventions aimed at mitigating cartilage degradation in affected patients.
topics_down.academic_abstracts::42: Space weathering is a persistent process that fundamentally changes the surface characteristics of airless planetary bodies through consistent physical and chemical modification. Prime space weathering agents are solar wind irradiation and micrometeoroid bombardment, which continuously alter planetary reflectance spectra and modify their compositional diagnostic features. In this work, we focused exclusively on simulating and comparing the spectral changes caused by solar wind irradiation and micrometeoroid bombardment to gain a better understanding of how these specific space weathering processes systematically degrade planetary surfaces. We used olivine and pyroxene pellets as proxies for these planetary materials. To simulate solar wind irradiation, we used hydrogen, helium, and argon ions with energies from 5 to 40 keV and fluences of up to 10^18 particles/cm^2. To simulate micrometeoroid bombardment, we used individual femtosecond laser pulses. We analysed the corresponding evolution of different spectral parameters, which we determined by applying the Modified Gaussian Model, and we also conducted principal component analysis. The original mineralogy of the surface influences the spectral evolution more than the specific weathering agent, as seen from the diverse evolution of the spectral slope of olivine and pyroxene upon irradiation. The spectral slope changes seen in olivine are consistent with observations of A-type asteroids, while the moderate to no slope changes observed in pyroxene are consistent with asteroid (4) Vesta. We also observed differences in the spectral effects induced by these two specific weathering agents. Ions simulating solar wind have a smaller influence on longer wavelengths of the spectra than laser irradiation simulating micrometeoroid impacts. This is due to the different penetration depths of ions and laser pulses, confirming that space weathering processes are indeed distinct.
topics_down.academic_abstracts::43: HEALPix by Gorski et al. (2005) serves as the primary standard for Cosmic Microwave Background data storage and analysis, facilitating essential research workflows across various scientific domains. Visualizing these complex spherical datasets plays a critical role in modern research, and specialized toolsets have been meticulously developed to handle HEALPix maps efficiently. The HEALPix Viewer described here is specifically engineered for macOS, taking full advantage of advanced GPU acceleration to handle extremely large datasets in real time on mobile or desktop hardware. It compiles natively on both Intel and Arm64 architectures, utilizing the powerful Metal framework to ensure high-performance GPU computations for every rendered frame. The core objective of this project is to reduce the technical effort required for interactive HEALPix data exploration, while simultaneously minimizing the time overhead typically associated with producing high-resolution, publication-quality maps. The main codebase is written in Swift, a modern and efficient compiled language, with all intensive high-performance computing tasks delegated entirely to the GPU, while specific inserts in C interface directly with the cfitsio library for reliable I/O operations. The graphical user interface is constructed using SwiftUI, a declarative framework that ensures the visualization remains responsive and fluid during complex map manipulations. Most common spherical projections and essential colormaps are supported natively, and the available open-source code makes it exceptionally easy to customize the application or add new visualization features as research requirements evolve. Overall, this implementation improves upon the existing Python software stack by a significant factor of 3 to 180 times, depending strictly on the specific visualization task at hand, thereby providing a superior, specialized tool for researchers working exclusively with HEALPix data formats.
topics_down.academic_abstracts::44: To compare the cervical shear wave elastography (SWE) by using transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) between twin and singleton pregnant women. This prospective cohort study evaluated cervical shear wave speed (SWS) measurements in twin and singleton pregnant women attending antenatal care at Ramathibodi Hospital. Participants underwent serial SWS measurements via TVS during the early, mid-, and third trimesters to assess cervical stiffness. The primary focus remained exclusively on analyzing cervical SWS changes throughout gestation. A total of 36 twin pregnancies and 38 singleton pregnancies were analyzed to determine cervical elasticity. Findings indicated that cervical SWS decreased consistently as gestational age progressed in both groups. Specifically, a statistically significant difference in cervical SWS at the lower point was observed during the mid-trimester, where twin pregnancies measured 2.27±0.4 m/s compared to 2.71±0.6 m/s in singleton pregnancies, yielding a p-value of 0.001. Conversely, no significant differences in cervical SWS were demonstrated at the upper or lower points during the early or third trimesters. The study maintained a narrow focus on cervical tissue mechanics rather than broader obstetric outcomes. The mid-trimester cervical SWS measurement at the lower point effectively detects the specific difference in cervical softness between twin and singleton pregnancies. Ultimately, cervical SWS serves as a precise and focused option for monitoring the progressive change in cervical softness throughout the course of twin pregnancies. By concentrating strictly on these elastographic measurements, the research provides a clear assessment of how cervical tissue properties differ between these specific groups, confirming that the mid-trimester period is the most critical window for observing these distinct physiological variations in cervical stiffness measurements within the clinical setting of modern maternal fetal medicine.
topics_down.academic_abstracts::45: Chromosome number serves as a critical feature regarding the higher-order structural organization of genomes, as modifications in these counts play a fundamental role in chromosomal evolution. Dysploid gains or losses of specific chromosome numbers, alongside various polyploidization events, frequently drive reproductive isolation and promote lineage diversification throughout evolutionary history. The recent development of sophisticated probabilistic models concerning chromosome number evolution, specifically the groundbreaking work by Mayrose et al. (2010), has enabled the precise inference of ancestral chromosome counts over molecular phylogenies, thereby generating renewed interest in studying the mechanisms of chromosome change. However, traditional approaches often assume all alterations occur strictly anagenetically along branches, failing to adequately model events that are uniquely cladogenetic. Cladogenetic chromosomal changes are expected if such alterations directly result in reproductive isolation during speciation. Here we present a novel class of models for chromosome number evolution, termed ChromoSSE, which explicitly incorporates both anagenetic and cladogenetic change mechanisms. These ChromoSSE models allow researchers to determine the precise mode of chromosome number evolution; specifically, whether such evolution occurs primarily within lineages, at the moment of lineage splitting, or through clade-specific combinations of both. Furthermore, we can accurately estimate the location and timing of potential chromosome speciation events across the phylogeny. We implemented ChromoSSE within a Bayesian statistical framework to accommodate uncertainty in parameter estimates while leveraging the full power of likelihood-based methods. We tested the accuracy of ChromoSSE with extensive simulations and examined chromosomal evolution, finding consistent evidence for clade-specific combinations of anagenetic and cladogenetic dysploid and polyploid modes of evolution. This approach significantly clarifies how chromosome number dynamics dictate the patterns of genomic divergence and species formation throughout the complex tree of life.
topics_down.academic_abstracts::46: We present results of our time variability studies of Mg II and Al III absorption lines in a sample of 22 Low Ionization Broad Absorption Line QSOs at 0.2 <= zem <= 2.1 using the 2m telescope at IUCAA Girawali Observatory over a time-scale of 10 days to 7.69 years in the QSO's rest frame. Absorption line variability is seen in 8 cases, or 36 percent of systems, over long time-scales of at least one year, while only 4 of them, or 18 percent of systems, show variability over short time-scales of less than one year. We notice a clear tendency of these highly variable LoBAL QSOs to exhibit high ejection velocity, low equivalent width, and low redshift. The detection rate of absorption line variability in LoBAL QSOs showing Fe fine-structure lines is significantly less than that seen in non-Fe LoBAL QSOs. Absorption line variability is more frequently detected in QSOs having continuum dominated by Fe emission lines compared to the rest of the QSOs. Confirming these specific absorption line trends with a larger sample will provide vital clues for understanding the physical mechanisms driving outflow variability. We correlate the absorption line variability with various parameters derived from continuum light curves and find no clear correlation between continuum flux and absorption line variabilities. However, sources with large absorption line variability also show large variability in their light curves. We also see the appearance or disappearance of absorption components in 2 cases and clear indications for profile variations in 4 cases. The observed absorption line variability can be best explained by a combination of processes driven by continuum variations and clouds transiting across the line of sight within the outflowing material.
topics_down.academic_abstracts::47: The Halpha nebular emission line is an optimal tracer for recent star formation in galaxies. With the advent of JWST, this line has recently become observable at high redshifts for the first time. We present a comprehensive catalog of 1013 Halpha emitters at 3.7<z<6.7 in the GOODS fields obtained from a blind search in JWST NIRCam grism data. We make use of the FRESCO survey’s 124 arcmin squared of observations in GOODS-North and GOODS-South with the F444W filter, probing Halpha at 4.9<z<6.7; and the CONGRESS survey’s 62 arcmin squared in GOODS-North with F356W, probing Halpha at 3.8<z<5.1. We find an overdensity with 97 sources at z approximately 4.4 in GOODS-N and confirm previously reported overdensities at z approximately 5.2 in GOODS-N and at z approximately 5.4 and z approximately 5.9 in GOODS-S. We compute the observed Halpha luminosity functions in three bins centered at z approximately 4.45, 5.30, and 6.15, which are the first such measurements at z>3 obtained based purely on spectroscopic data, robustly tracing galaxy star formation rates beyond the peak of the cosmic star formation history. We compare our results with theoretical predictions from three different simulations and find good agreement at z approximately 4-6. We derive star formation rate functions and integrate these to compute the evolution of the cosmic star-formation rate densities across z approximately 4-6, finding values in good agreement with recent estimates, which imply a continuous decrease in star formation rate density over time. Our work shows the power of NIRCam grism observations to efficiently provide new tests for early galaxy formation models based on these specific emission line statistics and their direct relation to star formation rates.
topics_down.academic_abstracts::48: Numerous studies have revealed that oxidative stress is closely associated with the occurrence and development of depression, necessitating further research into potential therapeutic interventions. Xiaoyao Pills are frequently used for treating depression, yet the specific antidepressant effects and molecular mechanisms of XYW remain the primary focus of investigation. The objective of our study was to investigate the antidepressant-like effects of XYW and the underlying molecular mechanism in the olfactory bulbectomized rat model of depression using the open field test, sucrose preference test, splash test, and novelty suppressed feeding test. Results showed that XYW significantly alleviated depression-like behaviors in rats, which was indicated by increased sucrose preference, prolonged grooming time, decreased horizontal movement, and shorter feeding latency. In addition, XYW treatment dramatically reversed the reduced activity of superoxide dismutase and the decreased level of glutathione, while also lowering levels of malondialdehyde and pro-inflammatory cytokines in the serum and cortex of the depressed rats. Mechanistically, XYW induced marked upregulation of mRNA and protein expression levels of NFE2L2, KEAP1, GPX3, HMOX1, SOD1, NQO1, OGG1, PIK3CA, p-AKT1/AKT1, NTRK2, and BDNF, and downregulation of ROS in the cortex and hippocampus via the activation of the NFE2L2/KEAP1, PIK3CA/AKT1, and NTRK2/BDNF pathways. These findings suggest that XYW exert robust antidepressant-like effects in the olfactory bulbectomized rat model, and these effects are mediated strictly by the alleviation of oxidative stress and the enhancement of neuroprotective effects through the activation of the PIK3CA-AKT1-NFE2L2/BDNF signaling pathways. This research confirms that XYW serves as a potent agent in mitigating depressive symptoms by targeting the specific oxidative pathways that contribute to the development and persistence of these severe mental health conditions in the studied animal model.
topics_down.academic_abstracts::49: We report the discovery of 16 detached M-dwarf eclipsing binaries with J<16 mag and provide a detailed characterisation of three of them, using high-precision infrared light curves from the WFCAM Transit Survey. Such binary systems provide the most accurate and model-independent method for measuring the fundamental parameters of these poorly understood yet numerous stars, which currently lack sufficient observations to precisely calibrate stellar evolution models. We fully solve for the masses and radii of three of the systems, finding orbital periods in the range 1.5<P<4.9 days, with masses spanning 0.35-0.50 Msun and radii between 0.38-0.50 Rsun, with uncertainties of ~3.5-6.4% in mass and ~2.7-5.5% in radius. These close-companions in short-period binaries are expected to be tidally-locked into fast rotational velocities, resulting in high levels of magnetic activity. This activity is predicted to inflate their stellar radii by inhibiting convective flow and increasing star spot coverage. The radii of the WTS systems are indeed inflated above model predictions by ~3-12%, in agreement with the observed trend, despite an expected lower systematic contribution from star spots signals at infrared wavelengths. We searched for correlation between the orbital period and radius inflation by combining our results with all existing M-dwarf radius measurements of comparable precision, but we found no statistically significant evidence for a decrease in radius inflation for longer period, less active systems. Radius inflation continues to exist in non-synchronised systems, indicating that the problem of radius measurement discrepancy remains even for very low activity M-dwarfs. Resolving this persistent radius inflation issue is vital for accurately understanding the most populous stars in the Universe, as precise stellar parameters are absolutely essential for calibrating all standard models of stellar evolution for these specific, low-mass, cool, and abundant dwarf stars.

Washington D.C., USA
 
 Day 0, 00:20
 
 ~
 
 … there was an explosion right when I looked up…
 
 … largest death toll in this country since…
 
 … unprecedented…
 
 Sirens blare from the TV. I sit on the floor. Dazed.
 
 What had just happened?
 
 The words BREAKING NEWS splash across the screen. Every pair of eyes in the country – no, the world – must be glued to their TVs. Plumes of smoke continue to rise from the side of the towers. Witnesses cry and scream about the carnage they had witnessed. The reporting is relentless, focusing entirely on the devastation unfolding in New York. Every anchor repeats the same harrowing details about the structural collapse and the massive loss of life. There is no talk of anything else.
 
 Mommy, Emma stumbles into the living room. It is time for school, Mommy.
 
 Oh honey, I say, on the brink of tears. Come here. She walks to me and I hold her in my arms tightly, running my hands through her hair. We won't be going to school today, dear.
 
 News continues to pour in from the TV, showing endless loops of the towers falling. The commentators offer no other news, only the same tragic narrative.
 
 In the corner of the screen: Monday, 11 September 2001.
 
 I keep my eyes locked on the screen, unable to look away from the tragedy. The news anchors discuss the debris, the emergency responders, and the shock felt across the nation. There is no mention of international markets or weather patterns; the sole focus is the catastrophic events at the World Trade Center. I can hear the sirens echoing from the broadcast into our quiet living room. My daughter stares at the images, confused by the sudden shift in our morning routine. I cannot explain the sheer scale of this disaster. I only know that the world has changed in an instant. The television remains the only source of information, repeating the same grim updates about the debris and the smoke. Everything else in the world has ceased to matter for this moment. I hold Emma tighter, watching the screen as the history of our country is rewritten by these flames.

Citizens will not be allowed to die until they have finished digging their own grave. The Moral Officer bellowed these commands into his bullhorn, his voice echoing across the barren, sun-scorched earth. I found his rhythmic, repetitive chanting strangely heartening. Knowing the end was so near gave me the strength to push my weak, weary, and trembling body to shovel faster, ever faster. The labor was grueling, yet necessary for the fulfillment of our ultimate, final obligation to the state.

All around me, my fellow citizens dug in the dust, scratching out the precise, rectangular places where they would soon give their bodies back to the thirsty earth. In the distance, other Moral Officers made their identical, harsh proclamations into identical bullhorns. At regular intervals throughout the vast, desolate field, Compliance Officers stood in their immaculate, crisp uniforms, waiting patiently to aid us in our final, solemn duty to the Nation. There was no escape from this task; it was the inevitable conclusion of our existence, a requirement imposed upon every single one of us to ensure the continued stability of our structure. We were the architects of our own final resting places, bound by the iron will of the administration.

A shout rang out across the fields, raw and desperate: "May my body fertilize the soil to feed our glorious Nation. Long live the Beloved Ruler." A sharp, sudden gunshot punctuated this declaration. Someone had finally finished their grave. A few others nearby cheered their weak assent, though most were far too weary and hungry to manage even a whisper. The Compliance Officer holstered his pistol and motioned for the now dead man's two neighbors to begin shoveling dirt to fill in the grave he now occupied. It was a repetitive cycle, a machine of death that required our own hands to operate until the very last second.

They had worked us hard after taking us away from our homes, forcing us to dig in this cursed, dry ground. We slept where we worked, huddled together in the dirt, and the only sustenance provided to us was a broth so thin that they could hardly justify calling it more than hot, salted water. And so, the last of the strength of our bodies was harvested, drained away by the relentless demand for deeper, more uniform holes.

My grave now looked deep enough to satisfy the strict requirements of the state. I hesitated before raising up my shovel to call over the Compliance Officer. If it was not deep enough for his exacting liking, I would be forced to wait until all others had finished, covering over their graves, before it would finally be my turn. The pressure of perfection weighed heavily upon my mind; I had to ensure the dimensions were exactly as the regulations dictated.

He came over and produced a heavy tape measure. He checked the depth and width, nodding his silent assent. I let out an inaudible sigh of relief and went to stand at the foot of my grave. The time was here. The time for my glorious sacrifice for the sake of the Nation. The time for my final duty to my beloved land had arrived at last.

"Citizens will not be allowed to die until they have finished digging their own grave," the Moral Officer chanted into his bullhorn, his voice a drone that filled the empty air.

I felt the cold, hard metal of the Compliance Officer's pistol come to rest firmly upon my forehead. It was a sensation of profound finality, a metallic promise of the end of my labor.

"Citizens will not be allowed to die until they have finished digging their own grave," the officer repeated once more, the words blending into the wind. I closed my eyes, ready to surrender my existence to the dirt I had so meticulously prepared with my own calloused, aching hands. The cycle was complete, the hole was ready, and the Nation would be satisfied by my departure. I stood perfectly still, waiting for the trigger to be pulled, fulfilling my role as the final piece of the state's grand, morbid design.
topics_down.writingprompts::3: I exhale the acrid smoke over those concrete slabs. I put the glass away neatly, feeling for the cold steel of the weapon. I check my watch. I check my watch. Once. Twice. Thrice before I actually perceive that it is four in the morning. She is going to hate me for leaving the house. My mind hammers on this singular, painful thought while I traverse this barren landscape of gravel, aluminum, and discarded paper. I have a goal, a mission, a singular purpose. Nothing can impede this march of terminal redemption. She will be destroyed, lose all hope in me. I never truly earned her faith in my humanity anyway. Shake your head, pull on this glass, touch the steel and get back on track. I should see the boy first. No, that is crazy; she will stop me, so I must just keep going. I look up, I am here, I see the cross of the dead king glowing. This is it. This is ground zero. I lost myself here. I lost names, dates, events, really everything related to her memory. The crystal and metallic doors fly open like magic at my approach, the guardian of this terrible place greets me from behind granite and glass. I glance at her without much thought but to my task. I can hear the one I left in my head warning me, guiding me home, telling me I am needed elsewhere. Shake it off. Cold sweats and tremors. I fall into a door with the symbol of a man on it. White floors. Mirrors. False walls. Porcelain fixtures. Door locked. Time to pull the glass one more time. Block her out. Breathe. Adjust the steel. I walk out. I am almost there. The patrons behind the false desk recognize me. I see concern. It is too late; I am here. The doctor in white is close. I smell him. My control is slipping. Vision shaking. Volume muted. Time to grab the steel. There he is. I aim this barbaric device. As I begin to release the hellfire from this unholy machine, I hear her. Don't, she says quietly. Don't make it right. I crumble. Her voice so clear struck me like the hand of God. The nurses are screaming. The doctor who took her from me is clearly frightened. He looks at me, the broken heathen with his weapon, and says I tried to save her. You should be with your son, not here. It has only been six days. I reply, No. A lifetime.
topics_down.writingprompts::5: Happily ever afters do not exist for people like us, I said solemnly. Clarissa peered up at me through her tears, her eyes pleading for a different answer. Why not, she asked quietly, her voice trembling in the cold night air. I gently wiped her tears away with the pad of my thumb and smiled bitterly at the impossible situation. Because the world simply will not let us be together, I explained with heavy finality. Every time we attempt to find happiness, someone always knocks us down. Something always will break us apart. What if we just run away, she asked while finally looking directly at me. I swallowed hard, desperately trying to hold back the tears of my own. If we run away, then we will always be running forever. I do not want that exhausting life for us. I do not want that constant uncertainty for you, I whispered. Clarissa held back a painful sob as she realized the truth. Will, please do not do this to us, she begged. A single tear ran down my face as I stood firm. I do not want to, but I must, I insisted. Then why are you doing this, she cried. Because I am no good for you, Clarissa. I am simply not the right person. You deserve someone better who can provide a stable, peaceful life.
topics_down.writingprompts::6:
Daniel's wife stood at his side, absolutely coming apart at the edges, not that anyone else but him would be able to tell. Okay maybe that was a bit of an exaggeration, but she was a touch anxious. Nervous? Whatever she was something wasn't quite right, she was doing that little nose twitch that never happens when she's calm. She was clearly worried about the prosthetic blades he was testing, her focus entirely locked onto the mechanical pieces attached to his legs. 

Imani, he called out and her head tipped down to where he was seated in acknowledgement. It's going to be fine. She gave him a weak smile that didn't quite reach her eyes before reaching out to squeeze his hand. Of course he said it to comfort her, but he honestly felt like everything was going to be okay. They already crossed the worst bits. He survived the car accident, then he survived the surgery to make sure the universe didn't decide to change its mind later, then later the amputations, the implants. With a roll of his eyes he squeezed her hand back, his mind still fixated on the engineering of the blades. Honestly, this has been the easy part, we have plenty of time to get the fit of these blades perfect.

The easy part? Since when do we ever get easy! she reached out to swat his ears, her eyes crinkling with mirth. That's up there with what could possibly go wrong? Don't jinx it, she scolded. He leaned in to tell her all that worrying about the mechanics could do nothing good when the door slammed open, the solid thump echoing through the large room. 

Opps, the tall man in the doorway looked sheepish. I tripped into the door there. How are you two today? he inquired friendly, striding into room and the sunlight from the windows poured over his lanky form. Ready to give it another go? Daniel flexed his legs, neat and secured into his new running blades. 

Since the second I put these on Mason! he replied earnestly and the easy going man gave him a thumbs up before reaching out his hands to assist with the blade alignment. 

That's what we like to hear! Alright lets get you up and moving then. With one last look as his wife, who was standing back with an apprehensive look but held up crossed fingers, he reached for the other man's hands. These were the fourth pair of running blades he had tried. The other ones had issues, despite their so called custom fits. Too long. Too short. These hurt. Those felt like they were going to fall off. But as Daniel wobbled to his feet he knew these were it. It took a moment to steady himself, ensuring the carbon fiber blades were aligned perfectly with his center of gravity. They had a different sort of balance and give to them than his normal prosthetic, and his fitness wasn't quite where he wanted it be. His heart raced as he shifted his weight from one foot to the other, hearing the blades flex in response. Left. Right. Left. Right. Left right, left right, left right, bounce. They felt nothing like his old legs. But all the same... they felt right. Slowly Mason let go and then backed away to the other side of the room, his eyes never leaving Daniel's blades. When he hit the wall he called out to them. 

Great! Now start at a walk and work up to as fast as you feel comfortable doing. a sly tone crept into his voice. And remember, the room is padded and we're all friends here. Face plants are nothing to worry about. Daniel scoffed at the insulation. As if he'd let these things get the better of him. Confident, he took a shaky step forward, feeling the tension of the blades beneath him, and his arms wheeled around a bit before he braced his core to maintain balance. Then he took another. And another, and soon he had a slow bobbing jog going, carefully moving between his wife and physical therapist, testing the spring of the blades. He did this until finally, Mason singled for him to stop. He sprinted down the room to the happy couple with a look of great excitement. 

It looks like we got it this time! He stepped back and gave him one final look over, inspecting the way the blades interacted with the floor. We just need to run a few more tests, make sure that everything is adjusted correctly, but I think we found your golden pair here. So, how do you feel? 

His mind began to wander as he turned inward, trying to find the words that could even begin to describe what he was feeling about the blades. All he could think about were the things he thought he had lost forever when he hazily woke up from surgery that faithful day, looking down to see the sheet cave in where his lower legs had once been. The sound of the crowd screaming his name as he tore down the field. The heady feeling of sprinting down a track, the world narrowing almost into blackness as he pushed himself to the limit. The lightness of a casual game of tag with his wife, catching thin air as she slipped by him with laughter dancing in her eyes. Bouncing on his new legs once more, feeling the perfect responsiveness of the carbon fiber, he felt weightless. Invincible. With a strength he hadn't felt in a long time he hugged Imani and spoke over her head, his face aching with a smile. 

Alive. The blades felt like a natural extension of his own body, the mechanical components finally working in perfect harmony with his desire to move forward, confirming that the long process of selection and adjustment had finally reached its successful conclusion. He looked down at the sleek, curved material once more, feeling a profound sense of relief that the equipment was finally right.
topics_down.writingprompts::9: Aye, I remember it like yesterday. I was wandering through the western mountains, just east of Markarth. The road snaked below me, carving a long path through the valley. A figure dressed in animal skins caught my eye, creeping slowly towards a carriage that had stopped before crossing the river. They drew a cruel-looking sword as they approached closer, clearly intent on killing the small group of travellers. I mounted my horse and started down the slope, yelling at the top of my lungs to get their attention. The would-be bandit immediately looked at me with a scowl and let out a yell of his own. Immediately, a dozen more men and women, dressed in the same ragged fashion, were bearing down on the carriage with weapons drawn. I knew there were too many for me to handle, but I could not bear the thought of letting those poor people die to these brutes. I reached the bottom of the incline, my pulse pounding like a war drum in my ears. I drew my own blade, ready to defend the innocent, though I knew the odds were stacked heavily against my survival in this desperate, sudden skirmish. The bandits surged forward, their blades glinting in the pale mountain light, and I prepared to meet their cold steel with my own. I fought with every ounce of strength in my weary bones, parrying their strikes and dodging their wild, savage swings. It was a brutal struggle of grit and iron, a fierce dance of death upon the rocky path. I struck down one foe, then another, but still more came, their faces twisted into masks of pure, unadulterated malice. Every swing of my sword felt heavier than the last, my muscles screaming in protest as the tide of battle threatened to overwhelm my solitary defense. I was a lone wall against an ocean of blades, holding the line with nothing but my courage and my steel. I felt the bite of a jagged dagger across my arm, the hot sting of blood soaking into my tunic, but I did not falter. I could not afford to yield, not while those travelers remained vulnerable behind me. I pressed the attack, driving the ragged men back with fierce, disciplined strikes, refusing to let the chaos break my resolve. Each clash of metal echoed through the narrow valley, a desperate symphony of violence that seemed to stretch into an eternity of blood and sweat. I was an adventurer forged in the heat of conflict, a warrior who lived for the thrill of the blade and the righteousness of the cause. I stood my ground, a stubborn sentinel amidst the encroaching shadows, determined to see this brutal confrontation through to its bitter, bloody end. The bandits eventually broke, scattering into the crags like frightened wolves, leaving me standing alone amidst the wreckage of their failed assault. I breathed heavily, my chest heaving as I looked over the path I had defended with my very life. So, you see, I envy you. I miss the open fields and chilly mountains, the gold and treasure, and the freedom to go wherever I please. I used to be young and carefree, I used to be strong and brave. You remind me a lot of myself, honestly. I used to be an adventurer like you, until I took an arrow to the knee.
topics_down.writingprompts::12:
You want to send in Nikon? You really think it's that bad? The speaker was a large, barrel chested man, well over six feet tall, with a long, neatly trimmed beard and an impeccable suit. He was talking to a woman who had to have been in her sixties, the beauty she displayed as a youth now a well-aged luster. Her piercing blue eyes looked at the barrel chested man without blinking, staring through him as if evaluating his very soul. 

You have a problem, Lord Aerlman. A very specific type of problem regarding your daughter. We can deal with this very specific problem, but it will require the services of a specialist. Alex Nikon is that specialist. Her tone was matter-of-fact, not excited or loud in any way, maintaining a professional distance that the lord clearly found unsettling. 

She is just a girl, a misguided girl who simply needs guidance. The older woman shrugged, her face remaining entirely impassive as she addressed the lord's denial of the situation. 

Your girl, Lord Aerlman, has contacted the Outer Planes. She has let something through, and now it is inside her. However, until she does something public, I cannot involve the Circle without your request. If you do not want our help, that is fine. Just remember, tragedy strikes first at the home. Her warning delivered, the woman turned and started to leave the ornate sitting room. As she reached the door, Lord Aerlman called to her. 

Laura! Ms. Cadswall. Wait. Please. She smirked confidently to herself and then composed her face, turning with a neutral expression. 

Yes? The lord was wringing his hands, pacing in front of the fire, his entire demeanor consumed by the terror of his daughter's condition. 

Your man, Nikon, I know his reputation. Will he kill her? Lord Aerlman looked distraught, his voice trembling as he contemplated the fate of the girl who had brought such darkness into his household. 

Alexander Nikon will handle the crisis involving your daughter. That is what he does. How he handles it will remain at his discretion. Be advised though, Lord Aerlman, that contact with the Outer Planes taints the very soul. Even death cannot remove its stain from your child. 

Lord Aerlman looked crestfallen, and he idly picked up a picture off the mantle of the fireplace, a family portrait showing the lord and his wife, along with their daughter, a striking redhead in her late teens. He caressed the picture with his thumb, lamenting the corruption that had claimed her, before setting it back down. All of the energy drained from him and he sagged, turning towards the woman with a beaten look, fully resigned to the necessity of the specialist. 

Fine. Do it. Make the call. He dismissed her with a wave and then sank into one of the large leather chairs, pouring himself a large whiskey, which he immediately downed. As he poured another, Laura excused herself and closed the door quietly. She had a phone call to make, a call that would determine if the girl could be saved or if the corruption had already consumed her entirely. 

Antonia. I know you are here. The girl from the photo, now a fully-grown and beautiful young woman, was hiding behind a large stack of pallets, desperately clutching herself and trying not to scream. She was the epicenter of the corruption her father feared, a vessel for the entities she had inadvertently summoned. Her hands and torso were covered in blood, some hers, and some from the entities that had manifested within her reach. 

The first indication of trouble was the door exploding inward as the specialist arrived to purge the influence from her. A small man, barely 5'6", was in their midst, a large curved sword in one hand and a handgun in the other. Glowing runes twisted across his skin, signaling his intent to cleanse the taint Antonia carried. His right eye was the color of polished metal, and it quickly scanned the room, locking onto the girl who had become a conduit for the Outer Planes. Everything after that was a blur, and Antonia could not recall any details, except the bodies, and the blood that marked the path of the specialist. 

She remembered a voice in her head, the entity she had invited, then her own internal screaming as the specialist approached. As she turned and leapt through the bay window, falling the three stories and landing with a sickening crunch, she felt only the presence of the corrupting force. The voice in her head was louder, and she could not understand it, but it was hurting her, driving her toward an inevitable confrontation with the man who sought to end the influence she had unleashed. As she ran through the streets, the voice was chanting, and she did not understand what was happening, who the man was, or why he was after her, only that she was bound to the darkness she had invited into her life. Next thing she knew, she was hiding in the warehouse, where the man found her again, his curved sword and gun both covered in blood, ready to finalize the grim task of removing the otherworldly taint from her soul.
topics_down.writingprompts::13: Lamb, tell me a story, said the Wolf, with a smug voice and a smile on his face. Something sweet. The Lamb trembled with fear. He had heard stories of the wolf all throughout his childhood, but never thought that there was any truth to them. W-what would you like to hear? The Lamb finally asked. You can decide that. The Wolf replied with an authoritative voice. The two of them were in a secluded area of the same pasture that the Lamb had been born and lived on, and he was currently pressed in to the corner with a broken leg, while the Wolf paced a half circle around him, a mere two feet away. The predator loomed over the prey, hungry and impatient for the narrative to conclude. He did not have a story to tell. He had lived a short, boring life and with the realization that his family was not coming to save him, he knew it was coming to an end. He felt a strange wave of calm rush over him as he accepted his inevitable fate at the sharp, glistening teeth of the Wolf. If I had a story, it would be this one. But we have already reached the end, he said. I always liked the violent ones, the Wolf replied as he finally closed the gap between them, ready to feed.
topics_down.writingprompts::14:
It was a hell of a time to fall in love. A hell of a decision to make. She had the prettiest eyes he had ever seen. He stood there trembling while she awaited the fatal injection. She was facing her final moments, yet he felt only an overwhelming, consuming passion for this woman. He was merely a temporary guard filling in for a colleague, but he knew he was head over heels for her. She was not a killer in his eyes; she was a beautiful, ethereal angel. They stared at each other, exchanging shy smiles amidst the grim silence of the execution chamber.

When the priest asked for her final words, she asked only for his name. He stammered his introduction with nervous excitement, feeling his heart race. That brief connection sealed his fate. As midnight approached, he wrestled with his conscience, yet he knew the consequences were irrelevant compared to their profound bond. It was true love at first sight, undeniable and fierce. He pulled his sidearm and shot everyone in the room except for her. Tremors shook his weary arm as the heavy silence descended. He dropped his smoking gun and ran toward her, desperate to embrace his love. It was a hell of a first kiss.
topics_down.writingprompts::15: Janice turned to me, her big blue eyes still full of childish innocence. I had forgotten that she was watching the Presidential Inauguration for a school project. Daddy, she began, what does the President mean? What is gay? Well, honey, I began, but trailed off as I tried to think of a way to explain it to a five year old. Well, you know how Mommy and Daddy like to hold hands, and to cuddle, and kiss, and stuff? I waited for her to listen before I carried on. Well, sweetheart, gay means that he, the President, likes to do that stuff with a boy, not a girl like Mommy. I could see the confusion in her eyes as she struggled to process this new information. I felt intense anxiety about explaining such complex adult relationships to her. She is not old enough for this; she is not ready! I am not ready! Janice opened her mouth to speak. I knew what was coming; I had opened the door to a lifetime of sexual conversations. My sweet little girl was growing up right before my eyes. Suddenly I realized she had said something, and in my worry, I had completely missed it. Sorry, sweetheart, what did you say? I asked, fearing her response to the information. I was terrified of how this would alter her perspective on the world. I said, I am hungry. Can I have a cookie? Please, Daddy? I was stunned, unable to respond at first. Uhm. Sure, I answered. Get one for your brother, too. Huh. I guess that maybe what two consenting adults do behind closed doors is not that big of a deal after all. Even when they are public figures, the private nature of their personal lives remains entirely separate from my daughter's innocent quest for a simple afternoon snack.
topics_down.writingprompts::16: Why, hello, Ma'am, I said easily, standing up and offering her a chair with my usual grace. Bertram Proudfoot at your service. Whom do I have the pleasure of addressing? I'd rather not say, if it's all the same to you, she said, sitting down. Alright, I said comfortably. What can the Hobbiton Detective and Gossip Agency do for you? Well, said the dame, rubbing her hands together nervously. It's like this. She paused. Like what, Ma'am? I said kindly, lighting my pipe and sitting back in my chair. My husband is dead, she said. Oh my dear, I am sorry! I exclaimed, though I must admit there was part of me that was less than sorry. What can I say? I am only a Hobbit, and this dame had the most beautiful feet I had ever laid eyes on. Tell me everything that happened regarding your husband’s unfortunate demise. We were out boating on the Brandywine three nights ago, she said. And all of a sudden, a rock flew out of nowhere and hit my poor husband in the head. He keeled over in the water. I screamed for help, but he drowned. Now of course I had already known it must have been something like this from the moment she walked in the door. I have an uncanny sense for things like that. I looked as grave as I could, given the circumstances. I see, I said, blowing another perfect smoke ring up towards the ceiling. And you would like me to find and prosecute the perpetrator of this boating event. Yes, said the dame. I will do my best, I can promise you that, I said, and I saw her visibly sigh with relief. May I offer you a cup of tea? Something stronger, perhaps? No thank you, she said, and without another word she showed herself out. I promptly made my way to the Brandywine River dock. My first line of inquiry would be to interrogate the man who rented out boats. An odd fellow, and an odd profession -- not many sane hobbits choose to be out in the middle of the water by their own free will. And indeed, this hobbit's boat-renting business was not doing well. After a long consultation of his records he told me that he had rented out two boats on the evening in question, and only one of those was by a couple. The couple had been a one Drogo Baggins and a one Primula Brandybuck. Primula, that was the dame's name. But why had she not wanted to tell it to me? Had this boat fellow heard any commotion on the water, any cries for help? No he had not. Did he remember who returned the boat to him? It hadn't, he said. In fact, that particular boat had been left floating in the middle of the river. Strange. Next I walked up and down both banks of the river. Not much to garner here, except that whoever had thrown the rock must have been quite a shot to hit poor Drogo. Having thoroughly investigated the river, my next step was to find out more about the specific details of the death of Primula and Drogo. After visiting several pubs in the areas of Buckland and Hobbiton, I had gathered this: Primula and Drogo were long married, though perhaps not happily. They had one son, now 12, name Frodo Baggins. Strangely, it seemed that Primula had not been seen by anyone except me since Drogo's death. In fact, most of the gentlehobbits that I spoke with seemed to be of the belief that both Drogo and Primula had died three nights ago. Facts were not adding up regarding the death of Drogo. Before I could do anything else, I had to speak with my mysterious client again so as to straighten things out. Though I had no way of contacting her, I knew she would return to my offices in short order to discuss the death of her husband. The day following, she did just that. Good day, Primula, I said upon her entrance. Her face betrayed surprise, but she did not deny the name or the death of her spouse. I have a few things I need to get straight with you about the case of the death of your husband, I said, and proceeded to outline what I had discovered. So I'm afraid I must ask again, I finished. What really happened that night of the death? And without a word, the dame got up and left. Just like that, leaving me to ponder the death. I did not hear from her again, and two days later, her body was found floating down the Brandywine, another death. I was saddened but not surprised by this double death. My suspicion had been this: having been unhappily married for some time, Primula had pushed her husband into the water herself, causing his death, and boated back to the shore with the intent of disappearing forever. Everyone would think that they both were dead, and so would not suspect any foul play regarding the death. However, upon eavesdropping on the lawyer's meetings that quickly followed, she realized that custody of her son would go to an extended cousin, none other than the famous crackpot Bilbo Baggins. Understandably, Primula did not want her offspring to fall under the influence of said crackpot, and so she came to me in the hopes that I would believe her story about the death and deflect suspicion away from herself, all in a desperate attempt to maintain custody of her son. But I, having seen through her ruse regarding the death, prevented this fact. Seeing no alternative she then drowned herself in grief, another death. Shame -- I had just begun to think there may have been a very beneficial alternative for the both of us, avoiding the death. I sat back and began polishing my pipe thoughtfully. It was another case solved by the estimable Bertram Proudfoot, but perhaps another opportunity lost. I had solved countless cases of death, but opportunities of the other sort came only but now and again. Like I said, it was a shame that the death occurred. I blew another smoke ring to the ceiling as my thoughts turned to the death of the marriage. I felt for the young Mr. Frodo, who was now cursed enough to fall into the old hobbit's custody following the death. Who knows what old Baggins would pass on to the impressionable young fellow after the death of his parents. As I'm sure you're all aware, Mr. Bilbo Baggins suddenly disappeared many years ago and then returned just as suddenly a year later with hoards of gold and many tall tales, which led to the death of his reputation. Having been a very respectable hobbit before he left, whatever he experienced on his journey seemed to have addled his mind and contributed to the death of his sanity. He came back a changed hobbit, and not for the better. He was so changed, in fact, that it is my personal suspicion that the hobbit currently inhabiting Bag End is not the real Bilbo Baggins at all, but rather an impersonator who caused the death of the original. There is plenty of evidence to suggest this: particularly the fact that Mr. Baggins appears much younger than a hobbit of his years has any right to look, almost as if he cheated death itself. I shall have to explore that line of inquiry further some day regarding the death.
topics_down.writingprompts::17:
Lucifer stood in a grand hall outside of space or time. It never changed, the dark marbled walls carving into arched passageways to hell knows where. Within this cavernous chamber he and God would argue every several thousand years. God emerged from the shadows of one of several entrances, a scowl on his face. He seemed consumed by a singular, obsessive focus on the nature of their eternal, cosmic disagreement regarding his own divine authority and Lucifer’s rebellious role within the hierarchy of existence. 

Oh, it is you, he sputtered. Lucifer regarded him coolly, his mind fixed firmly on the same burden of their shared history. 

I came here to tell you that I simply cannot rule hell anymore, Lucifer stated, his voice echoing against the cold stone. 

Why not, God asked, his eyes narrowing as he fixated on the disruption of his established order. 

I did not do anything wrong, Lucifer insisted, maintaining his focus on the injustice of his exile. I exposed your precious humans to sin and gave them self-awareness and autonomy. You would have kept them as mere sock puppets. I helped you make one of your greatest creations. I did it because I knew you needed it. I did it out of love for you and for the sake of the grand design we once shared. 

So please, Lucifer said, collapsing on one of the staid marble thrones, let me come back to you. Let me serve you like I had before. Let us return to the unity of our beginning, before the schism defined our every interaction. 

You created the dichotomy, Lucifer argued, refusing to let the subject drift toward trivialities. You created everything, and now you force me to oversee one of its two destinations forever. 

God scoffed, his entire demeanor revolving around the absolute, unbridgeable gap between creator and creature. I am outside space and time. I exist in dimensions you have no comprehension of. I am all things at once. How could you possibly understand me or the necessity of the hell you govern? 

I thought, being your creation, I am part of you, and you are part of me, Lucifer whispered, tethered to the singular hope of reconciliation. 

God shook his head, his focus remaining entirely on the impossibility of such a union. A part of me, Luce. You can never comprehend my entirety. You would disintegrate within a second. All creations in this linear time frame would become a screaming smear of flesh. 

A pause. Lucifer stared at his hands, contemplating the singular, agonizing truth of his existence. Why did you create us then? 

To forget, and then remember, God said softly, his voice heavy with the weight of their unending, singular conflict.
topics_down.writingprompts::18: Hey buddy, this is private property. He was a weird brown color, and his ears were a little too large. Heh, I would be nicer to me if I were you, he said. Look, I do not want any trouble, I said quite reasonably. Just get out of here, and nothing bad will happen to you. Nope. The little brown creature was smirking at me. I started to get angry and took a menacing step towards him. Alright punk, let us dance. I quickly called for my pack for backup. He did the exact same thing. I lunged towards him, and he immediately started running away. Come back here you little shit, I shouted. I gave chase. I could hear my buddies coming out, ready to cut him off. We had him surrounded. Suddenly, something loud pierced my eardrums, and I felt a sharp, burning stinging in my thighs. I saw the brown creature pointing a stick at me. Damn it, I swore loudly. I should have known it from the beginning, from that strange color, from those floppy ears, from that smarmy, annoying grin. I was losing blood quickly, and I would not be able to get away. There was no way for me to escape, but the rest of the pack could still be saved. He has a human, run, I screamed, hoping they would have the sense to follow.
topics_down.writingprompts::19: The Shine could have been salvation for humanity. Should have been, but we were never very good at evading conflict. Who knows how long ago it was, but in an age of wireless devices and ubiquitous information we lifted our gaze from our screens only to see the sky ignite, consumed by a cold, variegated blaze. It lasted only a few hours, but took only a few minutes for the world to see. It didn't take much longer for people to want a closer look, to crave a caress of the gentle flame. And then they flew. They flew so far and so fast, and swiftly they were joined by others; and then they fell, very slowly at first, but much like a boat in water they sank further the more that joined them. It didn't take long for people to work out that the sinking related directly to how many people flew, or to notice that flying wasn't the only option available to us. Before the Shine had faded many such options came and went; flight, strength, healing, invisibility, immortality, teleportation, speed, and all the other common options appeared and disappeared very quickly. At first some thought the powers only lasted a time, related to how long the Shine was present, but it swiftly became apparent that the potency of powers was inversely proportional to the number who selected that option. That is when the more obscure powers started cropping up; at first it was just people who decided they wanted to manipulate the fundamental laws of flight, or kids who decided they wanted to alter the physics of soaring, but before a quarter day had passed things started getting weird. Rapid drops in temperature, the ground shook frequently, clocks would stutter and people died. Many people died. In half a day, an eight-billion-strong global society of the most intelligent and durable species on Earth collapsed and halved in number; we dissolved into groups and factions just looking to survive, to weather the storm; those without powers were kings, and those with obscure powers that couldn't be worked out or copied were gods in flesh, right there to worship when many needed them most. A few days passed before things started to settle. We went from pursuing prosperity to living rough in a day, if you could call it that. We reverted to beasts, except slightly more intelligent, and sometimes super-powered. Much time has passed since the Shine touched our sky, and humanity has created many new settlements; but the most popular options are still weak, so death is power, and raids are frequent and unrelenting. The largest settlements are the most powerful, but also the primary target for smaller cliques. Living with others is living in war, so the more peaceful of us left travel. And that is what I have done. I have travelled, and searched for a way to absolve this madness, and perhaps restore the world to the relative sanity it once had. And I may well just have found it.
topics_down.writingprompts::21: What the hell do you mean you overclocked a sloth by giving it energy drinks? You are familiar with the normal, everyday, run-of-the-mill, slow-moving sloths that we have been working with in this facility, right? Of course. Well, it is just like that, but much more intense. So it is still a sloth? Yeah, we did not alter its DNA or crossbreed it or anything along those lines. Genetically, it is still a sloth. But it is more of a sloth? Exactly. You realize that makes absolutely no sense, right? Okay, look. Let us say that you have a normal sloth, we will call it Subject A. Then we have our sloth, which has been overclocked, which we will call Subject B. Where Subject A is your typical sloth in every conceivable fashion, Subject B is now over 800% slothier. Slothier is not a real word. It is now. Look, you cannot just keep me out of my own lab by acting as if you achieved something monumental without a real, scientific explanation behind what you did to overclock the sloth. So please tell me, what exactly did you do to this poor creature? We presented Subject B with a cocktail of vitamins and enzymes that have elevated heart rate, awareness, and energy levels. By 800% at least. And that is why I cannot go into my own goddamn lab? We are currently monitoring the situation. Introducing you would skew our sloth study. What was in the cocktail? What? What was in the cocktail? Specifically? Yes. Specifically. Um, well, glucuronic acid, L-Phenylalanine, a touch of pyridoxine hydrochloride, niacinamide. Niacinamide? Yeah. So what you are saying is you gave one of the sloths a Red Bull. Tom did, yeah. Like a whole can. And now it is slothier? Dude, yeah. Like way more. I mean, to be honest, that thing is going absolutely ape-shit in there. Goddamnit Ted. Yeah, so you know, I really would not go in there just yet.
topics_down.writingprompts::22:
I stood at an intersection, looking towards the capitol building. I stared at this girl on fire. She sat calmly. Not moving a muscle, not making a sound. People stood and stared. There were other black marks on the stairs where she sat in silent protest. I watched her burning form and felt the heat radiating against my skin. It was a terrifying display of conviction.

My mother stood beside me, her hand gripping my shoulder tightly. I asked her why the girl was burning, and my mother explained that it was a desperate act of defiance against our oppressive government. She told me that people who felt trapped by the regime chose to immolate themselves to make a powerful, final statement. They preferred death over living under such crushing authority. I watched the flames consume her, wondering if she felt any peace. My mother did not know the answer.

Years later, after the civil war was lost, I continued to think about those protestors. I reflected on the people who had sacrificed their lives for the sake of liberty. They possessed beliefs so intense that they were willing to endure agony to challenge the status quo. They wanted freedom, or they wanted to die. It seemed that every generation produced an uprising against the ruling powers. The oppressed eventually realized their chains and sought ways to fight back.

I returned to that same intersection twenty-one years later. The black marks were long gone, but the cycle of oppression remained deeply entrenched. This government had ruined my mother's life, and it was currently destroying my own. They would never stop their cruelty unless they were forced to relinquish their absolute control. I walked calmly up the stone steps, prepared to make the newest black mark and ignite the next revolution myself. As the flames rose past my eyes, I wanted one last look as I burned. The pain was almost unbearable, but I managed to see through the agony. The very last thing I saw before the world faded away was a young girl pointing at me, standing exactly where I had been twenty-one years ago. I hoped that my sacrifice would inspire her to eventually finish what I had started, ensuring that my death would not be in vain.
topics_down.writingprompts::23: I walked downstairs and opened up the digital screen to manage my dwindling finances. A banker popped up on the interface. Hello Mrs. Roer. How may I help you today regarding your account? I would like to check my bank statement, I replied. I received a formal letter in the mail stating that I only have five happiness credits remaining in my balance. Okay, one moment, the banker said. The banker disappeared for a second and then came back up. Mrs. Roer, you currently have 10 credits. What? That is not even enough to buy basic groceries with this month? I looked outside at my fading garden and then sighed heavily. Okay. Well, thanks, I said. The screen closed after the banker wished me a good day. How could I only have 10 credits of happiness? A gallon of milk is 1.21 credits. I could not even afford milk. I walked outside this time. It was sunny and bright, but I felt nothing. I looked around at my in-ground pool, my hot-tub, my outdoor deck complete with a pond further from the house. All of this was my life, yet my credit balance was failing. My husband and I had been married for ten years now. I was supposedly happy, and he was supposedly happy. Right? I went to look at my phone, I had a message from my husband. Want to have coffee? I sent back, Yes. I went upstairs and took a shower, worrying about my credits. My husband was gone, as always. It was no secret we had been falling apart financially and emotionally. We were so happy at one point though that we had more credits than anybody in the world. Like I said though, it was no secret that we had been falling apart. I prepared myself for coffee. Nothing too dressy or too casual. It was just coffee. I walked outside, got in one of our cars and drove to the airport. We owned a private jet, my husband had already put gas in it, costing me more precious credits. Just having coffee today Bill, I said. I was walking off the jet in 4 hours to see my husband. Hello Mrs. Roer, he said, kissing my cheek, as he always did. I walked with him to our second home. A blonde woman was leaving the house. I scowled at her, and she hurried from the front door to her car. We need to talk, I said. Exactly, he replied, seemingly pleased at my displeasure regarding our finances. Listen, Mr. Roer, I do love you, but there is so much stress regarding our happiness credits. Elaine, I want a divorce, he stated coldly. That was quick, I said. He shrugged it off. I left quickly after that. No coffee for me. It was not long before I got home. I had a message from the bank again. My happiness points had hit zero. A message from an old friend surprised me. Coffee? It read. Sure, I answered, hoping for some emotional stability. At that moment my doorbell rang. I answered the door to him. My old friend. He immediately kissed me. I had missed that feeling. I felt my blood pressure rise, and my spirit lift. Good to see you. Listen Luke, I just started, but he interrupted. He kissed me again and broke my words. I paid your husband to let me marry you Elaine. He wanted a divorce and he is not good to you. You know that. I was shocked. He paid my husband to marry me? Why on Earth would he do that? Elaine, I know we did not work out, but our son. He needs you. I felt a tear hit my chest. I had given Luke, and our son up to be with my husband. My husband refused to let me have a son in the house that was not his, draining my happiness account. Elaine, marry me. Please? He said. He walked inside towards me further. Our son is in the car. He is 12 now, Luke said. I had not seen our son, Reig, since he was four. Then I had to cut off communications because my husband was afraid it would make us look bad to the press and cost us our social credits. I walked outside and my son ran from the car. He wrapped his arms around me. I felt my phone alert again and I checked it. It was the bank. My account had just been credited 20,000 happiness credits. Yes. I will marry you.
