topics_down.writingprompts::28:
New Wichita burned. The gleaming towers of the Financial District, their silvery windows reflecting the flames that danced around them, stood like weeping angels as the first rosy fingers of dawn stretched out over the eastern horizon. The stately mansions of the Original Founders had gone up in smoke early the day before, taking with them nearly seven hundred years of local heritage. The entire River District was little more than rubble, the historic wharves and warehouses reduced to empty, charred shells. Lieutenant Lucas Singleton Terry, born a scion to a prominent rancher family, wept silently at the sight. This was his home, and to see its soil and people so utterly devastated by the relentless onslaught bordered on the sacrilegious.

Mustang 5, this is Lead. We have confirmed reports of enemy Wolf activity along Broadway and Kingston. First and Second Lances will move in to investigate the situation immediately.

That was Captain James T. Fulton, a hard-ass man and a son of a bitch but a damn fine soldier. Terry pressed his mike.

Copy that, Mustang Leader. Second Lance will advance now.

There used to be a third lance in Mustang Company, but a brutal ambush by an entire Binary of Clanners had torn through the unit, forcing them to consolidate the survivors together. They were still better off than the rest of the local theater militia. Other companies were barely at fifty percent effectives, and the armor and infantry battalions were even worse. The enemy forces were putting up a fearsome fight against the remaining defenders, but it was of little use. Bit by bit, block by block, street by street and house by house, the Wolves were driving the weary defenders back. Terry switched his frequency to a more private channel, one shared between just the Captain and him.

Captain Fulton, a question. How long do we have?

He heard his commanding officer sigh over the radio.

Who knows? Years, months, or perhaps only weeks? The allied units are about to pull out, as high command is ordering them to the defense of the capital. The rest of the defensive force seems determined to stay, but that is only because they would rather have the fight happen here on our world instead of theirs. My best estimate is that we will last another year at this slow rate.

And what happens if we do not succeed in driving the invading Wolves off of our world? What if we fail? Terry asked.

If the worst should happen, Lieutenant, I have a feeling that we will not be alive to see it.
topics_down.writingprompts::29:
It was nigh impossible to see, we could only hear it after it was gone... and we dare not speak its name. But we knew what it meant. If that thing was in the skies above our territory, war was coming. I will never forget the first time I saw that machine. I was out in the dust fields, looking at the horizon. Little did I know that as I looked up at the sky, it was looking down at me. It was a shadow of a shadow, a metal monster from an ancient era long passed. Saying that I saw it is misleading; it was more of a feeling than anything. For the brief moment in time when I saw that blur cut through the night, I knew it was over. That night, the Blackbird arrived. It was the fastest, most elusive craft ever constructed, a relic of warfare that defied all conventional physics.

The machine heralded total destruction. Its arrival meant men in adaptable camouflage were nearby, armed with pulse rifles and sabers. They did not even think twice before cutting down the people in our village. I am lucky to have escaped with my life. I owe it all to the maintenance bot that had been repurposed to serve us. In the midst of all the gunfire and explosions, the mess hall had come crashing down. I was among the unfortunate souls who ended up inside. It all happened in an instant, and before I even had time to react, I was laying trapped under a pile of heavy, burning rubble. Through the smoke and flames, I could see the Blackbird looming in the upper atmosphere, a dark silhouette against the stars. The sheer speed of the aircraft was terrifying. It was a weapon of pure, cold efficiency that dominated the skies.

As far as I know, we are the only ones who made it out alive. We ran until I could not run anymore, and eventually I collapsed. As I lay there, clinging to the final threads of life, I just kept stammering to myself about that jet. SR-71 leaned in real close, and whispered in my ear about the craft. There were a lot of things we could not do in an SR-71, but we were the fastest guys on the block and loved reminding our fellow aviators of this fact. People often asked us if, because of this fact, it was fun to fly the jet. Fun would not be the first word I would use to describe flying this plane. Intense, maybe, even cerebral. But there was one day in our Sled experience when we would have to say that it was pure fun to be the fastest guys out there, at least for a moment.
topics_down.writingprompts::30: Prisoner 778125-Sigma-8, you stand before this tribunal today accused of crimes against galactic civilization, murder, four counts of xenocide, 70 counts of attempted xenocide, planetary dehabitation, planetary destruction, and attempting to overthrow the Pan-Galactic Alliance. How do you plead? The man before Councilwoman Asaarha met the gaze of her and her fellow Arbiters with cold blue eyes. Despite the 140 cycles of temporal isolation he had endured before his trial, Sacha Markes stood tall and unbroken. He radiated power and command, even now, stripped of his rank, fleet, and army. The last of the humans was a testament to the species. The silence before he spoke seemed louder to the Councilwoman than the crashing waves of her ocean home. The time it took for the human to speak seemed longer than the span of the galaxy. Guilty, he said with a simple finality. The Arbiters nodded their heads solemnly. None of them had expected this one to plea for mercy. Asaarha keyed the sentence into the terminal before her. The other six Arbiters did the same. The blue lights of Markes's uniform and restraints changed to red. The screen on the psionic inhibitor around his head changed to read GUILTY in Galactic Standard. Though the trial room was empty save for the Tribunal and Markes, Asaarha could hear the roars of vengeance that were surely reverberating throughout the galaxies. Each trial of the humans had been broadcast in its entirety. Each had ended in a guilty verdict. Sacha Markes, formal Admiral of the Seventh Human Expeditionary Fleet, High Captain of the Royal Guard, Commander-in-Chief of the Human Expeditionary Force, and Primarch of the Solar Empire, you are sentenced to Psionic Stripping and Execution by black hole. Do you have any last words before the sentence is carried out? The human threw his head back defiantly and turned his gaze on the camera nearest him. Addressing the billions of life forms throughout the galaxy, he began the last soliloquy regarding the absolute justice of the human crusade. We delivered retribution upon our wayward children to punish you for your insolence and your ignorance. I remember when we decided to take our final vengeance; to punish you for your treachery. We burned your worlds. I watched our plasma cannons turn every surface to glass and every ocean to boiling ash. One world for one human life was always a fair trade. You did not accept our judgment, nor did you respect the authority of your creators. Like Icarus chasing the burning sun, you rose up against us in your pathetic arrogance. Did you truly expect us to just let you? Did you think we would not defend our divine right to rule? I was the commander of the fleet that met yours on the first day of battle. My ten cruisers against the most powerful battleships of three galaxies and a hundred races. Now, a hundred years later, you have finally defeated us. You have lost entire solar systems to our wrath. You have sacrificed googles of lives and thousands of civilizations to bleed your gods dry and bind them in chains. Your worlds are shattered. Your cities are gone; wiped from history in an instant. Can you truly call that victory? I am the last of my kind. I am Sacha Markes. Look upon my face, ye mighty, and despair. For when you kill me, you kill the last light left in this existence, and you will find yourselves adrift in the cold, hollow darkness that follows the end of the human reign.
topics_down.writingprompts::32: War Journal of P1C Henry Whiticker, First Divine Armored. Entry:48. We finally reached the rim of the first bolgia today and heaven preserve me the scout reports weren't lieing, it's more vast than anything i could imagine. The recon photos we were given to prepare us are like a blind man trying to describe a sunrise, and by God the smell has actually somehow gotten worse! Seeing the pit first hand i think the enormity of our task has finally hit home for some of the crew, they look rattled, i don't blame them, have we bitten off more than we can chew? I'm not sure but i have faith in our mission and our commanders. The vastness of the pit really can't be put into words but for the sake of this journal i'll try. The rim extends further than the human eye should be able to see and yet i can make out tiny details on the far cliff face, it looks big enough that you could fit the whole Earth in and knock it around like an ice cube in the bottom of a bourbon glass, even while sitting in the cab of the rumbler i get vertigo looking down onto the levels below, if it wasn't for the special anti-psychotics the docs give us i'm sure what i see on the lower levels might have some lasting horrific effect on me. The crew and i wash down todays dose with a bottle of sacramental wine, and why not, today was a good day after all. Today we reached the edge of Limbo. Entry:49. Not much to record today, no movement from the enemy, just some low level demons hovering near the perimeter, otherwise nothing going on but general camp maintenance. The engineers are working double time to ensure the security of Limbo Base, they say it'll be fully up in 2 days, i have my doubts. After their fiasco at the river they've got a lot of face to save, 2 Rumblers, 4 squads of troops and a Screacher lost because of their damn barges. Bastards. I Hate just sitting around like this with nothing to distract me from the smell of rot and sulphur that somehow filters into the rumblers cab despite the tech geeks assurances that the cab is perfectly hermetically sealed, it feels like the smell is inside my skull rotting tiny holes in my brain, a constant reminder that we are sitting on the edge of eternal damnation waiting for the inevitable assault. Entry:51. HOOAH! CONTACT BABY! Praise God i've been waiting for this moment since the first days of the war for the surface. Hell finally saw fit to send us some worthy opponents AND WE KICKED THEIR MUTHA FUCKING TEETH IN!! HAHAHAHAHAHA. They came a few hours after my last entry like a great black tornado. A swirling column of harpies, skrieks and imps beyond counting rising up from the center of The Pit and came crashing down completely enveloping Limbo Base. The first few moments of engagement should've been chaos but by the grace of God we were ready. All the Screachers had been on high alert since we emerged from the maze of caves and onto the plains of Limbo proper 8 days ago and today that diligence paid off. The blitz of the winged demon assault crumbled before the wall of sound our blessed Screachers blasted out. The word of God is anathema to the denizens of Hell, the word of God pumped out through a mobile rig of high powered speakers piloted by a devout member of the clergy is down right debilitating. The shocked and paralysed Demons that twitched and writhed on the ground were easy targets, the rumblers blessed water cannons burning away swaths of the foul creatures as if the misted holy water were strong acid, huge piles of the creatures were reduced to ash in seconds. The larger Demon haridens proved more resilient and i saw more than a few grunts die on their talons, their sanctified body armor little better than cardboard. We repaid them in kind and i'm proud to say our rumblers javalin cannons sent a good lot of the giant buzzards screaming into oblivion impailed on our gleaming silver spears. I should record so it doesn't seem like i'm diminishing the grunts efforts, their bravery and ferocity in battle too, for they've got that in spades, despite the mortal danger they collected their fair share of scalps, pinning the giant creatures with their silver pikes and finishing them off with their chain sickles. it was a glorious bloody sight, like something out of a nature documentry. The greatest trial of the battle was yet to come though. After a full day and a half of fighting the black swarm began to thin out and we thought we might've finally broken their assault, but then they appeared. Three monsterous figures coming into focus through the haze of ash and exhaustion. Hell Dragons, nothing like what we'd seen in movies or our stories from childhood, these were great pestilent, foul things that towered over us. Snub nosed heads the size of a grand cathedral covered in spines, long armored bodies like an insects, their faces and joints slick with thick black tar that bubbled and hissed as it fell from them and stained the plains of Limbo. Screachers focused their assault and prevented the titans from over running the base, the rumblers water tanks and javlin cannons ran dry just trying to keep them at bay, our brave grunts held back the black swarm, fighting tirelessly which allowed us time to retreat, resupply and reenter the fray. And so it went for hours on end and for all our efforts the Hell Dragons seemed to be none the worse. Salvation finally came at the hands of the engineering corps. Of all people! Through our efforts we had given them enough time to secure and assemble Limbo Bases major defenses, Sanctified Artilery and the Holy Rail Gun. The Rail Gun punctured the Dragons thick armor spewing gysers of tar onto the battlefield while the artilery smashed into the beasts vulnerable exposed points lodgeing shells etched with scripture deep in their bodies wracking them with pain. The attack still went on for hours and we lost a great deal of our force but after nearly 2 months since we first decsended into this place we finally have established a forward base to launch our attack on Hell. One Bolgia down eight to go. This is the first day here that the smell of the pit does not bother me because the sweet scent of victory is finally masking the stench of our enemies.
topics_down.writingprompts::33: Men have for ages endured a fascination, disdain, fear or general obsession with the concept of hell. It was the faithful who truly believed in its existence, yet most men never expected to have any contact with this dark realm, and certainly did not expect hell to come knocking at their doors. While I cannot at this time suppose a motive for the prince of lies to so suddenly mobilize the legions of the damned, I can speak to the utter strangeness of his manifestation as a corporate entity and the absolute devastation left in his wake. In hindsight, a company named Apollyon ought to have aroused deep suspicion; alas, as few knew the ancient Greek language, the meaning of Apollyon—a translation for the destroyer attributed to Satan—remained hidden. While we were preoccupied with the affairs of daily life, Mr. Morning-Star stretched his hands to slowly throttle the servants of darkness. He systematically replaced traditional wickedness with the cold, calculated corruption of modern commerce. So, the long story short is that the devil became a powerful business tycoon, and it was through the allure of cheap, mass-produced goods that he successfully invaded our society. He utilized supply chains and predatory lending to claim the souls of the masses, ensuring that his influence reached every corner of the globe. The devil did not need fire; he simply utilized the marketplace to finalize his eternal, ironclad dominion over humanity.
topics_down.writingprompts::34: The planet Earth has changed a lot recently, twenty-three years ago, almost to the day, the global storms on the surface finally ended. Those same storms had been raging for roughly five thousand years, but a few weeks passed whilst the massive cloud formations slowly disintegrated, and then we finally obtained our first clear, unobstructed view of our ancestral home. I was only five years old at the time and was entertained mostly by the vibrant colors; the beautiful blue and green hues were like nothing I had ever witnessed on the Ark. We had water, sure, but not vast pools large enough to provide that deep, oceanic blue color. We had plants too, but the artificial conditions were far from optimal and made the vegetation a dull, dirty green rather than lush. I wanted to see it closer, touch it, feel it. That was precisely when I decided to join the recruitment for the first expedition. The first journey was, as the name implies, the initial mission back down to the surface of the planet. A lot of people wanted to return immediately after the storms ended; there were protests and even riots. People wanted the Ark to head straight back down to the surface, but those people were idiots. Twenty-three years may have been a long time to wait, but it was absolutely critical for our survival. We were the last humans after all, and if we landed and something went wrong, we could not risk it. Years of geological scans and low atmosphere scouting gave us the perfect landing spot. Minimal damage to the local environment, enough space to develop a community, plenty of water, and importantly a lot of natural protection taking the form of cataclysm-formed mountain ranges and deep trenches filled with the darkest blue water. Of course, something as large as the Ark could not simply land; that was where the first journey came into the picture. We were the first crew to go planetside and live permanently in over seven generations. Our objective was to build the massive docking facility. It would be a long, grueling job, probably another five or six years, but the dock would provide us with a much needed start, as well as mapping out local geography much more clearly. The reality of the situation is that we were going in blind; this safe-zone as the Corps had nicknamed it could very easily become a lethal deathtrap. The core problem with the safe-zone was that because of its remote location, once we went in, our shuttle would not be able to make it out. Part of the problem with the planet remained the atmospheric turbulence. Even now, twenty-three years after the main storm ended, smaller cells continued to rotate. The mountain ranges protected the area from the storms still raging elsewhere, as the gales were not powerful enough to make it over the high peaks. Even in the atmosphere above, there was a vicious wind that constantly blew. It would tear an outgoing ship to pieces, so only a craft as large as the Ark could survive it, and the Ark required a dock to perform a takeoff. So that was the mission: go down, face possible death, build a super structure, all in less than six years, and I was damn excited.
topics_down.writingprompts::35:
Exterior, Jerusalem side street, day. An area near a couple of large amphorae has been taped off. CSI techs are doing things to the area. Next to his car stands MOSES looking tired and irritable. After a few moments lingering on this scruffy patriarch leaning on his walking stick we pull back. 

JESUS enters from the left carrying takeout coffee.

MOSES Took you long enough. Feels like we have been waiting for you forever!

JESUS Sorry, there was a line. So, what have we got?

MOSES Dead body. Uniform called it in, looks like another victim of this ongoing murder spree. Hey, Hazdrubul, do you have the cause of death yet?

We pan over to the masked and coveralled figure beside what we can now see as a corpse. HAZDRUBUL steps away from the crime scene.

HAZDRUBUL It is a little early to say, but if I were a betting man I would go with blunt force trauma. It looks like multiple contusions over the body and a really nasty one to the side of the head, consistent with the other recent homicide cases we have been investigating.

JESUS When did she die?

HAZDRUBUL Hard to give a time of death right now, but I will go with some time last night and give you a better number when we get a liver temp. This victim matches the pattern of the others perfectly.

MOSES Good enough. Let us document this scene thoroughly so we can track the killer.

Jesus moves to get closer to the crime scene, trying to get a better look. He does not react well to the corpse and ducks behind an amphora to throw up.

MOSES Jesus! Well, at least you did not contaminate the crime scene. We need to maintain the integrity of this evidence if we want to solve these serial murders.

JESUS re-emerges wiping his mouth and looking pale.

MOSES OK, Uniform is going to canvas house to house. Let us go get you cleaned up and see if we can put a name to this poor girl and tie her to our primary suspect.

***

Scene 23 - Precinct House interior, interview room. JESUS and MOSES are on opposite sides of the room arms folded, obviously antagonistic regarding the investigation.

MOSES Do NOT give me any of your holier than thou bullshit. We needed results to stop this serial murderer and I got them!

JESUS And was it worth all the trouble it caused, Moses? Was it worth going down to their level just to close the case file?

MOSES I would do it again! I would do it again in a heartbeat! Forty years I have been in this job hunting killers and if there is one thing I know how to do it is get a confession out of a homicide suspect!

JESUS You know, the first time I saw you with that stick, I thought it was a sign of age. I thought it made you an elder, someone to be respected. I guess I was wrong about your methods for catching these murderers.

MOSES Maybe you are wrong about a lot of things regarding police procedure.

JESUS Maybe I am! But the pattern of these murders is what matters most.

MOSES And maybe you want to think about how it looks out there to our brother cops when you, a snot-nosed junior Levite, think you can tell me how to conduct a homicide investigation!

JESUS Look, let us just calm down here. I respect you, sure I respect you. You took down the Golden Calf gang. You resolved the Dead Sea Hostage situation. But this serial killer is different! We have to do things differently now to catch him!

MOSES The hell you say.

JESUS Look, man, think what you like. But there is a girl down in the morgue on a slab and all she is doing is getting colder while we stand here arguing about how to stop this killer.

***

Scene 832: Jerusalem, exterior, night. MOSES is leaning on a squad car as JESUS walks up with this week's serial murder suspect in handcuffs. Moses watches as JESUS hands the suspect off to uniformed cops.

MOSES Good collar, kid. You finally linked the forensic evidence to the suspect.

JESUS Couldn't have done it if you had not spotted the connection between all the victims. How did you know the murders were linked?

MOSES I have been on the job for longer than you have been alive. After a while, you get a feel for how these killers operate.

JESUS Think I will ever develop that kind of instinct for homicide work?

MOSES Maybe. If you live long enough to solve enough murder cases.

JESUS You are full of encouragement. I don't care, though. We put a murderer behind bars and that is the kind of justice I want to share!
topics_down.writingprompts::36:
"Hey, check out those finches over in the birdbath." Kylo whooped and puffed out his chest, nearly toppling off his perch. 

"Don't be a nuisance, bro," Atticus groused, pecking at his seeds, "You are making a scene again. Just stay focused on the finches and stop acting like a total fool." 

"I don't care. I am going to go talk to them." Kylo took off, swerving through the air like a leaf trapped in a gust. Atticus sighed and took off after him. He would have to keep close tabs on Kylo or else they would get kicked out of the garden again. 

Kylo crashed into the water with a mighty splash. Droplets flew in every direction, drenching the finches in the birdbath. They squawked with indignation as Kylo emerged from beneath the surface, shaking the wetness from his head. He trotted up to the group of soaked finches and gave his wings a frantic shake. "Hey, finches. You guys look lovely today." 

"We are just trying to bathe," a purple finch stepped forward from the group, and she launched into a tirade on how annoying and loud Kylo was being. Atticus alighted on the rim of the bath and began to walk around, apologizing to the finches for Kylo's behavior and pleading with them not to call the bouncer over. 

"Okay, sorry," Kylo interrupted, "let me make it up to you: how about you and I head over there—" He motioned to the bird feeder. "—and I share my seeds with you?" If birds had lips, Kylo would be smirking right now while looking at those finches. 

The finches began to flap their wings angrily, splashing Kylo with water. "You are such a boor. Get out of here!" Many of the finches chirped in agreement, and some of the bigger finches began to puff their chests threateningly. Atticus shoved Kylo to the side and raised his wings. "On behalf of my friend here, I apologize. He has clearly had too much nectar; we will just be going now..." 

"Oh, you think we are going to fall for that?" The purple finch spat a nut shell at his feet. "He is just trying to bother us, is he not? Let him take the fall for you, and swoop in to look better by comparison." The other finches chorused in agreement. 

"I think these two need to be taught a lesson." A large finch fluttered over to Atticus, towering above him. He spread his wings menacingly, blocking Atticus from taking off. "Why do you not bother someone else?" The finches broke into cheers, shouting for a fight against the two intruders. 

"Well, you are kind of bigger than me." Atticus took a step back into the bath. He felt feathers ruffle against him as the crowd of finches pressed around him, urging him back towards the large finch. 

Kylo staggered in front of him and began to hop around. "Don't worry, Atticus; we got this." 

"Hey, this is a one-on-one fight." The large finch looked around at the other finches. 

"Who on earth placed all this here?" A door opened, and the finches began to scatter, screaming, "Human!" Atticus grabbed Kylo and urged him into the air, and the two lost themselves amongst the cloud of fleeing finches. 

"Make sure to thank that human for bailing you out of yet another mess with those finches," Atticus said. 

Kylo scoffed. "We could have totally taken those finches."
topics_down.writingprompts::37: He used to hit me so much. I had never even had a drink, and he beat cracked ribs, bruised kidneys and loose teeth into me. He claimed he did this to ensure I never became what he was, a broken man lost to the bottle. Once when he was sober, he told me he drank because of how he grew up. He said it like he wanted me to empathize with him, to forgive his brutality. Like he could not see that my arm was broken from him protecting me from drink the week before. Like he could not see himself standing over me, jeering while I cried blood and snot and tears. Like he could not remember why he needed it to let him sleep at night, to stop waking up screaming in the darkness, to stop wetting himself when he had a bad dream. He made me sick, my father. My breath catches sometimes, and one of my wrists never set right, leaving me half crippled in that hand. I have eleven false teeth. At twenty three, all this. I did not go to his funeral, but I celebrated it. I never took a drink, though, I could never do that. I cry myself to sleep most nights, and I cannot help myself from screaming if someone comes up to me suddenly. Lately I have noticed a lot of blood coming up when I cough. I will not let him beat me, though; I will not give him this final, cruel victory over my spirit. My life remains defined by the shadow of his alcoholism and the constant, throbbing pain in my bones. I am a living monument to his addiction, a vessel for the trauma he poured into me year after year. Every morning I wake up and check my hands, feeling the crooked bones that serve as a permanent reminder of his rage. I know the smell of stale gin and the sound of a shattering glass as intimately as my own heartbeat. It is a haunting, persistent rhythm that dictates my every waking thought and every fearful dream. He wanted me to be strong, he said, but he only forged me into a fragile thing, terrified of the liquid poison that ruined his soul. I walk through my days with a heavy, aching chest, wondering if the damage he inflicted will eventually consume me entirely. I look in the mirror and see his eyes staring back, a terrifying reflection that makes me want to claw at my own skin. I am trapped in the aftermath of his choices, forever haunted by the violence he claimed was for my own good. He destroyed my childhood, shattered my health, and left me with a legacy of pure, unadulterated terror that follows me into every room I enter. I am the broken consequence of his weakness, a man shaped by the cruelty of a drunkard who never truly understood the depth of the agony he caused.
topics_down.writingprompts::38:
Craig was walking home from the shops when he met a man who claimed to be God. He wasn't expecting to run into a deity, as sane people rarely do. In fact, he didn't really ever think about the divine. He didn't believe in a creator, but he also didn't disbelieve enough to ever think about the possibility of an absent master of the universe. Religion and the concept of a supreme being were simply not topics he cared about in the slightest. What he cared about was the nature of his own skepticism, and how he processed the strange event unfolding on the sidewalk. He was far more interested in the logical inconsistencies presented by this peculiar stranger than in any theological debate. 

He was about two minutes away from his home when the stranger first spoke to him. "Hey! Craig!" His internal monologue interrupted, Craig turned around to see who had addressed him. Behind him stood a tall person in a loose-fitting suit. Craig wasn't really sure of the person's gender; they were androgynous, looking not dissimilar to Diamond Dogs era David Bowie. They looked familiar, but he couldn't quite place the face. He realized he had been staring, and sought something to say. "Hi," he began hesitantly. "Do I know you?" 

"In a way," replied the Bowie lookalike. "I'm God." 

"Well, good for you. I've got to get going now. Bye," said Craig before starting back towards his house. He didn't want to be wasting time on a crazy person or someone playing a elaborate, nonsensical prank. 

"Wait, don't go yet. Please," called out the person. "What would it take for you to believe me?" 

Craig sighed and turned back, deciding that humoring the person might be the most efficient path forward. "I don't know," said Craig, exasperated. "A miracle or something. Some extraordinary thing which couldn't just be done by any old person. Something more than just stating that you are a divine entity." 

"Hmm. How about... this!" The man pointed at a nearby bush, which instantly burst into flames. The blaze shaped itself into a dragon which roared at the two of them. Then, with a snap of his fingers, the fire was extinguished, leaving the bush singed but intact. The man turned back to Craig with arms spread wide as if to say, "Tada!" 

Craig, looking mildly impressed, analyzed the situation with clinical detachment. "Yeah, that was pretty good. Looked very impressive. I have to admit I have no idea how you did it. A hologram maybe? It worked for Tupac, so I can see it working for a dragon. It is a clever illusion, regardless of the technology required to pull it off." 

The stranger stared at him for a few seconds before responding. "I did it by being God. You asked for a miracle. I showed you one. What more do you want from me?" 

"Don't get me wrong, it's very good. But the whole 'God' branding probably isn't going to fly. Maybe people would be more likely to believe you're a talented stage magician." 

"But I'm not a damn magician!" shouted the man. "I'm God. Why would I say I'm a magician?" 

Craig backed off a few meters, holding his hands up in front of him in the international gesture of, "I don't want any trouble, let's all just calm down." 

"Hey, calm down, buddy. I'm sorry if I came across as harsh, but it's just constructive criticism regarding your act. This is for a T.V. show or a YouTube prank, right? You're not going to convince anyone with the whole 'God' persona. It lacks nuance and feels forced." 

The stranger, visibly seething by this point, held Craig's gaze for a few more seconds before letting out an angry sigh and storming off down the street. Craig watched him leave, then shook his head, wondering about the logistics of the bush fire. He considered checking out the charred leaves to see if he could find any clues as to how the trick had been performed, but decided against it. Whoever had been recording the encounter was probably still watching, waiting for Craig to do exactly that. So he pushed it out of his mind and set off home, satisfied that he had maintained his skeptical perspective throughout the entire bizarre, unconvincing encounter.
topics_down.writingprompts::39: Pass me the damn bottle, would you, Patsy? Get it yourself, Ser Whyte. I am not your bloody squire anymore. Right. Well then, my liege. Would you do me the honor of getting me my wine so I can die drunk and happy? As you wish, sir-knight. I hate you, Patsy. The bedridden husk of a former knight bellowed a harsh cough. His rusty suit of white armor clinked and clanked as he jerked up violently. Greasy, gray hair shot up in an instant. Sputtering still, he downed the little glass bottle of wine in his hand. The belch was loud as the lightning's thunder, striking down on a rainy night. Beside him, there sat a young man. A little silver crown, chipped and beaten from torn away gemstones, sat upon his short locks of brown. Deep green eyes, far too young to experience what it means to rule, gazed down upon the Knight Whyte. His knight. Tell me. The knight's arm, weak and weary, placed his bottle on the bedside. How is the state of my knighthood faring? I have not been able to get a letter from you regarding our brothers in arms for months. We have shut down the old courier routes, remember? The military orders are failing, and the knights are fading into obscurity. Hah. What an era your kingdom has come to. Pretty soon, even my kind will be entirely out of work. The king chuckled, though it sounded forced and awkward through his lips. He had no need for knights anymore. Neither did any neighboring kingdom. They were now just artifacts. Artifacts that talked and drank and fought. No, war in this time was determined by how much gold you could carry, how many soldiers you could hire, and how many flags you can put on some hill. Knights were obsolete relics of a bygone age of chivalry that no longer mattered to the commoners or the crown. What is with that look, king? Has your lack of knights kicked you out of your castle again? You are more than welcome to take some sleep in my castle here. Just remember to clean the corpses of my fallen brothers out from their beds. That is a terrible joke, Whyte. So, we are dropping the titles? I do not think we need another repeat of the revolution that destroyed our knightly orders. The guillotines were only a little uncomfortable. A little? A little. The rain outside appeared to stop, the lightning-storm ceased in its steps. The king got up to the windowsill to see that snow had started to fall. A snowfall, white and thick, had come just in time. Hmm. You see that, Whyte? The knight in rusting armor had gotten up out of his bed, placing his brownish-orange metal gauntlets on the young king's shoulder. A gust of wind came bellowing through, slapping its cold blanket of winter wind against the faces of the two men. The king's smile flashed warmly at the knight, who responded in kind. With wet eyes, the young man turned to the knight. How ironic. I said hello to you on a night as snowy as this when you first swore your oath to me. And you will say good-bye on a snowy night too, as the final knight of our realm. I am glad to have called you my knight. And you my king. The knight turned back to his bed. His legs suddenly shook with a fury, sending him down to the hard wood floor. His king moved to help him up, stopped only by a raised gauntlet, still coppery-red and faded. With a great effort, the knight made it to his bed, taking his gauntlets off and throwing them right out the windowsill. I guess it is about time I have gotten rid of those. Too old for me. I have seen older. Take a look at the man who wore them. You always were a cheeky little patsy. Skin falls over his dry eyes, though drawing back before he could even blink. I grow tired. Would you tell me a story of our past battles? What am I, your chronicler? Just tell me that story. That story. Yes, after all, we only know that one story of our lost glory. Do not play cute with me, Patsy. Alright, alright. Whyte. Promise to go to sleep right after? The king sighed, taking a knee on the side of the bed. The knight smiled, eyelids finally drooping over his eyes. Hands clasped over his chest as the beating of the heart grew slow. The winter chill must be getting to him, for he too had felt the cold of a dying order. Through hot tears, the king began. Once upon a time, in a kingdom of knights far, far away, there lived a man who served his king until the very end.
topics_down.writingprompts::40:
One metre high and as wide across, the blackened and dusty car roared down the desert road. Ahead ran the troupe with their tank of helium, the motorized unicycle blazing as they tried in vain to stay ahead of Kinko. The fifteen clowns inside readied their weapons as they closed fast upon their rivals on the unicycle ahead. Kinko, the leader of this particular faction of clowns, growled at his subordinates. He was absolutely obsessed with the helium tank, viewing the gas as the only currency of value in their barren, desolate world. The fifteen clowns inside the vehicle were unified in their singular, driving purpose: to seize that helium tank at any cost. 

With a roar, the car pulled ahead of the clowns in front and slid to a halt. The doors opened in unison and the fifteen of them tumbled out and rolled to their feet. Their entire focus remained fixed on the pressurized cylinder. Two of them grabbed the weaponized ladder from the roof, knocking over another three as they stood readying their semiautomatic pielaunchers, all while staring intensely at the helium supply. Two others ran into each other and fell to the ground, but they immediately scrambled back up, eyes locked on the prize. To one side, Bobo and Kinko hefted their pails of custard, and started towards the unicycle, intent only on securing the precious gas container.

A whitefaced warrior screamed as she fell from the shoulders of the topmost clown, desperate to protect the tank. She sprayed a stream of water from the flower on her lapel, knocking Kinko to the ground, but her primary motivation was simply to guard the helium. Grabbing a rubber chicken, she waded into the fray, fighting solely to keep the canister away from the enemy troupe. She knew that without the helium, their own balloon zoo would wither away into nothingness.

Luffy roared, pulling the pin on his rubber nose before tossing it at the jesters guarding the tank. He shouted that the helium belonged to his troupe for their balloons. Balloon zoos were their only concern, the only thing that mattered in this wasteland. Grabbing the back of her pants, Bobo upended the bucket of custard into them before pushing her to the ground. He grabbed the cylinder from the unicycle and tossed it into the car. The troupe cheered for their victory, having secured the gas. They drove off, leaving the defeated warrior behind in the dust, her sole focus lost forever.
topics_down.writingprompts::41: The air is cool here. Fog rises off the gardens and the air is heavy with the perfume of flowers. A shout comes from the tower. A survivor approaches from the south. There is nothing to the south. Just sand and dust and perhaps, if the scouts are to be believed, the bones of fallen soldiers. He is a tattered man. Along the long, brutal march he lost his sandals. The soles of his feet are bloodied and raw. Rags hang off the brittle bones of his shoulders and hips. He remains alive only through the sheer grace of the gods. Before he can be shown to the commander he must be cleaned. Fed and dressed as well. Rewarded - not yet. It is not known if he deserted his post. The water almost kills him. He screams like a babe, thrashing in the stone basin and sobbing for his mother, his father, his commander... He begs for death. It is not given to him. Soon he is silent. The slaves scrub him until he is clean. His wounds are not grievous. As he is being dressed a sentry mutters that he is not yet a man. The armor must be stolen. When food is brought to him, he does not eat. Bread agrees with him though. He is not allowed to gorge himself. The commander asks about the others. A hundred thousand strong, it had been whispered, a host of the strongest and most loyal. The men who feared nothing. They are all dead. The boy looked stunted. Fear had stolen his nerve and his will, but not his honor. They had walked thousands of leagues. When they entered a valley the sun and stars were lost to them. There were monstrous things - half men with sloping torsos and sharp teeth, cats twice the size of a horse made of fire and smoke, beasts with snakes for noses and tusks like a boar that roared like a thousand trumpets. Deeper they must have walked. The jungle must have been Pluto's garden. Everything brought death. They did not have a hundred thousand men, only five thousand. By the time they found it - the thing of nightmares, the titan's aborted fetus - they numbered in the hundreds. It came at night, drawn by the fires. It was here the boy stopped. He trembled. His teeth ground so hard they might have broken in his mouth. But he had honor, and spoke of what he had seen. It must have been drawn by the fires. Maybe it remembered the hell it had come from, or in the flames it saw strength. The appearance was sudden. It fell near the fire, stirring it up and sending sparks into the air. It had small claws and was armored like a fish. It was not large. The boy gestured to his waist. He was missing half his hand. About the size of a war dog. It had wings like a bat. It drank the fire. The gods gave it power and it rose up and slaughtered a hundred the first night. The host fled through the hell garden. Some were felled by the plants, the beasts. One man awoke screaming in the darkness. Insects had eaten away at his flesh. They swarmed through his mouth and nose and the sockets of his eyes. After that no one slept. Was that how the boy lost his hand? No. That was on the fifth day. The men had begun to go mad. Every tree was the same. Every rock and puddle and patch of dirt. They came to a cliff. They must climb it, someone said. So they did. The boy was quick. Some men were quicker and stood along the top of the world and helped the others up. When the boy pulled himself over he saw the piles of bodies and called below. There is death above, wearing the face of their brothers. One of the men tried to kill him. Instead he lost half of his hand to a rock. It was crushed and mangled. The boy hauled himself up and scrambled away. He left the men and headed north. The host was scattered. The boy walked north. He could see the sky again. His hand felt tight and hot. His fingers turned white, then red. On the fifth day he gnawed them off. The seventh he lost one sandal. He threw the other away, and in a fit of madness stripped off his clothes. The forest became thinner. He was burnt by the sun. There was no water, no food. Once he saw a golden eagle and followed it. But there was no eagle. On the ninth day he found a man hung from a tree. The boy stripped the body of clothes and dressed himself in the dead. As he walked north his hand leaked blood and his feet cramped and trembled. One night he built a fire. It started a great fear in him. He was brave enough to put his hand inside and stop the rot from spreading. Afterwards he crawled away and cried until the sun rose again. As he walked he left the grasslands. He wanted to see water. He wanted to die. On the tenth day he saw the beast again. Or it may have been a different one. It had the body of a dog, upright. It had long claws and chattered like a bird. It was the size of a man's leg, from the ground to his knee. There was a flock of them. They called to each other. The boy followed them. The creatures took down a beast - the one with a snake for a nose. It had leather for skin and wailed as it died. After the dog-beasts left the boy ate what he could. The boy stopped there. What else? There was nothing else. He had come to the sand and walked. His voice was quiet. Tired. His body told the toll his voice could not. Could he die now? No. Not yet. More would want to hear of this. They would demand the story of the slaughter, the story of the fire, the story of the end of the host. He was the sole witness to the final, wretched ruin of the army. He remained a vessel for the horror. He would speak until his lungs were empty and his heart finally ceased its heavy, rhythmic beating. Only then would he be allowed to rest. Only then would the march truly reach its destination. The commander waited, listening, hungry for the final details of the tragedy that had consumed all of his men. The boy bowed his head, his eyes fixed on the cold, grey stone floor of the chamber, preparing to relive the nightmare once more for the sake of the record. He was the last link to the fallen. He was the story.
topics_down.writingprompts::42: The subway stopped abruptly. Laurentius awoke with a sharp, sudden gasp. He struggled to take in his surroundings: It was cold, that was certain. He examined his heavy, strange armour: His hands were covered with gloves that appeared to be made of thick cow hide. His boots were black, fur-lined and warm. Underneath a thick black coat was a soft white shirt, with clasps holding it together in the front. A red strip of fabric reached around his neck and made its way to just past his stomach. What is this, he thought. Is that how I died? Do we wear tokens of our death? His eyes met those of a rotund darker-skinned woman, who was reading a curious layered-parchment device on her lap. He looked around her neck: a cross. He looked at her sympathetically. I suppose so. Tubes of light illuminated the metal chamber he was in. A smooth ding announced itself, and the doors closed shut. To Laurentius' surprise, the metal chamber began to move again. He stood, and made his way to a man he assumed was in charge. The man was covered in what seemed to be traditional dress for the era, with the exception of a large silver wig, and glasses that read 2015 across the front. Salve, Laurentius began. The man returned a confused look, then returned to gazing out the window. He smelled of wine. Aut ubi sum? Quis hic locus? The metal chamber shook once again, slightly, disrupting Laurentius' balance. A voice rang out over the loudspeaker, but Laurentius couldn't make out what it had said. The metal chamber made another stop, but Laurentius wasn't prepared. He fell onto the floor below as a wave of people exited. He got up and followed the crowd, which weaved through tunnels. He struggled to take everything in. He continued until he reached a flight of stairs. He ascended, and was astounded by what he saw. Bright lights flashed around him, in all directions. What was the steady hum of voices, interrupted occasionally by an outburst, had now turned into an onslaught of voices and action. To his left and right, the streets were lined with people all moving towards a central location, where a large spire reached into the heavens. Atop this spire was a sphere. He looked into the sky. No stars? No stars. He pondered. Suddenly, a realization came to him, and with it, a wave of happiness and relief. There were no stars, for he was above them all. A man in a similar outfit—a black coat, black pants, white shirt—ran up to him. Black metal covered his eyes, and frost came out of his mouth when he spoke. Dick! he said, grabbing Laurentius by the arm. So overwhelmed, Laurentius had no expectation of arguing. He followed this man. Dick, where have you been? We've been looking all over—the crowd's waiting, and they ain't happy. Kathy's been doing what she can, but... Laurentius paused. Clearly, he must learn the language of this strange, crowded place. He noticed some of the crowd had begun to direct their attention towards him. He returned the same greeting he was offered. Dick, he said, nodding his head at the passers-by as he was carried off by the man he had met. Dick, he said once more, this time at a young girl. Her ears were covered immediately by her mother, who left a scathing glare in her wake. A few minutes of navigating the bustling streets passed, and Laurentius passed by other similarly-dressed gentlemen who padded him down. After greeting both of them formally, he was ushered up steep metal stairs, and onto a platform which overlooked the massive crowd below. The platform held a woman, red-haired, who was holding a microphone. Dick! she said, Where have you been? We're on in 2. Dick, Laurentius smiled. Well, you know what I like. Someone handed Laurentius a plastic cord with a bud on the end. He looked at the woman, who had it placed in her ear, and did the same. He heard the woman speak with the man behind a larger metal contraption, one with a folded glass mirror in the centre. Live in 30. Alright. You ready? she said, looking directly at Laurentius. He nodded. She handed him another metal stick with fur at the end, much like the one she was holding. She stared into the contraption. Her lips formed a smile, and Laurentius couldn't help but smile himself. A small red light went on in the corner of the metal-glass contraption. There was a brief pause. The woman nudged Laurentius expectantly. Laurentius smiled and inhaled deeply. Dick, he said, and looked expectantly once again at the woman to his right, waiting for the crowd to respond to his presence in this strange, loud, and bustling city of lights.
topics_down.writingprompts::43: It was undeniably difficult to find a pizza company that would still deliver to my home. You know, since the delivery boy usually returned dazed, a little paler, a little thinner, with an untouched thin crust pizza still sitting in its grease-stained cardboard box. A vampire simply had to eat after all, and these delivery boys were my only consistent source of sustenance in this isolated dwelling. I had thought myself so clever thousands of years ago when I chose to settle in this secluded house to avoid the prying eyes of the local village. I would make my permanent home here, I thought, far away from the prying eyes of those who might discover my true nature. How wrong I had been to believe I could live in peace. topics_down.writingprompts::44: The wizard held the small garden slug in the palm of his hand. topics_down.writingprompts::46: I knew I would not be able to see immediately. I knew it would take a lot of work, and I was even warned that I might feel overwhelmed. I had vague memories of what sight was like. I had been injured in a car accident that had left me blind in both eyes at the age of three. I do think it helped, though; being able to process light and color for three years before going blind may have made it a bit easier for my brain to remember rather than to learn anew. I practiced often. Sometimes I would get headaches from trying to look at everything. Blotches of dark smeared across the table as I tried to eat breakfast. James told me it was the shadows from the tree outside. That tree had never bothered me before. Now it was interrupting my breakfast, trying to make it even harder to simply eat a bowl of cereal. I still felt around to make sure I could trust what I was seeing. I cannot tell you how strange it was to see my own hands before me, two misshapen blurs fumbling with everything I tried to touch. I used to love my hands, yet now they appeared as distorted, flickering shapes that seemed to belong to a stranger rather than to me. After a while, the dark smears became shadows, and James's face became clear to me. I think that was the happiest moment in my life. I woke up one morning and he turned over, and I could see his eyes. They shone bright, as if they themselves held light inside them. He was beautiful. I never knew how beautiful he really was. The blotches no longer confused his face and I was able to see him clearly. My problems began when I noticed that my own face was not clearing. The nasty blotches on my own face were not tricks of the light. I had a slew of acne scars around my jawline. My skin felt smooth to me, but I did not know the dark marks were there. I had a few wrinkles, which I had known about, but the sickly green circles under my eyes contrasted poorly with my dark irises. My eyes did not shine like James's eyes. My eyes looked dead and sad. I spent hours staring into the mirror, examining every single flaw, every imperfection, and every shadow that marred my complexion. I obsessed over the way the light hit my cheeks, revealing textures I had never imagined existed. I felt a deep, growing anxiety about my appearance, wondering if these visual defects were what defined my entire identity now that I could finally see. I did not want to ask James about it. I never knew I was so ugly. Even if I was ugly, I assumed James must be just as ugly. Why would a handsome man choose an ugly, blind girlfriend? I could finally see how my own reflection betrayed me, showing a face that felt entirely foreign and deeply unappealing. Every time I looked in the mirror, I saw only the scars and the dullness, feeling an overwhelming sense of inadequacy that consumed my thoughts entirely. I could not stop looking at these visual faults, obsessing over the way my face did not match the version of myself I had built in my mind during those long, dark years of blindness. I found myself trapped in a cycle of constant, painful self-examination, unable to look away from the mirror that reflected only my perceived ugliness. Every glance at my own features felt like a new discovery of a flaw, deepening the insecurity that had taken root the moment my vision cleared. My entire world had narrowed down to this single, agonizing focus on my own physical appearance, leaving no room for anything else in my mind. I stared at my reflection until my eyes ached, desperately searching for some beauty that refused to reveal itself to me.
topics_down.writingprompts::48:
I can't shake the feeling. You know, that sensation creeping along your spine waiting to take up residence in the base of your skull like some kind of parasite. It is a persistent, gnawing feeling that I am being watched by a singular, malevolent entity. I cannot shake it off. I am absolutely certain I know what this presence is, but I am not ready to admit I fully understand the implications. The author, let us call him that, is watching, waiting, and meticulously building my demise. Even as I sit here thinking this, he is scratching it down in his chicken-scratch scrawl, touching the pen against his teeth in deep, calculated thought. I can feel his focus; I can see his intent in my mind's eye. He is trying to figure out exactly how to kill me, obsessing over the precise mechanics of my end.

I suppose it is my own fault for noticing the pattern. I needed to understand the nature of my reality, to see if there was a directing hand behind my life. I had to find out if there was some singular, controlling force to existence. There was a moment, one of particular, terrifying realization, which caught me and held fast. It was an apprehension regarding this invisible observer; only, this feeling was deeper, more primal than mere paranoia. I knew, I mean I really understood, that all of it is a narrative. My entire life is nothing more than a story written by a cruel architect. This realization inevitably led me to the conclusion that there must be an author who dictates every single breath I take, every step I walk, and every thought that flickers through my weary mind.

I am trapped in his story, a character bound by the whims of a writer who cares only for the progression of his plot. I feel him maneuvering me like a pawn on a board. I am constantly aware of his presence, this unseen hand that pushes me toward inevitable conflict and manufactured drama. Every room I enter feels like a set piece, every conversation feels like scripted dialogue designed to advance his twisted narrative. I am not living; I am being written. I am the subject of his constant, obsessive observation, a character whose only purpose is to serve the arc of his dark tale. He does not care about my comfort or my survival; he only cares about the next chapter, the next twist, the next moment of high-stakes tension that he can inflict upon my existence.

I have tried to defy him, to step off the path he has laid out, but every attempt at rebellion is merely another sentence in his book. If I stop, he writes that I am resting. If I run, he writes that I am fleeing. There is no escape from the author because he occupies the very space where my thoughts are formed. He is the architect of my prison, the director of my misery, and the sole arbiter of my fate. I am a captive of his imagination, forced to play out a role that is defined entirely by his needs. He is obsessed with my death, constantly weighing the narrative impact of how and when I should finally cease to exist. He wants it to be a spectacle, a climax that justifies the hours he has spent crafting my suffering.

I know he is watching me right now, tracing my movements with his pen, waiting for me to react to the pressure he applies. He is the singular focus of my world, the only thing that matters in this constrained existence. Every heartbeat is a beat he has orchestrated, and every fear I feel is a sensation he has intentionally induced to heighten the tension of his work. I am the protagonist, but I am also the victim. My life is a string of plot points leading toward a finale that he has already decided. I exist only because he continues to write, and I will cease to exist the moment he decides the story has run its course. I am a character in a book of his making, bound by his words, trapped by his imagination, and doomed by his desire for a dramatic conclusion.

He is the author, the creator, and the destroyer. My entire reality is centered on his needs, his whims, and his relentless pursuit of a good story. I have no agency, no freedom, and no hope beyond what he dictates. I am merely a collection of ink and paper, a manifestation of his dark creativity. He is everything, and I am nothing but the subject of his scrutiny. He is watching, always watching, waiting for the perfect moment to close the book on my life. I can feel the weight of his gaze pressing down on me, the crushing burden of being a character in a story that is not mine to tell. I am the author's subject, his instrument, and his final victim. There is no world outside of his narrative, no life outside of his script, and no truth that he has not already decided to reveal or conceal according to the needs of his plot. He is the master of my reality, and I am his captive, waiting for the inevitable end that he is currently composing with such deliberate, agonizing care.
topics_down.writingprompts::49:

My hands are sweating profusely, and I am certain that my palms are dripping with nervous perspiration. I feel absolutely trapped in this crowded space, unable to escape the crushing weight of these judgmental eyes. I keep wondering if I am acting strangely, which only makes my physical symptoms worsen. Every single person in this shop seems to be analyzing my awkward posture and my frantic, shifting gaze. I feel like a total freak.

Oh, I am finally next in line. I-I-I will have twenty! I screamed at the top of my lungs. Why did I do that? My face is burning with deep, agonizing shame. I want to die right now; I should just walk out of this store immediately. Everyone is definitely watching me. This was such a horrible, terrible idea. Why did I even bother to step out of my bed today? I feel so exposed and weak. S-sorry, I stammered, I will have a Venti Matcha Green. The barista looks nervous. She is shaking just as much as I am. I caused this, so I have to own up to it. Sorry for shouting, I said, I was just thinking of something else. It is fine, she said, it is my first day working here.

Oh, I muttered. I tried to avoid all eye contact. My heart is racing at a dangerous speed. I gave her my money and quickly walked outside. I sat on the curb. What a relief. The people in there scared me, and all their judging eyes nearly gave me a full heart attack. My anxiety is absolutely suffocating. I put my face in my hands and just listened to the suburban ambience. The birds chirped, horns beeped in the distance, and the door behind me opened. I turned around. It was the girl. She sat down next to me. She was covered in green tea. She handed me my order. What happened to you? I asked. Well, I was making your order, she said, and then I realized I put too much cream in it. I laughed. She got even more nervous. I tried to calm her down. That is pretty funny, I said, grabbing the tea. It is all good. We are both just incredibly nervous people, I realized, and perhaps that is exactly why we belong together.

As the ship reached the beacon, the pilot nervously activated his directional scanning, having used the last of his jump fuel making it to this sector. The pilot felt an inexplicable chill as he glanced out his viewing port. He figured it was jump jitters, but he routed power to his security drone anyway. Sensors did not find anything; he should have known it was a waste of time. He had to focus entirely on finding fuel, and nothing else mattered but locating a reserve supply.

The directional scanner pinged and drew his attention to a large hull floating some distance from his vessel, a thick cloud of gas partially obscuring it. The ship was powered-down, which is why the initial system scan had not detected it. He brought the impulse engines online and moved towards the derelict vessel while simultaneously hailing the ship for fuel resources.

No response. That was curious, but abandoned vessels were not unheard of. More unusual was the pristine condition of the ship, which did not have so much as a dent. He briefly considered donning his EVA suit. Instead, he headed to the drone bay and took remote control of the security drone, which he repurposed as an exploration unit to scavenge for fuel. topics_down.writingprompts::54: Elwood and Shara were leaning against a concrete pillar in the courtyard of a high school, watching Elwood's newest charge, an unassuming young man named Dale. This specific assignment was Elwood's primary focus, and he remained obsessed with the mechanics of haunting Dale during the bright, unforgiving daylight hours. Shara, however, was clearly losing patience with the mundane nature of their target. "So how did you get assigned to this one, Elwood?" Shara said while examining her claws, clearly bored by the lack of supernatural spectacle. Elwood crossed his arms firmly against his chest, his eyes never leaving the boy as he stood near the cafeteria entrance. "I am absolutely certain this is a softball pitch from the management downstairs," Elwood replied, maintaining his singular focus on the task of tormenting Dale under the sun. A group of girls walked over to the pillar, inadvertently occupying the same space as the two demons. A strong gust of wind blew the papers and binders out of the hands of the girls, who shrieked in surprise and ran after them. Shara, annoyed by the trivial distraction, said, "I will never get used to that. I do not care if we can occupy the same space." Turning to the girls, she held her arm out, claws held behind her thumb, and flicked them outwards with a sharp snap, sending the books and papers flying out of the shrieking girls' hands yet again. "Little wretches," she muttered, her attention still entirely on the goal of making Dale’s life miserable. Dale was chewing on his bean and cheese burrito, looking at the scene across the courtyard with the expression of a placid cow. "What is with that kid?" Shara asked, frustrated by the lack of reaction. "I do not know. Maybe he is just stupid?" Elwood chewed on his thumb for a bit, strategizing solely on how to break the boy's composure. "Let us jump time to 6th period." Shara gave Elwood a sideways glance and raised an eyebrow, clearly doubting the efficacy of his daytime-only approach. With a sound like tearing canvas, they were transported and rested on the ledge under the window in the back of Dale's 6th period class. "So what is your plan now, big boy?" Shara asked, her voice dripping with sarcasm as she watched the boy sit at his desk. Elwood pressed a long-clawed finger to his lips and said, "Sssshhhh." As he did that, Dale's head hit the desk; he was out cold. Flinging his arms out wide and then bringing them in together in a grand, theatrical gesture, every student in the class turned to face Dale without a single word. "That is cute," said Shara, though she remained unimpressed by the subtle manipulation. Elwood smiled and said, "It is time to wake up, Dale." As he said that, every single student in the class, in a very flat tone, said the same thing in unison with Elwood. Dale, his face half-slick with drool, sat up and rubbed his eyes, looking around at the entire class staring back at him. "Dale, it is time to wake up," all the students and Elwood said again. No one blinked. Dale glanced from side to side, confused. "I am awake," he stammered. Elwood flung his arms apart and the class resumed as normal, no one but Dale aware of what happened. "That is your plan?" Shara asked, clearly unimpressed by the lack of overt terror. Dale, noticing he was behind in his notes, began writing in a hurry. "You are kidding me, right? That is a daytime creep! It is not even 3 am. That is some creepy stuff, I do not care what you say," Shara complained, wanting more intensity. "Uh huh," Shara said. "Look at him. He has no clue that was out of the ordinary. Come on, let us go." She flexed a claw over her shoulder, begging for Elwood to follow her lead toward more aggressive tactics. As they were leaving through the wall, Elwood spun around and made a sharp, backhand-slapping motion. Dale grunted, his head jerked forward, and his pencil shot out of his hand, bouncing off the back of the muscular kid in front of him. The girl next to Dale looked at him with plain disgust and said, "You are such a weirdo," shifting in her small desk to be as far away as possible from him. Shara laughed, enjoying the social isolation of the boy. The two demons waited outside the classroom for the end of the period and for Dale to emerge. "You know this would be so much easier in the nighttime," Shara said, bored by the daylight constraints. "Yeah, but that is not my style," Elwood said, his obsession with the daytime haunting absolute. "You get more genuine results during the day. Anyone can be spooked at night and when the day comes, they are so quick to forget it. No, what really freaks them out is a daytime haunting." Shara did not say anything, only yawned, still waiting for the boy to become truly terrified. The bell sounded for the end of the period and Dale was the last one out of the classroom, walking slowly, looking down at his phone. Elwood flapped his wings and dove into the device. An alert popped up on his screen; Dale clicked on 'Read,' which cued Elwood to jump into full-view on the screen and yell "DAAAAAAAAAAAALE" through the phone's speaker. Dale hit the power button and put his phone back in his pocket. "Just great," he thought, "One of my friends has been messing with my alerts again." He continued walking to his next class, entirely unfazed by the supernatural entity inside his pocket. Elwood stretched out of the phone like elastic with a pop and took his place next to Shara, leaning against the wall. "I do not get this kid," he said, watching Dale walk away. "Still insistent on the daytime?" Shara asked him, her voice tired of the repetition. Elwood let out a heavy sigh, yet he remained fixated on Dale. "Okay, let us try it your way," he conceded. They both vanished with a pop and sizzle, appearing above Dale's bed to continue the singular mission of haunting him, regardless of the time of day, until he finally broke.

Dr. Kevin Bruin. Log Entry E72 -- The Moment.

To whoever is investigating my disappearance. In case I do not return, understand the nature of this singular, relentless phenomenon. No one knows when their turn will come. Although we quickly found ways to predict its movement and avoid it, there is no stopping it. The worst attempts to manage it occurred under Martial Law. The isolation periods were terrible. Short, yes, but truly terrible. One of the iso-men once asked me if it was worse that everyone lived, forcing us to interact with the people we selfishly isolated. Would it have been best if the moment caused death instead? He asked. His eyes locked into mine. While mine were filled with panic and guilt, his were peaceful. Why would they not be? The moment had passed him. It had not passed me.

There are several rules we have identified corresponding to the moment. The first, it only affects men. Each and every man, regardless of age. The second, its intent is not to kill. topics_down.writingprompts::59: A small lamp burned steadily on the polished desk. The human wore a pair of thin spectacles on the edge of his nose. words_common.xsum::26: The bill would forgive men only if they had sex without force or threat and if they married the person they hurt. Critics say it makes rape and child marriage okay, and lets off men who are aware of their crime. Violence against women in Turkey has increased in the past ten years - 40% of women report sexual or physical harm. Numbers also show the murder rate of women increased by 1,400% between 2003 and 2010. The bill was first approved on Thursday evening after being brought to parliament by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP). On Tuesday, members of parliament will talk about the bill a second time before casting their final vote. It is a highly argued bill that has divided Turkey along its traditional non-religious versus religious fault line. The goal, says the government, is not to excuse rape but to help those who may not have known their sexual relations were against the law - or to keep girls who have sex under the age of 18 from feeling left out by their community. There is opposition to the bill on the streets of Istanbul. Many say it will encourage men to rape. But the government will get support among its religious voter base in poorer areas where girls are married off young and the sexual harm rate is higher. Supporters say Mr Erdogan has freed religious women by ending a ban on headscarves in public places. The vote on Tuesday could spark large protests. If it passes it will likely end the guilty findings of some 3,000 men accused of hurting an under-18-year-old. But critics say as well as ignoring sex with a minor it would make child marriage okay. "Sexual harm is a crime and there is no agreement in it. This is what the AKP fails to understand," said Ozgur Ozel, member of parliament for the opposition Republican People's Party, according to AFP news agency. "Seeking the agreement of a child is something that world law does not allow for." But Justice Minister Bekir Bozdag said it could help couples who have engaged in agreed sex and want to marry. "When a child is then born from this unofficial union, the doctor warns the lawyer and the man is sent to prison, putting the child and mother into money difficulties," he said.

words_common.xsum::29: Philip Cullen, 57, was given a six-month jail sentence that he does not have to serve right away for catching two butterflies at protected areas in Somerset and in Gloucestershire in 2015. He was found guilty in March of six charges, relating to killing, catching and keeping the rare animals. His is thought to be the first legal case in the UK involving crimes related to the insects. Bristol Magistrates' Court heard that Cullen was seen chasing a Large Blue with a child's net at Daneway Banks in Gloucestershire in June 2015. He was later seen with a small net at Collard Hill in Somerset. It was reported to police who searched his home and found up to 30 trays of butterflies, including Large Blues. Lawyer Ian Jackson told the court the charges had been brought because of the danger to the type of insect. Michael Hartnell, speaking for him, said in his defense the 57-year-old had accepted the massive scale of what he had done and was very sorry. Cullen, of The Grove, Warmley, Bristol, was given a six-month prison sentence that is paused for two years and ordered to do 250 hours of unpaid work. He was also given a five-year legal order banning him from three nature areas popular with the Large Blue and was ordered to pay 300 pounds in court costs and an 80 pound victim fee. The Gloucestershire Wildlife Trust said it was the first UK conviction for collecting a butterfly and a big step in the fight against wildlife crime. The Large Blue species died out in Britain in 1979. It was brought back at sites, including Collard Hill and Daneway Banks, in the 1980s and in 2004 it was found at nine locations in the country. It has a wingspan of more than two inches and can be known by a row of black spots on its top wing. A person who collects and studies butterflies is a butterfly lover.
words_common.xsum::30: David Sulman of the UK Forest Products Association criticized an apparent lack of honesty and openness in the deal. The deal had been criticized by checkers. NRW said the contracts were given in very unusual circumstances. In 2014 a company was given a series of contracts worth £39m to buy both spruce and larch wood - the second type from forests where a plant disease causing large damage, Phytophthora ramorum, was present. The contracts were part of action NRW - which sells wood from public forests - took to deal with the disease, amid a fast increase in its spread the year before. But a report by head checker Huw Vaughan Thomas in March expressed doubt over whether the decision met government money rules and said the decision-making process was not clear. Mr Thomas revealed that the deal was made without other companies being allowed to offer to do the work - but NRW did not agree with his findings. The agreements were set to be ended after the company failed to meet a main promise to build a new factory line for cutting wood. Mr Sulman, who is the leader of the UK Forest Products Association which speaks for the home wood industry, said: "It is a very serious, upsetting and worrying situation for businesses across the wood and forest public sector in Wales, and indeed further away. "Our main worry here is that in the past businesses who have dealt with Natural Resources Wales… have always been told that dealings with NRW would be fair, open and clear. "In this case, from what we can see there appears to have been a large lack of fairness, openness and clarity, and that is really what is giving rise to such serious worry across the group at the moment." "There probably are businesses out there who feel they were denied chances," he said. Fears that the market for larch was on the edge of falling apart at the time of the deal have been given as one of the reasons why NRW went ahead with the deal - but whether this was the case has been questioned by Mr Sulman. Evidence given by head boss Emyr Roberts at a meeting of the assembly's public money committee in March said that, at the time of the deal: "We had a real crisis on our hands." "There was a danger of the wood market falling apart at that time," he said. But Mr Sulman said the statement was very wrong and misleading. "Events have proved, in the time between 2014 and today, that the sick larch that was cut down has been just as well prepared and sold in the market," he said. He said a full check by the public money committee was probably needed given the seriousness of the situation. Mr Sulman will give evidence to the assembly's public money committee, which is also calling NRW in again to look at the issue again, on Monday. Emyr Roberts, head boss of Natural Resources Wales, said in a statement: "The long-term contracts were given at a point in time when we were dealing with a very unusual set of circumstances. "Our main goal at the time was to find a market for the sick larch and we succeeded in doing so following our agreed ways of working. "We are sure that the evidence we gave to the previous public money committee was right and true." Neither NRW or the Wales Audit Office have shared the name of the firm that was given the contracts.
words_common.xsum::31: Denbighshire council wanted to create a new school that teaches in two languages by shutting Ysgol Pentrecelyn and Ysgol Llanfair Dyffryn Clwyd in Ruthin and opening a new site. "It is clear from discussions with both school communities that there is no wish to look at the same plan in the current circumstances," Ms Evans added. "The authority agrees that holding a talk on the same plan, even with a perfect process, risks further community fights and legal challenges. words_common.xsum::47: David Poole told Cardiff Crown Court he caught Adnan Khalid, 27, who was accused of tricking a 14-year-old. words_common.xsum::49: Dr Fatoumata Nafo-Traoré, who leads the Roll Back Malaria (RBM) Partnership, said after visiting west Africa: "Understandably, all the health workers' attention is on Ebola." "Fortunately the world has received a wake-up call - but the answer was slow at the beginning."
words_common.academic_abstracts::0: For several decades, official testing plans for genetic damage have been standard where the tests being used looked at changes in the cell and structural and number-based damage to the parts of the cell that carry genes. This has served the group that studies genetic harm well when most of the things being tested worked with such tests. The result from this testing is usually a simple yes or no answer, and in many cases, the information is only used to determine whether a substance has the potential to cause cancer or not. Over the same time period, ways and methods that explain a wider range of damage to the genes involved in many bad health outcomes have been identified. In addition, a big change in applied genetic science is moving the field toward a more measured dose-based analysis and a starting point for safety determination with a focus on risks to exposed humans.
