Pass me that bottle, would you, Patsy? 
 
 Get it yourself, Ser Whyte. I am not your servant anymore. 
 
 Right. Well then, my leader. Would you do me the favor of getting me my wine so I can die drunk and happy? 
 
 As you wish, sir-knight. 
 
 I hate you, Patsy. 
 
 The sick, dying man who used to be a knight let out a loud, hard cough. His old suit of white metal armor made loud noises as he sat up quickly. Messy, gray hair stood up in a second. Coughing still, he finished the little glass bottle of wine in his hand. The burp was loud like the sound of thunder, hitting hard on a rainy night. 
 
 Beside him, there sat a young man. A little silver crown, broken and worn from missing pieces of glass, sat upon his short hair of brown. Deep green eyes, far too young to understand what it means to lead, look down upon the Knight Whyte. His knight. 
 
 Tell me. The knight's arm, weak and tired, put his bottle on the side of the bed. How is Isabella doing? I have not been able to get a letter from you for months. 
 
 We have shut down the mail service, remember? The delivery service handles shipping for boxes, but messages go through that fancy electronic message system. 
 
 Ha. What a time your land has come to. Bows that shoot steel and fire. Writers who control entire towns. Pretty soon, even my kind will have no work left to do. 
 
 The king laughed, though it sounded fake and strange through his lips. He had no need for knights anymore. Neither did any nearby land. They were now just old things. Old things that talked and drank and fought. No, war in this time was decided by how much money you could carry, how many people you could take, and how many flags you can put on some hill. 
 
 What is with that look, king? Has that queen kicked you out of your home again? You are more than welcome to take some sleep in my room here. Just remember to clean the dead bodies out from their beds. 
 
 That is a terrible joke, Whyte. 
 
 So, we are dropping the fancy names? I do not think we need another repeat of Georgie starting another fight against the leaders. The machines that cut off heads, they were only a little uncomfortable. 
 
 A little? 
 
 A little. 
 
 The rain outside seemed to stop, the storm of lightning finished its work. The king went up to the window to see that snow had started to fall. A snowfall, white and thick, had come just in time. 
 
 Hmm. You see that, Whyte? 
 
 The knight in rusty armor had gotten up out of his bed, placing his brownish-orange metal gloves on the young king's shoulder. A burst of wind came rushing through, hitting its cold blanket of winter air against the faces of the two men. The king's smile flashed warmly at the knight, who smiled back in the same way. With wet eyes, the young man turned to the knight. 
 
 How strange. I said hello to you on a night as snowy as this. 
 
 And you will say good-bye on a snowy night too. 
 
 I am glad to have called you my knight. 
 
 And you my king. 
 
 The knight turned back to his bed. His legs suddenly shook with a force, sending him down to the hard wood floor. His king moved to help him up, stopped only by a raised hand, still red and faded. With a great effort, the knight made it to his bed, taking his heavy gloves off and throwing them right out the window. 
 
 I guess it is about time I got rid of those. Too old for me. 
 
 I have seen older. Take a look at the man who wore them. 
 
 You always were a funny little patsy. Skin falls over his dry eyes, though pulling back before he could even blink. I grow tired. Would you tell me a story? 
 
 What am I, your mother? 
 
 Just tell me that story. 
 
 That story. Yes, after all, we only know that one story. 
 
 Do not play games with me, Patsy. 
 
 Alright, alright. Whyte. Promise to go to sleep right after? 
 
 The king sighed, taking a knee on the side of the bed. The knight smiled, eyelids finally falling over his eyes. Hands joined over his chest as the beating of the heart grew slow. The winter chill must be getting to him, for he too had felt the cold. Through hot tears, the king began. 
 
 Once upon a time, in a village far, far away...
words_common.writingprompts::40:
One metre high and as wide across, the blackened and dusty car moved fast down the desert road. Ahead ran the group with their tank of gas, the motorized one-wheeled bike moving fast as they tried in vain to stay ahead of Kinko. The fifteen clowns inside readied their weapons as they closed fast upon their rivals on the one-wheeled bike ahead. 
 "Boffo, Luffy, Bobo," said Kinko, "bad clowns messed with us for the last bad time. When we catch up to those guys, I want you to really hurt their backsides. Hit them so bad that they can honk their noses from the inside." They nodded, and gripped their big wooden sticks all the tighter. 
 
 With a roar, the car pulled ahead of the clowns in front and slid to a stop. The doors opened together and the fifteen of them tumbled out and rolled to their feet. Two of them grabbed the long ladder from the roof, knocking over another three as they stood getting their pie-launching guns ready - and the same three again as the original two turned to see what they hit. Two others ran into each other and fell to the ground, lying flat and still. To one side, Bobo and Kinko held their buckets of pudding, and started towards the one-wheeled bike. 
 
 "Bad people!" screamed a white-faced fighter as she fell from the shoulders of the top clown. Rolling as she landed, she sprayed a stream of water from the flower on her shirt, knocking Kinko to the ground with a very funny sound. Grabbing a rubber chicken from the driver, she jumped into the fight, knocking Kinko's clowns over like bowling pins. "That gas is ours!" 
 
 "No it is not!" yelled Luffy, pulling the pin on his rubber nose before throwing it at the funny people falling from the bike seat. "That gas is ours, for our balloons! Balloon parks are ours, you hear? Ours!" Grabbing the back of her pants, Bobo dumped the bucket of pudding into them before pushing her to the ground. As she bounced up and started running in circles, he grabbed the tank from the bike and tossed it in the car. "Our group!" he cheered, as the rest of the clowns piled into the car. One started the front handle to life, and with a happy song, they drove off down the road, to their big tent in the empty land. 
 As they disappeared in the distance, the white-faced fighter sadly blew her horn, and watched the dust cloud fade away.
words_common.writingprompts::41: The air is cool here. Fog rises off the gardens and the air is heavy with the smell of flowers. A shout comes from the tower. Stranger coming from the south. There is nothing to the south. Just sand and dust and perhaps, if the wild people are to be believed, the bones of monsters. He is a messy man. Along the march he lost his shoes. The bottom of his feet are bloody. Rags hang off the bones of his shoulders and hips. He is only alive through the kindness of the gods. Before he can be shown to the leader he must be cleaned. Fed and dressed as well. Rewarded - not yet. It is not known if he ran away. The water almost kills him. He screams like a baby, fighting in the pool and crying for his mother, his father, his leader... He begs for death. It is not given to him. Soon he is silent. The workers scrub him until he is clean. His wounds are not bad. As he is being dressed a guard whispers that he is not yet a man. The metal suit must be stolen. When food is brought to him, he does not eat. Bread agrees with him though. He is not allowed to eat too much. The leader asks about the others. A hundred thousand strong, it had been whispered, a group of the strongest and most loyal. The men who feared nothing. They are all dead. The boy looked small. Fear had stolen his courage and his will, but not his pride. They had walked thousands of miles. When they entered a valley the sun and stars were lost to them. There were giant things - half men with leaning bodies and sharp teeth, cats twice the size of a horse made of fire and smoke, animals with snakes for noses and long teeth like a wild pig that roared like a thousand trumpets. Deeper they must have walked. The thick woods must have been a place of total death. Everything brought death. They did not have a hundred thousand men, only five thousand. By the time they found it - the thing of nightmares, the giant's lost child - they numbered in the hundreds. It came at night, pulled by the fires. It was here the boy stopped. He shook. His teeth ground so hard they might have broken in his mouth. But he had pride, and spoke of what he had seen. It must have been pulled by the fires. Maybe it remembered the bad place it had come from, or in the flames it saw strength. The appearance was sudden. It fell near the fire, stirring it up and sending sparks into the air. It had small claws and was covered like a fish. It was not large. The boy pointed to his waist. He was missing half his hand. About the size of a hunting dog. It had wings like a bat. It drank the fire. The gods gave it power and it rose up and killed a hundred the first night. The group ran through the death garden. Some were killed by the plants, the animals. One man woke up screaming in the darkness. Bugs had eaten away at his skin. They filled his mouth and nose and the holes of his eyes. After that no one slept. Was that how the boy lost his hand? No. That was on the fifth day. The men had begun to lose their minds. Every tree was the same. Every rock and puddle and patch of dirt. They came to a high wall. They must climb it, someone said. So they did. The boy was quick. Some men were quicker and stood along the top of the world and helped the others up. When the boy pulled himself over he saw the piles of bodies and called below. There is death above, wearing the face of their brothers. One of the men tried to kill him. Instead he lost half of his hand to a rock. It was crushed and broken. The boy pulled himself up and ran away. He left the men and headed north. The group was spread out. The boy walked north. He could see the sky again. His hand felt tight and hot. His fingers turned white, then red. On the fifth day he chewed them off. The seventh he lost one shoe. He threw the other away, and in a fit of madness took off his clothes. The forest became thinner. He was burnt by the sun. There was no water, no food. Once he saw a golden bird and followed it. But there was no bird. On the ninth day he found a man hanging from a tree. The boy took the clothes off the body and dressed himself in the dead man’s gear. As he walked north his hand leaked blood and his feet cramped and shook. One night he built a fire. It started a great fear in him. He was brave enough to put his hand inside and stop the rot from spreading. Afterwards he crawled away and cried until the sun rose again. As he walked he left the grassy fields. He wanted to see water. He wanted to die. On the tenth day he saw the beast again. Or it may have been a different one. It had the body of a dog, standing up. It had long claws and talked like a bird. It was the size of a man's leg, from the ground to his knee. There was a group of them. They called to each other. The boy followed them. The creatures killed an animal - the one with a snake for a nose. It had leather for skin and cried as it died. After the dog-beasts left the boy ate what he could. The boy stopped there. What else? There was nothing else. He had come to the sand and walked. His voice was quiet. Tired. His body told the hard story his voice could not. Could he die now? No. Not yet. More would want to hear of this. He remained here, waiting for the truth to be told by his tired lips.
words_common.writingprompts::42:
The train stopped suddenly. Laurentius woke up with a sharp breath. He worked to look at his surroundings: It was cold, that was for sure. He checked his clothes: His hands were covered with gloves that looked like they were made of cow skin. His boots were black, lined with fur and warm. Underneath a thick black coat was a soft white shirt, with small hooks holding it shut in the front. A red piece of cloth went around his neck and hung down to just past his stomach. "What is this," he thought. "Is that how I died? Do we wear signs of our death?" His eyes met those of a round darker-skinned woman, who was reading a strange folded-paper device on her lap. He looked around her neck: a cross. He looked at her with pity. "I guess so."

Tubes of light lit up the metal room he was in. A smooth sound played, and the doors shut closed. To the surprise of Laurentius, the metal room began to move again. He stood up, and made his way to a man he thought was in charge. The man, covered in what looked like normal clothes for the time, except for a large silver wig, and glasses that read "2015" across the front.

"Hello," Laurentius began.

The man gave a confused look, then went back to looking out the window. He smelled of wine.

"And where am I? What is this place?"

The metal room shook once again, a little, hurting the balance of Laurentius. A voice spoke out over the speaker, but Laurentius could not tell what it had said. The metal room made another stop, but Laurentius was not ready. He fell onto the floor below as a group of people walked out. He got up and followed the crowd, which moved through tunnels. He worked to take everything in: Musicians lined the covered street. Few sellers, from what he understood. He kept going until he reached a set of stairs. He went up, and was shocked by what he saw.

Bright lights flashed around him, in all ways. What was the steady hum of voices, broken sometimes by a loud sound, had now turned into a rush of voices and movement. To his left and right, the streets were lined with people all moving toward a middle spot, where a large tall tower reached into the sky. On top of this tower was a ball. He looked into the sky.

No stars?

No stars. He thought. Suddenly, a realization came to him, and with it, a wave of happiness and relief. There were no stars, for he was above them all: Could these be the fields of the dead? They were more beautiful than he had ever thought.

Suddenly, a man in a similar outfit – a black coat, black pants, white shirt – ran up to him. Black metal covered his eyes, and cold air came out of his mouth when he spoke.

"Dick!" he said, grabbing Laurentius by the arm. So shocked, Laurentius had no thought of arguing. He followed this man.

"Dick, where have you been? We have been looking all over – the crowd is waiting, and they are not happy. Kathy has been doing what she can, but..."

Laurentius paused. Clearly, he must learn the language of the place he had arrived in. He noticed some of the crowd had begun to look at him. He gave back the same greeting he was offered.

"Dick," he said, nodding his head at the people as he was pulled off by the man he had met.

"Dick," he said once more, this time at a young girl. Her ears were covered quickly by her mother, who gave him a mean look as they walked away.

A few minutes of walking through the busy streets passed, and Laurentius passed by other dressed men who patted him down. After greeting both of them in a formal way, he was led up steep metal stairs, and onto a flat space which looked over the huge crowd below. The space held a woman, red-haired, who was holding a small handheld speaker. "Dick!" she said, "Where have you been? We are on in two."

"Dick," Laurentius smiled.

"Well, you know what I like."

Someone handed Laurentius a plastic cord with a small plug on the end. He looked at the woman, who had it placed in her ear, and did the same. Maybe this was part of the welcome ceremony.

He heard the woman speak with the man behind a larger metal machine, one with a folded glass mirror in the center.

"Live in thirty."

"Alright. You ready?" she said, looking directly at Laurentius. He nodded. She handed him another metal stick with fur on the end, much like the one she was holding. She stared into the machine. Her lips formed a smile, and Laurentius could not help but smile himself.

A small red light went on in the corner of the metal-glass machine. There was a short pause. The woman pushed Laurentius to start.

Laurentius smiled and took a deep breath. "Dick," he said, and looked expectantly once again at the woman to his right.
words_common.writingprompts::43:
It was hard to find a pizza company that would still bring food to my house. You know, since the delivery boy usually came back confused, a little paler, a little thinner, with an untouched thin crust pizza still in its box.

A vampire had to eat after all.

I had thought myself so clever all those thousands years ago. Rome! Home of every religion but the one that mattered, away from those bad crosses made of cheap wood that had begun to rest against every doorway in Jerusalem. I would make my home in Italy, I thought. Never would the new faith follow me to what had been the greatest nation the world had ever seen!

How wrong I had been.

Almost overnight the preachers had shown up, and within a century there was a cross on every door and a church on every block. I was trapped, certain death just waiting outside if I so much as poked my head out of my beautiful wood door.

Outside, I could sense three children giggling as they pushed each other outside on my doorstep. Finally, one of them jumped up to ring the doorbell, and giggling, they ran away. Ringing the doorbell of the lonely person, and escaping to tell the story! How very exciting.

I hate humans, I said to myself.

Looking through the seemingly 800th phone book they had left stuck in my mail slot the last year, I tried to find a restaurant that maybe had not heard the story of the feared Pale Master of The Takeout.

One could hope.
words_common.writingprompts::44:
The wizard held the small garden slug in the palm of his hand.

He was Marvolio IV. He had called up monsters the size of castles, he had made new rivers, he had figured out a spell that stopped you from getting nose itches when your hands were busy. He would not wrongly call a slug when he was looking for God?

He carefully placed the slug down. Even if it obviously was not God maybe it was God's favorite slug or something.

He spent hours looking through his notes, measuring the holy calling circles, checking the basic liquids for any dirt or things that did not belong. A mistake was somewhere in here. The slug chewed at the corner of his work book.

After the moon began falling to the ground and the sun started peeking over the horizon God decided to speak.

LETTUCE

Wh-what Marvolio whispered. The voice had appeared directly in his head and though his mostly sane mind could barely take it. He knew. He knew that voice was the voice from which all started and all were kept alive. He knew that voice was older than time. He knew that voice came from the three inch slug on his work bench.

BRING ME LETTUCE. IT IS NOT WISE TO REFUSE ME.

Marvolio walked in a haze into his kitchens and found a basket of lettuce. He looked at it. It was a bit soft and old and some blue fuzzy stuff had begun creeping around the edges. Wizards did not go in for vegetables much.

Though the slug was on the opposite side of the house its voice sprang again unwelcome into Marvolio's brain.

YES THAT WILL DO NICELY.

Surely not, I mean for God? It is not- I mean? I can run down to the market and get some of that black Italian cabbage tha-

NO I LIKE IT LIKE THAT. NICE AND SOFT.

Marvolio talked to himself in a strange way as he brought the rotting vegetable back to the one true boss of life.

God enjoyed the lettuce completely while Marvolio sat and talked to himself some more.

WELL.

Well what? - I mean Um, Yes- L-lord.

YOU WANTED TO KNOW SOMETHING? YOU PUT A LOT OF EFFORT INTO BRINGING ME HERE SO YOU SHOULD PROBABLY ASK.

Oh um. Well. Why did you make everything? I mean there is so much pain and-

LETTUCE.

I do not think I have any more.

NO I MADE THIS WORLD TO GROW THE CORRECT KIND OF LETTUCE. THIS IS THE MOST LETTUCY OF ALL POSSIBLE WORLDS.

That actually explains a lot.

If God could move his shoulders he would have, instead he stared at Marvolio with no feeling in his eyes with his holy stalks.

Should I try to send you back.

NO JUST PUT ME OUT IN THE BACK GARDEN THAT IS A GOOD LAD.

Marvolio never spoke of his time, nor did magic again, but he did take up gardening and became famous across the land for his impressive variety of award winning lettuce and cabbages.
words_common.writingprompts::45:
I don't know Sharon, I'm just tired of it Markond leant back in his tall chair made of the bones of many a dead hero. I sit in this home all day and night waiting on some poor normal group of new travelers to walk in. I'm just feeling unhappy with my work.

Well honey, perhaps it's time for a change? Maybe a new start?

But we have a great money situation, a beautiful cave to raise some dead people and I have a safe job.

Marky, it doesn't mean anything if you're not happy. You always dreamed of opening that hotel remember She walked over and gently rubbed his shoulders. We used to talk about it on those long cold nights before you became powerful, we would buy an old farm building and fix it up, let the rooms out, make our own beer, cook meals and hire a music player or two.

Of course I remember but that was nothing but a silly dream, there's no way a dead magic man could run a pub, it's just... not the normal thing to do.

Marky, baby, who cares what the normal thing is? Lets do it! There's that bad little pub down the road which you send your helpers to so they can spread lies of your gold but that's our only competition! We've got the whole business area covered!

You know what Sharon, you're right, you're always right. Lets do this baby.

6 months later, Markond stood cleaning a cup with his favorite cloth. A warm smile crossed his face. The pub was busy, the fire pit burned warmly in the middle of the room and the singer sang songs of heroes of old. Sharon was serving a group of loud Dwarves and she had never looked more beautiful to him, not even on the day he took her from her home. Everything was perfect.
words_common.writingprompts::46:
I knew I would not be able to see right away. I knew it would take a lot of work, and I was even warned that I might feel very stressed. I had fuzzy memories of what sight was like. I had been hurt in a car crash that had left me unable to see in both eyes at the age of three. I do think it helped, though; being able to handle light and color for three years before going unable to see may have made it a bit easier for my brain to remember rather than to learn all over again. 
 
 James helped me a lot. Sometimes I would close my eyes to get around like I had before. He would suddenly get in front of me and block my way, teasing me. It was not mean; if I complained, he would raise his arms out and stop my movement until he closed them around me, hugging me tight. 
 I will not let go until you open your eyes, he would say. No one had ever loved me this much. I could hear it in his voice and feel it every time he hugged me. 
 
 I practiced often. Sometimes I would get headaches from trying to look at everything. Spots of dark smeared across the table as I tried to eat breakfast. James told me it was the shadows from the tree outside. That tree had never bothered me before. Now it was getting in the way of my breakfast, trying to make it even harder to simply eat a bowl of cereal. I still felt around to make sure I could trust what I was seeing. I cannot tell you how strange it was to see my own hands in front of me, two oddly shaped blurs moving around with everything I tried to touch. I used to love my hands. 
 
 After a while, the dark smears became shadows, and James's face became clear to me. I think that was the happiest moment in my life. I woke up one morning and he turned over, and I could see his eyes. They shone bright, as if they themselves held light inside them. He was beautiful. I never knew how beautiful he really was. 
 
 The spots no longer confused his face and I was able to see him clearly. My problems began when I noticed that my own face was not clearing. The bad spots on my own face were not tricks of the light. I had a lot of skin scars around my jawline. My skin felt smooth to me, but I did not know the dark marks were there. I had a few lines, which I had known about, but the unhealthy green circles under my eyes looked bad against my dark eyes. My eyes did not shine like James's eyes. My eyes looked dead and sad. 
 
 I did not want to ask James about it. I never knew I was so ugly. Even if I was ugly, I thought James must be just as ugly. Why would a handsome man choose an ugly, blind girlfriend? I could finally see how women looked at him. Nobody ever looked at me that way. A trip to the food store used to be a fun time for both of us. Now, it was another chance to see every other woman- who he could easily have if he wanted- stealing quick looks at him, or smiling if he looked at them. 
 
 I have no idea what to think. Sometimes I think he smiles back at them. I caught him looking at two women walking by us at a restaurant. My stomach was in knots. I did not say anything. I just stared down at my food and tried not to lose my hunger. 
 Is something wrong? James asked. 
 No, why? I said, forcing my scarred face into a look of fun. 
 Just asking, he said. I love you, he said, with a smile. 
 
 I wish I could believe it.
words_common.writingprompts::48:
The Author 

I can't shake the feeling. You know, that sensation creeping along your back waiting to take up space in the base of your head like some kind of bug. It's a feeling you cannot name that you are being watched. I can't shake it off. I am sure I know what it is, but I'm not ready to admit I know. The... writer let's call him. He is watching, waiting, building. Even as I think this, he is scratching it down in his messy handwriting, touching the pen against his teeth in thought. I can feel it; I can see it in my mind. He's trying to figure out how to kill me. 

I suppose it is my own fault. See I kept asking, I needed to understand. I had to find out if there was some guiding hand to life. If people had a goal, a reason, I needed to know what goal we worked toward. There's a moment, one of real understanding, which caught me and held fast. Like my fear regarding someone watching me; only, this feeling was deeper, more basic. I knew, I mean really understood; all of it is a story. Life is a story. Which naturally led me to the conclusion -- there needs to be a planner, a writer. 

The car almost hit me. I had a feeling of pressure against my chest getting close to the point of panic. I didn't cross when the green man showed on the crossing light, instead I took a step back. My gut feeling tingled. The taxi driver never saw me, I hadn't seen him either. His drunk moving vehicle slammed into the same traffic light post I had been, until recently, standing by. Can I tell you how bad that is, I have this understanding, followed by a sudden feeling of fear. If I hadn't listened to my inner warning, I might have been crushed between the taxi's car and the hard place which was the traffic light pole. I turned my eyes upward, burning eyes and tight jaw not stopping me, and yelled at whoever worked at making this story. 

"What the actual hell was that?" I said. 

Okay, so I realize my choice of words probably did not fall into the definition of careful, but hell we're talking about some kind of god-figure deciding on my time to die. 

*Are you sure?* My logical brain asked. 

I thought about my position, both in the physical and beyond the physical sense. 

*Yeah, I'm really sure,* I replied to myself inside. *How else do you explain the sudden realization and then my almost immediate death. There's a writer and he doesn't want to be known.* 

I'm not sure how I knew the writer didn't want to be known, or the fact he was a man, but I figured it was something in my general make-up giving me the knowledge. Oh don't get all fancy and preach at me now, I'm not talking religion or spirit stuff, I want to live damnit. I stood, still staring up at the sky, trying to show my total disgust and frustration when the light pole made a noise, in a way that was not normal. I moved my head so my eyes were even with the pole. 

The metal looked bent, and I realized that the car had burst into flames. 

*When had that happened?* I thought. *Nevermind, run stupid.* 

My inner talk is not always the most kind; I'm a blunt sort. So, I ran. What I was running from, if Mr. All-Knowing writer was already in my head, he could follow me anywhere. Hell, I could have a sudden memory, and he could hit me with a large truck. If this writer decided I was going to die, why didn't he do it already? 

*Damn me,* I thought. *It's about the drama; the story.* 

"Sick person," I said. I knew he'd hear me, or he'd write that in his childish handwriting, knowing I meant it for him. 

*What if I stop?* 

I looked up again, and said, "What are you going to do with a character who won't do what you say, huh?" 

Naturally, he didn't answer. It wasn't like I expected a voice from the sky, but I figured he might strike me down with lightning or something, I mean he potentially has it within his power, right? He might decide my knowledge of the plan made me a problem. 

*What the hell is the plan anyway?* 

I don't know, I guess the plan is for me to die. Perhaps, he's not into the normal stuff. Maybe, just maybe, he wants my death to be something big, something of a show. I bet that's it. I got the feeling again; a gut punch to my stomach making my insides feel sick like they were coming out, and the noise in my stomach suggested I take a step back. I did. Something went through the skin in my back. It was a smooth, easy motion that opened the skin. I felt the warm blood mixing with my sweat as it soaked the back of my flannel shirt. 

A quiet voice whispered in my ear. "Hello main character," she said. "I'm the one against you, the writer says hello." 

That was all she said. She didn't have a smell, like you would expect. She was a ghost from the shadows. I don't know who she was, or why her, but she'd made it clear... I was right. Take that jerk. I didn't have the strength to say it, but I know he heard me. 

Everything is just a story that he writes for his own fun, and I am stuck in the middle of it. I will keep fighting, even if he wants me to end. I will stay here and be the person I choose to be, even if he tries to make me someone else. This is my life, even if he holds the pen.
words_common.writingprompts::49:
Will life get any better? How is tomorrow's weather? Oh God, that girl is looking right at me. She probably hates me. Am I sweating? I think I'm sweating. Waiting in this coffee line is killing me. These people are looking right at me. My hands are sweating right now, they're probably dripping. 

Oh, I'm next in line. "I-I'll have 20!" I screamed. WHY DID I DO THAT!?! Kill me now, I might as well just walk out. Everybody was watching me. It was a horrible idea. Why did I even step out of bed today? "s-Sorry," I said "I'll have a Large Matcha Green." The person making coffee was nervous. She was shaking as much as I was. I did this, I have to own up to it. "Sorry for shouting. I was thinking of something else." "It's fine," she said "It's my first day ever working." 

"Oh," I muttered. I tried not to keep eye contact. My heart was racing. She has such a cute voice. I gave her my money and walked out. I sat on the curb. What a relief. The people in there scared me, and all their judging eyes nearly gave me a heart attack. That girl, she was cute though. When was the last time I had actually ever talked to a girl? 1st grade? It didn't matter anyways, she probably thought I was a weirdo. I shouted at her. I put my face in my hands and just listened to the sounds of the neighborhood. The birds chirped, horns beeped in the distance, trees swished around, and the door behind me opened. I turned around. It was the girl. 

She sat down next to me. She was covered in green tea. She handed me my order. "What happened to you?" I asked. "w-Well I was making your order. Then I realized I put too much cream, and then I realized, wait, why did I put coffee in this, this is tea." I laughed. She got even more nervous. I tried to calm her down. "That's pretty funny," I grabbed the tea "It's all good." I sipped, it was bad. "Hey, you want to come over?!" she asked. It was weird, super sudden at that, and it made me nervous. words_common.writingprompts::50:
A wise man, in a rare attempt at humor, once said "Heaven was eating rich goose liver to the sound of horns."

Page of a journal of a cook - Recently Deceased.

As a cook, I fully agree with the rich goose liver but I have never had much of an ear for horns. Rich goose liver for those who do not know (and do not worry, many do not) is a dish as old as the art of cooking. Rich goose liver, French for fat liver, is the most important part of any self respecting cook. Take a duck, better a goose, but more often a duck. Cage it, give it no room, movement will ruin the feel. Take it by the neck and pump corn boiled in fat down its throat. Do this seven times a day, pump it plump. Kill the bird, remove the liver and a good cook would pay a high price for it. With mustard, with honey, with cut onions and dark vinegar. Never has anything been so delicious.

See, it is not the taste that turns people away, it is the way it is made. "Does the end justify the means?" is a question often asked. No, if you are without talent, if you lack a good tongue for food. Yes, Yes! Believe me anyone would scream "YES!" if they tried my rich goose liver. But then again, mine is different, mine is better.

See, they say that beauty is only on the surface. It is, and taste is far shallower. I am a cook. A good cook, not a good man but I say again: A GOOD cook. If I had been born a painter and my only source of red was the blood of the innocent, do not doubt that I would paint in red. Of course I was not born a painter, I was born a cook. A GOOD cook. Rich goose liver, as most cooks make it, is against the law in many countries: the UK, Germany, and Italy to name a few. Needless to say that I do not get my recipes from law books. Rich goose liver as I make it, is against the law in every country. The pope once spoke out against rich goose liver as mean, that was of course before he tried mine. Mine is different, mine is better.

A high church leader said to me that if god again came to earth, he would make sure I cooked. Another said that "I once spoke out against your dish Cook. I am sorry Cook. I owe you a thousand apologies Cook. I have now tasted your dish Cook, and I now know that the joy from the soft soaked flesh on my tongue is greater than all the pain of all the geese and ducks that God has ever tried to make." They were in wonder of me. Anyone who I convince to put aside their morals, will at the moment of eating my rich goose liver, be in wonder of me. Mine is different, mine is better.

People would kill for a spoonful, Good people, holy people, moral people… They would kill for a spoonful of my rich goose liver. Believe me, I would be very rich if I charged a million per pound. But I do not. I do not do it for power or money, I do it for the art. I am a cook, A GOOD cook, not a good man but I say again: A GOOD cook. My recipe is worth kingdoms, my dish has made kings weak at the knees. So weak that they kneel before me, the Cook.

My history will be my recipe. If you are reading this, good for you, you have received it. Here it is:

Take a baby, take it away, buy it, steal it, it makes no difference. Any child without parents will do. Boy or girl, it makes no difference. Black, White, Arab, Asian, it makes no difference. Though they must be newborn! They must be innocent, they must be tasty.

Cage it, give it no room, movement will ruin the feel. Take it by the neck and pump corn boiled in fat down its throat. Do this seven times a day, pump it plump. Two months should be enough. Add a pinch of salt and an ounce of butter for every pint of corn. Two pints of fat, for every pint of corn. Animal fat is best, the more fatty acid the better. When killed, take the liver and prepare it in the way you are most able. I would soak it in honey and mustard seed. Cooked sesame seeds, cut red onions and a tiny bit of rum.
words_common.writingprompts::51:
Kai went quietly back up the stairs from the kitchen. Getting found by Mom and Dad would be bad. Getting found with the extra broccoli that Mom planned to serve for dinner tomorrow night would be worse. Lucky for Kai, he would not have to eat any of it.

Closing his bedroom door behind him, the six-year old went straight to his closet. Bravely opening the closet, he smiled at the pile of eyes, hair and arms he found there.

Here you go, Blergh, Kai whispered. Blergh took the open plastic container with one arm and emptied the entire thing into a mouth the size of a basketball hoop before swallowing it all at once. Kai could never see if Blergh had teeth or not, but the monster never chewed.

Kai began laying a path of crackers out to the middle of the floor. Tempted by the salty circles, the monster slowly left the closet. Kai got a box out of his toy chest and dumped its things on the floor.

We are playing soldier games tonight, Kai said. Blergh just made a noise in agreement. Kai loved playing with Blergh because he could move lots of pieces at once and he was really good at pretending to be surprised when things blew up.

***

Julia used to be bothered when she woke up in the morning to find her son not only sleeping on the floor but also in the middle of a bunch of plastic men just waiting to be stepped on. By now it had happened so many times that being bothered was not worth the trouble.

Wake up, sweetie, she said, softly shaking his shoulder. How is Blergh?

As they walked toward the breakfast table, Julia got ready for another story about how Kai and his make-believe friend had beaten some big bad guy. Kids are so cute at that age.

***

Ten years later, Kai no longer had to sneak. All boys his age eat a lot in the middle of the night, right? Kai sat in front of his X-Box and passed one bag of chips and one bottle of soda to his left.

Here you go, Blergh. Blergh made a noise to say thanks before swallowing everything all at once. The guy still had not learned to chew. Blergh made a noise again and showed the tv, the three controllers in his arms and the fourth one at Kai's feet. They were all ready to play the game. It was going to be another great night.
words_common.writingprompts::52:
As the ship reached the light, the pilot nervously turned on his direction finder - he had used the last of his travel fuel making it this area.

The pilot felt a strange chill as he looked out his window. He thought it was travel nerves, but he sent power to his safety robot anyway. Sensors did not find anything; he should have known it was a waste of time. He had more important things to focus on like finding fuel.

The direction finder made a sound and drew his attention to a large body floating some distance from his boat, a thick cloud of gas partly hiding it. The ship was turned off, which is why the first system check had not found it. He brought the travel engines on and moved towards the empty vessel while at the same time calling the ship.

No answer. That was strange, but empty vessels were not unheard of. More odd was the perfect condition of the ship, which did not have even a small mark. He had found empty bodies before, but they were covered with burn marks from a light beam or short range machine, some sign of a fight was always clear.

He briefly thought about putting on his space suit. Instead he went to the robot room and took remote control of the safety robot - it was meant for boarding defense, but in a bad spot it could be used as an exploration tool.

Moments later the robot slid through the door, a smooth machine filled to the top with a group of light beams and close fight weapons that had saved the pilot's life more than once. He had plans for this body, and the robot went straight for the engine room. Any remaining fuel would be found there.

The problem with remotely controlling the robot was that it needed the full attention of the pilot. The door had not closed - if the pilot was paying attention, he would have noticed his door system had broken.

His dying screams echoed as he was torn to pieces.

The pilot should have known that giant alien spiders are no joke.

Like I said, time is really hard to count here. Even the sun, stars and moon do not act quite right. You get used to it though, and Mister Cthulhu does not exactly mind when I go to bed or when I get up. Mind you, if I do not do my job well, I get my soul eaten like a sweet cake and my body tossed into the baby pool. But I have been working here three years now, and I have not had one major big mistake in that whole long time.

I check the back wall of my ice cold black rock house, as that is where Mister Cthulhu usually leaves my to-do list. Sure enough, I find a young woman pinned to my wall with a big spear, her body moving and twisting in pleasure. My list is carved into her face, which means it is a short day at least.

Mister Cthulhu killed Death a few years ago, so no one really dies any more. I free the young woman and take the spear with me. I have a few things to do today.

I have to clean the inside of the temple of Yog-Sothoth, get the salt balance sorted out in the Deep One's baby pool, and give the Hydra some stomach medicine. Poor girl has been moving about for a few hours and hurting the Earth's coasts with big waves. I set that to be the first priority, as Mister Cthulhu does not like when other people kill his food.
words_common.writingprompts::54:
Elwood and Shara were leaning against a hard stone post in the open area of a high school, watching Elwood's newest target, a very normal young man named Dale.

So how did you get assigned to this one, Elwood? Shara said while looking at her sharp nails.

I am very sure this is a simple task from the bosses down below. Elwood said, arms crossed against his chest. A group of girls walked over to the post and leaned against it, sharing the same space as the two evil spirits. A strong gust of wind blew the papers and notebooks out of the hands of the girls, who yelled in surprise and ran after them.

Shara, annoyed said, I will never get used to that. I do not care if we can be in the same space as them. Turning to the girls, she held her arm out to them, sharp nails held behind her thumb and flicked them outwards with a snap, sending the books and papers again flying out of the yelling girls hands. Mean little things.

Dale was chewing on his bean and cheese burrito looking at the scene across the area with the look of a calm cow chewing on grass.

What is wrong with that kid? Shara asked.

I do not know. Maybe he is not very smart? Elwood chewed on his thumb for a bit, thinking of a plan. Let us jump ahead to the sixth class period.

Shara gave Elwood a look from the side and raised an eyebrow, Sure.

With a sound like tearing heavy cloth they were moved and sat on the ledge under the window in the back of Dale's sixth class.

So what is your plan, big boy?

Elwood pressed a long-nailed finger to his lips and said, Sssshhhh. As he did that Dale's head hit the desk, he was fast asleep. Flinging his arms out wide and then bringing them in together in a grand group gesture, every student in the class turned to face Dale without a word.

That is cute. said Shara.

Elwood smiled and said, It is time to wake up, Dale. As he said that, every single student in the class in a very flat voice said the same thing at the same time as Elwood. Dale, face half-wet with spit sat up and rubbed his eyes, looking around at the class looking back at him.

Dale, it is time to wake up. All the students and Elwood said again. No one blinked. Dale looked from side to side, I am awake. Elwood flung his arms apart and the class went back to normal, no one but Dale knowing what happened.

That is your plan? Shara asked, clearly not impressed.

Dale noticing he was a little behind in taking notes began writing in a hurry.

You are joking, right? That is a daytime ghost story! It is not even 3 am. That is some creepy stuff, I do not care what you say.

Uh huh. Shara said. Look at him. He has no idea that was not normal. Come on, let us go. She moved a sharp nail over her shoulder as she walked away, asking for Elwood to follow.

As they were leaving through the wall, Elwood spun around and made a hitting motion. Dale grunted and his head jerked forward, loose pieces of hair at the back of his head flying up, his pencil shot out of his hand and hit the back of the strong kid in front of him. The girl next to Dale looked at him with clear dislike and said, You are such a weirdo, moving in her small desk to be as far away as possible from him.

Shara laughed.

The two evil spirits waited outside the classroom for the end of the period and Dale. You know this would be so much easier in the nighttime. Shara said, bored.

Yeah but that is not my style. Elwood said, You get more real results during the day. Anyone can be scared at night and when the day comes, they are so quick to forget it. No. No what really scares them is a daytime haunting.

Shara did not say anything, only yawned.

The bell rang for the end of the period and Dale was the last one out of the classroom, walking slowly, looking down at his phone. Elwood flapped his wings and dove into the phone. A message popped up on his screen, Dale clicked on read which told Elwood to jump into full view on the screen and yell DAAAAAAAAAAALE through the phone speaker.

Dale hit the power button and put his phone back in his pocket. Just great. he thought, One of my friends has been messing with my alerts again. and continued walking to his next class.

Elwood stretched out of the phone like a rubber band with a pop and took his place next to Shara leaning against the wall. I do not get this kid. he said, watching Dale walk away.

Still wanting to do this in the daytime? Shara asked him.

Elwood let out a heavy sigh. Okay, let us try it your way. and they both vanished with a pop and a sizzle.

The two evil spirits burst into the space above Dale's bed and stared down at him, gently flapping their wings. So what do you do now? Elwood asked Shara, who only gave a half smile and stretched her index finger out in front of her and slowly curled it back into her palm. The bed sheet covering Dale was pulled off him in time with the moving of Shara's finger. Dale only scratched his stomach and rolled over.

Wow. I am just at a loss for words, Shara. That is some scary stuff, right there.

She narrowed her eyes at him and shot a hand out to grab something in the air. Dale screamed in pain. Shara then pulled her arm back and Dale flew off the foot of the bed and crashed against the wall, knocking several books off the shelf which fell one after the other onto the top of his head.

Elwood's mouth dropped open and he looked from Shara to Dale and back again. You have no soft touch at all, woman!

Just watch.

Dale stood up and picked up the books, putting them back on the shelf. The door to his room opened and his mom asked him if he was alright. Yeah, just had a really bad leg cramp and fell when I got up.

Oh for goodness sake! Shara said and threw her arms up.

Yeah, the heck with this kid. Elwood said and they both popped out of the air, leaving the room behind for good as they moved on to find another person to bother in the morning light.

words_common.writingprompts::57:
Dr. Kevin Bruin.. Log Entry E72 -- The Moment 
 - 
 To whoever is looking into my disappearing... In case I don't come back. 
 
 No one knows when their turn will come. Although we quickly found ways to guess its movement and stay away from it there is no stopping it. The worst tries came under strict military rule. The times spent alone were terrible. Short, yes but terrible. One of the men kept alone once asked me if it was worse that everyone lived. Having to talk with the people we selfishly kept away. "Would it have been best if the moment caused death instead?" He asked. His eyes locked into mine. While mine were filled with fear and guilt his were calm. Why wouldn't they be? The moment had passed him. It hadn't passed me. 
 
 There are several rules we have found matching the moment. The first, it only affects men. Each and every man. Regardless of age. The second, its goal is not to kill. While deaths have happened, usually on the very young or old, they can be stopped through medical help. Third, it affects men one at a time. Meaning only one man can feel the moment at once. There have been no reported cases of shared feelings. Four, its movement is based on how near you are. The closer you are to someone feeling the moment the more likely you are to be next. Five, it can't be held back by any physical wall. The keeping of a sick area failed. Once the moment had gone through the male population in the kept area it moved outwards. Sixth, it is possible to run faster than it. It moves at speeds similar to a normal human. Finally, the feeling itself is said to be very painful. 
 
 As to where I went. 
 
 I was asked what I thought the moment could be when I first started. I said something that could be explained! Watching, guesses, trials, testing month after month. A germ, tiny bug, parasite... mass panic none of it fit. There was no reason. When people talked about space visitors or a god's punishment I laughed saying science will find the answer. Eventually though it seemed no answer was coming. I doubted for a while. I started to believe the radical people. Few people know this about me. However, there is one more rule that I choose to accept that others don't. It is alive and thinks. And the end of all of us is its final goal. As a man of science I can't be scared anymore. I must test my guess. You will now understand why I am missing. Men my age are less likely to stay alive but we can find the answer, science will win. I have cut off my testicles on myself. By the time you read this I should be within the area where the moment is now. I wonder what people will think when they see a naked old man walking into the fire. Is he crazy? A religious nut? No joke intended. If I succeed, which I believe I will, you will probably hear stories before I can make it back. So the log. Stories of a crazy old man whose belief made him safe from the moment. Well that will be so. Know that it was belief that won. Belief in science. 
 
 If I don't return. Dan. Love always.
words_common.writingprompts::59:
A small lamp burned steadily on the polished desk. The human wore a pair of thin glasses on the edge of his nose. Stacks of paper occupied a far corner of the work surface. He read through pages at a time, writing notes on another sheet. Empty ink bottles on the floor suggested the man was rather busy. 
 
 From the entrance, Ronn got ready with his heavy stick, letting the heavy chains hang down, their sounds filling the room. But the man refused to look up at the people who had walked in. Instead, he held up a finger and continued reading. Ronn and the rest of his group looked at each other and shrugged their shoulders. For a moment, they stood still. With a disappointed sound of the tongue, the man put back the paper, pushed his glasses closer to his eyes, and called for his guests to come closer. They did. 
 
 Apologies, my friends, he said. His voice cracked slightly as though it had gone unused for some time. Come. Come. 
 
 The group of people on a journey stepped forward slowly. Wilm's head moved around as he looked for bad stones in the floor or another trap. The floor turned to green when the fuzzy edge of the rug stood before them. The group stopped. 
 
 Come, the man said quietly, any feeling of not wanting to wait impossible to see. 
 
 Firrel's shoe tested its weight against the rug. There was hard ground beneath. The rest followed his lead. 
 
 Wait! the man screamed. The group wasted no time getting into a defensive position, their weapons and shields ready. I meant the carpet. 
 
 The group looked towards their feet. The green fibers turned a purplish color as the blood from their bodies dripped freely. Querth's face turned red. 
 
 Sorry, the magic user whispered. 
 
 The man rolled his eyes. It is already ruined. Nothing we can do now. Let us just get this over with. 
 
 The group was finally within a step of the desk when the open hand of the man asked them to stop. The large groups of bad creatures had led them to that room. The supposed throne room of terrible bad things was little more than a study with a man who keeps books. 
 
 Well, then. I think congratulations are in order! The man clapped his hands together. Great job. I am Pollock and I will be handling your paperwork from here. 
 
 Paperwork? Edmund repeated. 
 
 Yes, answered Pollock. You are almost done in this terrible castle and on your way back home to enjoy the prizes. All that is left is to handle the last small things. 
 
 The group nodded in agreement, but kept their weapons close. The large groups they had to cut through in order to reach that room began to feel finished. 
 
 Excellent! Let us get started. In total you have killed… one hundred and fifty three goblins, twenty nine orcs, eighteen small monsters… and two dragons. Impressive. 
 
 Edmund smiled and turned the handle of his axe to catch the light to the sounds of pain from Ronn and Dismal. They had enjoyed the mess that had followed as it stopped their fellow fighter from bragging. 
 
 In addition, you broke down forty one doors, set off two fire traps, six sharp traps, three big rocks, and one acid spill. Plus, it says you freed the dark rooms of ten prisoners. 
 
 All in a day's work, Wilm added. 
 
 Quite, responded Pollock, not the least impressed. And adding up your little trip, that comes to a total of eight million, eight hundred thirty seven thousand, two hundred and fifty one gold pieces. 
 
 Even Querth's mind could not understand such a number. They were used to large prizes, but several hundred was the most any had ever seen. 
 
 We could not possibly carry that much money, Dismal said. Or spend it. 
 
 That is quite expected, Pollock laughed. You can just pay in small amounts over time. 
 
 Pay? shouted Firrel. What do you mean pay? 
 
 Your fines. Your damages. You cannot just go around killing things, damaging property, and setting off traps that require professional fixing. 
 
 But we were on a mission, asked Ronn. We were trying to save the village. 
 
 I see, said Pollock. Does that mean the village is going to pay the fines, fix the castle, reset the protections, mop the floors, hire the guards again, train the dragons again, and tell the families of those lost? The group stood in wide-eyed silence. I did not think so. 
 
 B-but, it was a mission, Ronn said again. 
 
 Do you have a paper, a legal permit for this mission of yours? Ronn shook his head. No need to answer, I already know you do not. If you had bothered to ask for one, this castle would have been better protected and I would not have been needed. Just a little sign at the start would have been enough to save us all the mess of your unplanned fight. 
 
 Who was supposed to file our permit? Querth asked the group. They thought about the question for a moment before turning to face their friend. You have ruined us! 
 
 I am sorry, cried Dismal. I did not know! I did not know this would happen! 
 
 The circle closed around him as the group looked to handle their greatest enemy: the enemy within. 
 
 The lesson is to tag your posts or else your friends will kill you.

words_rare.xsum::28: 1917 - Great Britain subjugates Palestine from the Ottoman Empire. words_rare.xsum::30: David Sulman of the UK Forest Products Association censured a palpable deficiency of candour and lucidity within the compact. The accord had been impugned by comptrollers. words_rare.xsum::31: Denbighshire council aspired to establish a nascent bilingual academy by shuttering Ysgol Pentrecelyn and Ysgol Llanfair Dyffryn Clwyd in Ruthin and inaugurating a fresh facility. words_rare.academic_abstracts::0: For numerous decades, regulatory appraisal frameworks for genotoxic impairment have been standardized wherein the examinations utilized scrutinized mutations and structural and numerical chromosomal aberrations. This has served the genetic toxicity community capably when most of the substances being scrutinized were amenable to such assays. The outcome from this testing is usually a dichotomous (yes/no) evaluation of test results, and in many instances, the information is merely employed to determine whether a substance possesses carcinogenic potential or not. Over the identical temporal duration, mechanisms and modes of action (MOAs) that elucidate a broader spectrum of genomic impairment involved in numerous deleterious health consequences have been recognized. Furthermore, a paradigm shift in applied genetic toxicology is propelling the field toward a more quantitative dose-response analysis and point-of-departure (PoD) determination with an emphasis on risks to exposed humans. This is directing focus toward genomic impairment that is likely to precipitate changes associated with a variety of adverse health outcomes. This paradigm shift is transitioning the testing emphasis for genotoxic impairment from a hazard identification only evaluation to a more comprehensive risk assessment approach that provides more insightful intelligence for decision makers regarding the potential peril of genetic impairment to exposed humans. To facilitate this more expansive context for examining genotoxic impairment, a next generation testing strategy necessitates taking into account a broader, more flexible methodology to testing, and ultimately modeling, of genomic impairment as it relates to human exposure. This is consistent with the larger risk assessment context being utilized in regulatory decision making. As presented here, this flexible methodology for examining genomic impairment focuses on testing for relevant genomic effects that can be, as optimally as possible, associated with a deleterious health effect. The most coveted linkage for risk to humans would be alterations in loci associated with human pathologies, whether in somatic or germ cells. The outline of a flexible methodology and associated considerations are presented in a series of nine steps, some of which can occur in parallel, which was formulated through a collaborative endeavor by leading genetic toxicologists from academia, government, and industry through the International Life Sciences Institute (ILSI) Health and Environmental Sciences Institute (HESI) Genetic Toxicology Technical Committee (GTTC). The ultimate objective is to provide quantitative data to model the potential risk magnitudes of substances, which induce genomic impairment contributing to human deleterious health outcomes. Any robust risk assessment commences with posing the appropriate risk management interrogatories in a planning and scoping endeavor. This step establishes the problem to be addressed (e.g., broadly, does genomic impairment necessitate being addressed, and if so, how to proceed). The subsequent two steps aggregate what is understood about the problem by constructing a knowledge base regarding the substance of concern and developing a rational biological argument for why testing for genomic impairment is required or not. By focusing on the risk management problem and potential genomic impairment of concern, the subsequent step of assay(s) selection transpires. The work-up of the problem during the antecedent steps provides the insight to which assays would most likely produce the most meaningful data. This discourse does not detail the wide range of genomic impairment tests available, but designates types of testing systems that can be highly advantageous. Once the assays are executed and analyzed, the relevant data sets are selected for modeling potential risk. From this juncture forward, the data are evaluated and modeled as they are for any other toxicology endpoint. Any observed genomic impairment/effects (or genetic event(s)) can be modeled via a dose-response analysis and determination of an estimated PoD. When a quantitative risk analysis is mandatory for decision making, a parallel exposure assessment endeavor is performed (exposure assessment is not detailed here as this is not the focus of this discourse; guidelines for this assessment exist elsewhere). Then the PoD for genomic impairment is utilized with the exposure information to develop risk estimations (e.g., using reference dose (RfD), margin of exposure (MOE) approaches) in a risk characterization and presented to risk managers for informing decision making. This methodology is applicable now for incorporating genomic impairment results into the decision-making process for assessing potential deleterious outcomes in chemically exposed humans and is consistent with the ILSI HESI Risk Assessment in the 21st Century (RISK21) roadmap. This applies to any substance to which humans are exposed, including pharmaceuticals, agricultural products, food additives, and other chemicals. It is opportune for regulatory bodies to incorporate the broader knowledge and insights provided by genomic impairment results into the assessments of risk to more thoroughly comprehend the potential of deleterious outcomes in chemically exposed humans, thus improving the assessment of risk due to genomic impairment. The historical utilization of genomic impairment data as a yes/no gateway for possible cancer risk has been too narrowly constrained in risk assessment. The recent advances in assaying for and understanding genomic impairment, including eventually epigenetic alterations, obviously contribute a greater abundance of information for determining potential risk to humans. Regulatory bodies need to embrace this paradigm shift from hazard identification to quantitative analysis and to incorporate the wider range of genomic impairment in their assessments of risk to humans. The quantitative analyses and methodologies discussed here can be readily applied to genomic impairment testing results now. Indeed, with the passage of the recent update to the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) in the US, the new generation testing strategy for genomic impairment described here provides a regulatory agency (here the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), but suitable for others) a golden opportunity to reexamine the manner in which it addresses risk-based genomic impairment testing (including hazard identification and exposure). words_rare.academic_abstracts::3: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) constitutes a rare monogenic malady characterized by nonmalignant neoplasms in manifold viscera alongside a high prevalence of epilepsy, cognitive impairment and autism. words_rare.academic_abstracts::5: Resumption of athletic participation regarding National Football League (NFL) competitors following sequestered anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) lacerations has been documented. words_rare.academic_abstracts::6: Pulmonary hypertension consequential to exertion serves as a harbinger regarding the hemodynamic gravity of mitral stenosis (MS). words_rare.academic_abstracts::7: The repercussions of persistent hepatic pathology regarding clinical trajectories in individuals afflicted with COVID-19 remain ambiguous. words_rare.academic_abstracts::8: The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) precipitated by severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2) has instigated a substantial quantity of fatalities globally. words_rare.academic_abstracts::9: Thermal energy and moisture accessibility represent two of the most paramount variables influencing every facet of an anuran's vital physiological mechanisms, including internal body temperature, transdermal evaporative water loss, and standard metabolic rate. words_rare.academic_abstracts::10: Chronotaraxis constitutes a profound dysregulation regarding the cognition of temporal sequencing. words_rare.academic_abstracts::11: Certain contagious maladies, including influenza, tuberculosis, and SARS-CoV-2, might be disseminated when pathogen-replete particulates ejected from a symptomatic individual are respired by another human, an occurrence designated as the airborne transmission pathway. words_rare.academic_abstracts::12: Compound fractures represent sullied lacerations harboring gram-positive and gram-negative microorganisms; consequently, expansive-spectrum antimicrobial pharmacotherapy ought to be integrated into the clinical regimen. words_rare.academic_abstracts::13: OBJECTIVE: Periodic configurations of adherence have been discerned regarding numerous health-associated pursuits such as nutritional restriction and physical exertion. words_rare.academic_abstracts::14: Disparities within the enteric microbial assemblage (dysbiosis) of vertebrates have been correlated with numerous gastrointestinal and autoimmune maladies. words_rare.academic_abstracts::15: We scrutinize the rationale underpinning the quantum acceleration—quantum paradigms necessitating fewer computational iterations than their conventional equivalents. words_rare.academic_abstracts::16: Cardiovascular pathology and clinical intervention may both precipitate an elevated hazard for thrombotic occurrences owing to altered hemodynamics within the myocardium, and consequently a transformation in the mechanical stimuli of hematological corpuscles traversing the chambers of the heart. words_rare.academic_abstracts::17: The pervasive ultra-high-energy (VHE, > 100 GeV) gamma-ray radiation discerned within the central 200 pc of the Milky Way by H.E.S.S. was ascertained to emulate the dense matter configuration in the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) up to a longitudinal interval of approximately 130 pc to the Galactic Centre (GC), where the flux precipitously diminishes. words_rare.academic_abstracts::18: These transnational clinical practice recommendations for developmental coordination disorder, inaugurated by the European Academy of Childhood Disability, endeavor to elucidate pivotal interrogatives regarding the nomenclature, diagnosis, evaluation, remediation, and psychosocial facets of this condition pertinent for clinical praxis. words_rare.academic_abstracts::19: Arterial hypertension potentially precipitates affective disturbances that might exacerbate or alleviate contingent upon the specific pharmacological antihypertensive agent administered. syntax_complex.xsum::1: By facilitating the development of a unique, non-invasive methodology for monitoring the physiological health of wild elephants, her persistent efforts have assisted scientists in India, primarily through the innovative technique of freeze-drying dung directly in the field to effectively preserve vital elephant hormones. Consequently, researchers discovered that stress levels in females were significantly more conspicuous than those observed in male elephants. Over a duration of five years, Sanjeeta and her colleagues meticulously collected more than 300 samples from 261 individual elephants inhabiting the biodiversity-rich Western Ghats, an endeavor she described by noting that she often hid and observed until the elephant defecated and moved away, later telling the BBC that these samples mean a great deal to her. The primary aim of this research was to evaluate the influence of the elephants' body condition on glucocorticoid metabolites, as animals such as elephants are subjected to various stressors throughout their lives, including threats from predators, food shortages, drought, and illness. Whenever any animal faces such stressful events, its body secretes hormones known as glucocorticoids, which are released into the circulatory system before being broken down into metabolites that are ultimately excreted through urine or faeces. Because the researchers maintain that collecting blood samples to assess stress levels is neither ethical nor feasible—given that immobilising the animals would inherently cause additional stress and thus bias the study—Sanjeeta explained that glucocorticoid levels were measured using faecal or dung samples. The team discovered that these metabolites in the dung remained relatively stable for up to six hours after defecation, although they preferred collecting samples as fresh as possible, as the dung begins to degrade through microbial activity after six hours. To prevent this degradation, the collected samples were freeze-dried in the field and stored at -20 degrees Celsius for further analysis. Stress levels for all elephants peaked during the dry season, when resources were low. Senior researcher Prof. Raman Sukumar noted that in a natural environment, large and long-ranging herbivorous mammals such as elephants may have to face various ecological challenges or stressful conditions, one of which is forage resource limitation, whether in terms of quality or quantity. Higher amounts of glucocorticoids generally indicated that the animal was more stressed, he added, reiterating that stress levels in female elephants were more conspicuous than in males, a trend that researchers say all mammalian systems would show. Dr. Sukumar and his team claim that their study is the first to examine the relationship between body condition, seasonality, and stress in wild Asian elephants using large-scale faecal sample collection for assaying glucocorticoid metabolites. The study also focused on finding possible answers to how elephant populations react to chronic stress and if superior nutrition from feeding on cultivated crops could help them reduce their physiological stress levels that might otherwise be enhanced through harassment by farmers trying to protect their fields. Furthermore, they examined the idea that body condition alone could act as an indicator of physiological health and fitness, scoring the animal's body condition on a scale from one to five, where one indicates a poor state and five indicates obesity. Published in the Oxford Journal Conservation Physiology, the study conclusively found that stress levels in Asian elephants peaked during the dry season when resources were low, while also concluding that poor body condition served as a reliable visual indicator of stress.

syntax_complex.xsum::9: Nadia Eweida, having taken her case to the ECHR after British Airways compelled her to cease wearing her white gold cross in a visible manner, received a judgment stating that the airline had failed to strike a fair balance between the religious beliefs held by Ms Eweida and the corporate desire to project a specific image. These four Christians had collectively brought cases against the United Kingdom government for its alleged failure to protect their rights, though ministers contested these claims, arguing that the rights of employees were only protected within the private sphere. The message emanating from Strasbourg indicates that, although individuals are entitled to hold religious views, that right is severely limited in the workplace whenever it enters into conflict with the rights of others. Ms Eweida, a sixty-year-old Coptic Christian from Twickenham in south-west London, informed the BBC that she was jumping with joy following the ruling, noting that the experience had not been an easy ride. Ms Chaplin, who resides in Exeter, was transferred to a desk job by the Royal Devon and Exeter NHS Trust Hospital for failing to remove a confirmation crucifix on a small chain, which she had worn to work for thirty years. The court maintained that the decision was necessary to protect the health and safety of nurses and patients. She stated that she believed British Christians would be devastated by the ruling. The former businessman, who has been in poor health, had been on death row for fifteen years but had his sentence commuted to life imprisonment in 2002.
syntax_complex.xsum::12: This development follows an incident in which a two-year-old girl, having been struck by a van and subsequently abandoned by eighteen passing individuals, currently remains hospitalized while fighting for her life. Although this proposed legislation might never actually be enacted, the mere discussion of such a measure underscores the profound level of national anger generated within China by this specific case. The fallout from this tragedy, which occurred in the city of Foshan located in southern Guangdong Province, continues to expand as provincial groups representing the ruling Communist Party, various government departments, and local associations deliberate upon a potential new law that could render it illegal for citizens to ignore those desperately in need of assistance. According to a report in the English-language China Daily, lawyer Zhu Yongping noted that many laws, including those forbidding drunken driving, have historically been passed in China following high-profile individual cases. While other media outlets indicate that the introduction of such a law will be formally debated at a meeting of lawyers next month, initial online polls suggest that a majority of the public remains against it, with one representative posting questioning whether anyone is actually paying attention to the necessity of being civilized first. Simultaneously, organizations in Guangdong are exploring alternative ways to encourage people to act with compassion when faced with an emergency, as the provincial government’s political and legal affairs committee utilizes its micro-blog site to gather opinions on how to guide brave acts for just causes and promote socialist morals. This intense national debate has been sparked by the accident last week involving the toddler Wang Yue, who was knocked down by a van while wandering through a market where her parents operate a shop. The driver sped off without checking on the girl’s condition, and over the following minutes, eighteen people passed the bleeding toddler—while another van ran over her legs—yet no one stopped to help, all of which was recorded by a surveillance camera and shown on television, triggering millions of internet comments expressing outrage regarding the refusal to help.
syntax_complex.xsum::13: Lord Naseby’s formal inquiry emerged directly from persistent complaints lodged by frustrated viewers regarding the muffled, mumbled speech characterizing various television productions, most notably the recent BBC drama SS-GB. In response to this specific parliamentary query, Minister Lord Ashton of Hyde firmly asserted that it would be fundamentally inappropriate for the government to intervene in such matters. This spirited debate within the House of Lords notably drew in prominent figures such as the acclaimed Downton Abbey writer Lord Fellowes and the distinguished House of Cards creator Lord Dobbs. While Culture, Media and Sport Minister Lord Ashton conceded that TV viewers should reasonably be able to hear and clearly understand their favourite shows, he simultaneously maintained that, because it is a long-standing principle that the government does not interfere in the operational activities of broadcasters, it would not be right for the government to formally consult on this specific issue. Lord Naseby, expressing significant disappointment with the minister’s dismissive answer, reminded the House of Lords that these pervasive problems originated back in 2014 with the drama Jamaica Inn, which triggered well over 1,000 written complaints to the BBC concerning the sheer inaudibility of the dialogue. He questioned whether it was appropriate for the ordinary viewer to rely upon subtitles just to decipher the spoken dialogue, further asking if the minister would recognize that someone must eventually lodge a formal complaint to Ofcom if he refuses to apply direct pressure on the chairman of the BBC. Lord Ashton replied by noting that, since 2014, the BBC has produced over 66,000 hours of new material, of which only six programmes have encountered reported audibility problems. Lord Fellowes, a Conservative peer and writer of dramas such as ITV’s Downton Abbey, argued that the unfortunate fashion for mumbled dialogue is hardly a modern invention, remarking that they experienced similar trouble during the 1950s and 60s, and insisted that the government has no proper role other than hoping the trend passes. After the minister suggested that one person’s mumbling might simply be another person’s atmosphere, Labour peer Lord Blunkett, who is blind, retorted that atmosphere is only acceptable if one can actually lip-read. For individuals like him, he told the peers, mumbling is not merely an irritant but an impossibility, prompting him to call upon the government to lean on the regulator Ofcom. Lord Dobbs suggested the problem might lie with modern flat-screen televisions, which are all screen with backwards-facing speakers, though he conceded that we are all getting older and perhaps deafer.
syntax_complex.xsum::14: Action was brought against Bideford Town Council by the National Secular Society, an organization acting after atheist councillor Clive Bone registered a formal complaint, which resulted in Mr. Justice Ouseley ruling that the prayers in question were not lawful under section 111 of the Local Government Act 1972. However, while issuing this decree, the judge noted that prayers could theoretically be said as long as councillors were not formally summoned to attend, a judgment that was widely perceived as a definitive test case capable of impacting local councils across the entirety of England and Wales. Mr. Justice Ouseley clarified that the prayers, as practised by Bideford Town Council, had been unlawful precisely because there existed no statutory power permitting the council to continue them. The National Secular Society, which argued that prayers had no place in a secular environment concerned with civic business, maintained that the inappropriate ritual breached articles 9 and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights, provisions designed to protect an individual's right to freedom of conscience and immunity from discrimination; nevertheless, the case was ultimately not won on those human rights grounds but rather on a technical point regarding the statutory construction of local government legislation. According to Robert Pigott, the BBC News religious affairs correspondent, judges have generally been unsympathetic to the Christian case whenever individuals have argued against obligations like advising homosexual couples, suggesting that the tide has been flowing quite firmly against Christianity in public life, a trend which has caused enormous concerns for the churches. These institutions claim that faith is being actively driven out of public life, and there exists substantial anxiety that this shift is not merely about religion in a vacuum, but rather about the fundamental values that underpin the British way of life. Conversely, figures associated with the National Secular Society argue that the Church and Christianity should not enjoy undue privileges in having their specific values and traditional practices upheld by the state. While an argument persists on both sides, it has been remarkably noticeable in recent years that the tide has turned against Christian practices which society had simply taken for granted for centuries.
