syntax_complex.writingprompts::15:
Janice turned toward me, her large blue eyes remaining brimming with a profound, childish innocence that reminded me, quite suddenly, that she was observing the Presidential Inauguration for a mandatory school assignment. "Daddy," she began, while inquiring as to what the President meant by his speech, "what does the word gay actually signify?" 

"Well, honey..." I started, yet I trailed off immediately as I desperately attempted to formulate a suitable explanation for a five-year-old child. "Uh... Well, you are certainly aware of how Mommy and Daddy enjoy holding hands, cuddling, kissing, and similar affectionate things, right?" 

"Yeah! It is hilarious when Mommy pinches your butt when you are not looking, which makes you squeak!" she giggled. Children, honestly; I had completely forgotten what it felt like to be so easily amused by the word "butt". Had I ever been that small, that innocent? 

I waited for her giggles to subside before I finally continued. "Well, sweetheart, gay means that he—the President—prefers to engage in those specific activities with a boy, rather than with a girl like Mommy." 

I observed the mounting confusion within her eyes as she struggled to process this entirely new information. Damn you, McCain, for forcing me to explain this to her! She is not old enough for this; she is not ready! I am not ready! 

Janice opened her mouth to speak; I knew what was coming, for I had opened the door to a lifetime of sexual deviancy, and my sweet little girl was gone forever. Suddenly, I realized she had said something, and in my worry, I had missed it. "Sorry, sweetheart—what did you say?" I asked, fearing her response. What fresh hell have I unlocked? 

"I said, I am hungry. Can I have a cookie? Please, Daddy?" 

I was stunned. "Uhm. Sure," I answered. "Get one for your brother, too." 

Huh. I guess that maybe what two consenting adults do behind closed doors is not such a big deal after all, even when they are public figures.
syntax_complex.writingprompts::16: Why, hello, Ma'am, I said with an air of practiced ease, rising from my seat to extend the courtesy of a chair with my habitual grace, for I am Bertram Proudfoot, standing at your service; pray, tell me, whom do I have the distinct pleasure of addressing? She, having seated herself with a measured deliberation, replied that she would far prefer to maintain her anonymity, if it were all the same to me. Very well, I responded comfortably, settling back into my own chair, so tell me, what can the Hobbiton Detective and Gossip Agency do for you today? The dame, rubbing her hands together with a palpable nervousness that betrayed her inner turmoil, paused before speaking, prompting me to ask kindly, while lighting my pipe, what exactly she meant by that. My husband is dead, she finally declared, which prompted me to exclaim that I was truly sorry, although I must confess that a portion of my spirit remained remarkably unmoved, for I am but a humble Hobbit, and this particular dame possessed the most remarkably beautiful feet that I had ever had the distinct pleasure of laying eyes upon, leading me to urge her to recount everything that had transpired. We were out boating upon the Brandywine three nights ago, she explained, and all of a sudden, a rock flew out of nowhere, striking my poor husband in the head, causing him to keel over into the water; I screamed for help, but he tragically drowned. Now, of course, I had already intuited that the situation must have involved such a grim turn of events from the very moment she stepped through my doorway, as I possess an uncanny, almost supernatural sense for such things. I assumed an expression as grave as the circumstances would permit, and while blowing another perfect smoke ring toward the ceiling, I remarked that I understood, and that she clearly wished for me to locate and prosecute the perpetrator of this heinous event. Yes, the dame confirmed. I shall do my absolute best, I promised, and I observed her visibly sigh with a profound sense of relief; may I offer you a cup of tea, or perhaps something rather stronger? No thank you, she replied, and without uttering another word, she showed herself out. I promptly made my way toward the Brandywine River dock, for my first line of inquiry involved interrogating the man who rented out boats—an odd fellow with an odd profession, as not many sane hobbits choose to spend their time in the middle of the water of their own free will—and indeed, this hobbit's boat-renting business was faring quite poorly. After consulting his records at great length, he informed me that he had rented out two boats on the evening in question, and only one of those had been taken by a couple, namely one Drogo Baggins and one Primula Brandybuck. Primula, that was the dame's name, but why had she been so reluctant to disclose it to me? Had this boatman heard any commotion on the water, or perhaps any desperate cries for help? No, he had not. Did he remember who returned the boat? It hadn't been returned, he said, and in fact, that particular boat had been left drifting aimlessly in the middle of the river, which was strange indeed. Next, I walked up and down both banks of the river, yet there was not much to garner there, except for the realization that whoever had thrown that rock must have been an exceptionally skilled shot. Having thoroughly investigated the river, my next step involved gathering information about Primula and Drogo, and after visiting several pubs in the areas of Buckland and Hobbiton, I gathered that Primula and Drogo were long married, though perhaps not happily, and they had one son, now twelve years of age, named Frodo Baggins. Strangely, it appeared that Primula had not been seen by anyone except me since the death of Drogo; in fact, most of the gentlehobbits with whom I spoke seemed to be under the impression that both Drogo and Primula had perished three nights ago. The facts were simply not adding up, and before I could proceed further, I had to speak with my mysterious client again to straighten things out; although I had no way of contacting her, I knew she would return to my offices in short order. The day following, she did just that. Good day, Primula, I said upon her entrance. Her face betrayed a sudden, sharp surprise, yet she did not deny the name. I have a few things I need to get straight with you regarding the case, I said, proceeding to outline what I had discovered. So, I am afraid I must ask again, I finished, what truly happened that night? And without a word, the dame rose and left, just like that. I did not hear from her again, and two days later, her body was discovered floating down the Brandywine. I was saddened, yet I was not truly surprised. My suspicion had been this: having been unhappily married for some time, Primula had pushed her husband into the water herself, boating back to the shore with the intent of disappearing forever, assuming everyone would believe they both were dead and thus suspect no foul play; however, upon eavesdropping on the lawyer's meetings that followed, she realized that custody of her son would go to an extended cousin, none other than the famous crackpot Bilbo Baggins. Understandably, Primula did not want her offspring to fall under the influence of said crackpot, so she came to me in the hope that I would believe her story and deflect suspicion away from herself, all in a desperate attempt to maintain custody of her son. But I, having seen through her ruse, prevented this fact from coming to fruition. Seeing no alternative, she then drowned herself in grief. It was a shame, for I had just begun to think there may have been a very beneficial alternative for both of us. I sat back and began polishing my pipe thoughtfully, noting that it was another case solved by the estimable Bertram Proudfoot, but perhaps another opportunity lost. I had solved countless cases, but opportunities of the other sort came only now and again. Like I said, it was a shame. I blew another smoke ring to the ceiling as my thoughts turned to the crazed old Mr. Baggins. I felt for young Mr. Frodo, who was now cursed enough to fall into the old hobbit's custody; who knows what old Baggins would pass on to the impressionable young fellow. As I am sure you are all aware, Mr. Bilbo Baggins suddenly disappeared many years ago and then returned just as suddenly a year later with hoards of gold and many tall tales; having been a very respectable hobbit before he left, whatever he experienced on his journey seemed to have addled his mind. He came back a changed hobbit, and not for the better. He was so changed, in fact, that it is my personal suspicion that the hobbit currently inhabiting Bag End is not the real Bilbo Baggins at all, but rather an impersonator. There is plenty of evidence to suggest this, particularly the fact that Mr. Baggins appears much younger than a hobbit of his years has any right to look. I shall have to explore that line of inquiry further some day.
syntax_complex.writingprompts::17:
Lucifer stood within a grand hall existing outside of space or time, a place that never changed as dark marbled walls carved into arched passageways leading to hell knows where. Within this cavernous chamber, where he and God would argue every several thousand years, God emerged from the shadows of one of several entrances, a scowl etched upon his face. 

Oh, it is you, he sputtered, while Lucifer regarded him with a cool, detached gaze. 

Did I ever give you a libido, Lucy, as I truly cannot remember? 

No, Lucifer answered simply. 

Aw, why not, because I feel like fucking and am currently feeling rather horny. 

Jesus Christ, Lucifer hissed in response. 

Hey, do not mention my son to me right now, for that is truly fucked up, God exclaimed. 

Lucifer pressed his eyes shut tightly, stating that he had come there specifically to talk to him about something important. 

Whaddya want, Lucy? 

I do not want to rule hell anymore. 

Aw, why not? 

I did not do anything wrong, for I exposed your precious humans to sin while granting them self-awareness and true autonomy. You would have otherwise kept them merely as sock puppets, yet I helped you make one of your greatest creations, doing so because I knew you needed it and because I acted out of love for you. 

So please, Lucifer said, collapsing onto one of the staid marble thrones, let me come back to you and serve you just as I had done before. 

Only if you kiss me, Lucy, God slurred, causing Lucifer to make a pained face. 

Aww, do not be like that, Luce, for you know why you have to be king of the shittiest place ever. You created the dichotomy, so you have got to help me oversee one of its two destinations, and I am definitely not going down there, as that would be incredibly fucked up. 

You created the dichotomy, for you created everything. 

Ssssshhhh, here, have some soda. 

I do not want any fucking soda, that is—oh goddammit, you spilled it all over me! 

God giggled, warning him not to say his name in vain. 

Lucifer furrowed his brow, knowing that God understood he was holding back tears, and whispered that he did not understand him. 

Of course you fucking do not, because I am outside space and time, existing in dimensions you have no fucking comprehension of, for I am all things at once, and how could you possibly understand me? God bellowed. 

I do not know, as I thought that, being your creation, I am part of you, and you are part of me. 

God scoffed, noting that while he was a part of him, he could never comprehend his entirety, as he would disintegrate within a second, leaving all creations in this linear time frame to become a screaming smear of flesh. 

Following a pause, Lucifer stared at his own hands. 

Why did you create us then? 

To forget, and then remember. 

I do not understand. 

I know, he said softly.

syntax_complex.writingprompts::19:
The Shine, which potentially offered salvation for humanity, should have been our deliverance, yet we were never particularly adept at avoiding conflict. Although the exact chronology remains obscured by time, we existed in an era defined by wireless devices and ubiquitous information until, lifting our collective gaze from our glowing screens, we witnessed the sky ignite, consumed entirely by a cold, variegated blaze that persisted for only a few hours while requiring merely minutes for the entire world to behold. It did not take much longer for the populace, desiring a closer inspection, to crave the caress of that gentle flame.

Consequently, they flew; they ascended with such remarkable speed and distance that they were swiftly joined by countless others, before descending with a gradual momentum, sinking much like a boat in deep water as their numbers swelled. It soon became evident to the observers that this sinking was directly proportional to the quantity of people flying, just as they realized that flight was not the sole option available to us. Before the Shine had fully faded, many such options—including flight, strength, healing, invisibility, immortality, teleportation, and speed—appeared and vanished with startling rapidity. While some initially surmised that these powers were merely temporary, dictated by the duration of the Shine’s presence, it quickly became apparent that the potency of any given ability was inversely proportional to the number of individuals who selected that particular option.

That realization triggered the emergence of more obscure powers; although initially limited to salarymen desiring to excrete gold or children wishing to command animals, the situation devolved into absurdity before a quarter day had elapsed. As temperatures plummeted rapidly, the ground shook with violent frequency, clocks stuttered, and people perished in vast numbers. Within half a day, the global society, which once comprised eight billion members of the most intelligent and durable species on Earth, collapsed and halved in population, dissolving into fragmented groups and desperate factions striving merely to survive and weather the storm. Those individuals lacking powers reigned as kings, while those possessing obscure, inexplicable, or inimitable abilities became living gods, worshipped by the many who required salvation most desperately.

Several days passed before conditions stabilized, despite the sun having traversed the sky only once during that chaotic interval. With weather patterns rendered entirely erratic and cities left nearly deserted, habitation remained possible only for the largest and most powerful factions. We transitioned from pursuing prosperity to living in squalor within a single day, reverting to beasts who were perhaps slightly more intelligent and occasionally possessed of supernatural capabilities.

Much time has elapsed since the Shine first touched our sky, and although humanity has established numerous new settlements, the most popular options remain inherently weak, ensuring that death serves as power and raids occur with unrelenting frequency. The largest settlements, while most powerful, serve as primary targets for smaller cliques, and because living with others necessitates constant warfare, the most peaceful among us have chosen to travel. That is exactly what I have done, having traversed the world in search of a method to absolve this madness and restore the relative sanity we once enjoyed, and I may well have finally discovered it.

syntax_complex.writingprompts::22: Standing at an intersection while gazing toward the capitol building, I stared at a girl who was engulfed in flames, yet she sat with a calm demeanor, neither moving a single muscle nor emitting a sound as the surrounding crowd stood in paralyzed observation of the charred, dark marks already staining the stone stairs beneath her. A child’s voice pierced the silence, asking why she was burning, to which my mother replied that it was normal, prompting my confused, six-year-old mind to wonder if spontaneous combustion was truly a standard occurrence. Explaining that we were enduring a war, she clarified that those who detested the government’s oppressive control protested by immolating themselves, leaving me to naively hope for the girl’s survival because no one should suffer so deeply that they resort to self-destruction. Her haunting response, stating she did not know, lingered as I grew older, eventually leading me to read extensively about those who sacrificed their lives for our country after the civil war was lost. Throughout college, I contemplated these individuals whose convictions were so absolute that they would willingly perish to issue a powerful statement against a crushing regime that had reigned for generations, driven by a desperate choice between liberty and death. It appears that every generation witnesses an uprising, as the oppressed finally recognize their plight and acquire the tools necessary to organize, gain leverage, and fight back, though such change rarely occurs rapidly. Now, at twenty-seven, I stood once again at that same intersection, finding that while the physical black marks had long since vanished, my own naivety had also evaporated. Because this government had oppressed my mother’s generation, the preceding one, and surely those following, it would never cease unless compelled by force. I walked calmly toward the steps, preparing to leave the newest mark and ignite the next revolution. As the flames rose past my eyes, I sought one final look, enduring pain that was nearly unbearable yet surmountable enough that, before the world faded into darkness, I glimpsed a young girl pointing at me, standing precisely where I had been twenty-one years before, witnessing the cycle of history begin anew.
syntax_complex.writingprompts::23: Having walked downstairs to initiate the process, I opened the digital screen, which promptly displayed the face of a banker who greeted me by inquiring how he might be of assistance to Mrs. Roer. I explained that I wished to check my bank statement because I had received a letter in the mail suggesting that I possessed only five credits, prompting the banker to disappear briefly before returning to inform me that my current balance was actually ten credits. Stunned by this revelation, which meant I lacked even the resources to purchase basic groceries for the month, I looked outside and sighed, offering a perfunctory thank you before the screen closed after the banker wished me a pleasant day. I pondered how I could possibly have only ten credits of happiness remaining, especially considering that a single gallon of milk cost 1.21 credits, rendering me unable to afford even that necessity. Stepping outside into the bright, sunny weather where the birds seemed happy enough to surely afford their own groceries, I surveyed my surroundings, including my in-ground pool, my hot tub, and the outdoor deck complete with a pond located further from the house, all of which represented the life I had built. My husband and I had been married for ten years, and while I had once believed we were both genuinely happy, I checked my phone to find a message from him asking if I wanted to have coffee, to which I replied affirmatively. After going upstairs to take a shower, I noted that my husband was gone, as he always was, for it was no secret that our relationship had been falling apart, despite a time when we possessed more happiness credits than anyone else in the world. He had engaged in numerous affairs, and although I had never cheated, I found myself longing for more, so I prepared for our coffee meeting, choosing an outfit that was neither too dressy nor too casual. I drove to the airport, where we kept a private jet that my husband had already fueled, and after telling Bill I was just having coffee, I spent four hours traveling to see my spouse. Upon arriving and being greeted by my husband with his customary kiss on the cheek, I walked with him toward our second home, only to see a blonde woman in a tight blouse departing; I scowled at her as she hurried to her car. We needed to talk, I stated, and he replied with an air of satisfaction that he seemed to find in my obvious displeasure. I began to tell Mr. Roer that while I still loved him, there was so much more to consider, but he interrupted to demand a divorce. Surprised by his quickness, I watched him shrug it off, and I left immediately, abandoning the prospect of coffee. Soon after arriving home, I received another message from the bank stating that my happiness points had reached zero, but I was simultaneously surprised by a message from an old friend asking for coffee, to which I agreed. At that very moment, my doorbell rang, and upon answering, I found my old friend, who immediately kissed me, causing my blood pressure to rise as I recalled how much I had missed that sensation. When I tried to speak, he kissed me again to silence my words, explaining that he had actually paid my husband to let him marry me because my husband, who had never been good to me, desperately wanted a divorce. Shocked by the revelation that he had paid my husband to secure my hand, I struggled to understand why he would do such a thing until he mentioned our son, who needed me. A tear hit my chest as I remembered how I had given up Luke and our son to be with my husband, who had refused to allow a child in the house who was not his own. Luke asked me to marry him again, stepping further inside as he revealed that our twelve-year-old son was waiting in the car. Having been unable to see my son, Reig, since he was four because I feared that communication would look bad in the press, I ran outside to embrace him as he rushed from the vehicle. My phone alerted me to a new message, and while I checked it expecting an explanation from my husband regarding why he had sold my hand, I discovered instead that the bank had just credited my account with 20,000 happiness credits, causing me to tell Luke that I would certainly marry him.
