The gleaming towers of the Financial District, their silvery windows reflecting the flames that danced hungrily around them, stood like weeping angels as the first rosy fingers of dawn stretched out over the Eastern horizon. The stately mansions of the Original Founders had gone up in smoke early the day before, taking with them nearly seven hundred years of Dixie heritage, while the River District was left as little more than rubble, its historic wharves and warehouses becoming empty shells. Lieutenant Lucas Singleton Terry, who had been born a scion to a prominent rancher family, wept at the sight because this was his home, and to see its soil and its people so cruelly hurt bordered on the sacrilegious.

Mustang 5, this is Lead; we have received reports of Wolf activity along Broadway and Kingston, so the First and Second Lances will move in to investigate. That was Captain James T. Fulton, a man known for being a hard-ass and a son of a bitch, yet he remained a damn fine soldier nonetheless. Terry pressed his mike, acknowledging the order by stating that he understood, confirming that the Second Lance would advance. There used to be a third lance in Mustang Company, but an ambush by an entire Binary of Clanners had torn through the unit, forcing them to consolidate the survivors together. They were still better off than the rest of the Dixie Cavanaugh II Theater Militia, as Bronco and Stallion companies were barely at fifty percent effectives, while the armor and infantry battalions were faring even worse. The First Buena Guards and First Bolan Jaegers were putting up a fearsome fight against the rest of Clan Wolf's Gamma Galaxy, but it was of little use, for bit by bit, block by block, street by street and house by house, the Wolves were driving the Steiner defenders back. Terry switched his frequency to a more private channel, one shared between just the Captain and him.

Captain Fulton, I have a question regarding how long we have left, Terry asked, hearing his commanding officer sigh heavily over the radio. Who knows, perhaps years, months, or merely weeks? The First Buena is about to pull out, as the fucking Acting-Archon Brewer is ordering them to the defense of Tharkad. The Bolan Jaegers seem determined to stay, but that is just because they would rather have the fight happen here on our world instead of theirs. My best estimate is that we will last another year at this rate. And what happens if we fail to drive the Wolves off of Dixie, Terry asked, to which Fulton replied that if the worst should happen, he had a feeling they would not be alive to see it.
syntax_complex.writingprompts::29:
Because it was nigh impossible to see, we could only perceive the entity after it had vanished, and though we dared not speak its name, we understood its grim significance; if that manifestation haunted the skies above our territory, war was surely approaching. I shall never forget that initial encounter, occurring while I was stargazing in the dust fields with Roy, unaware that as we observed the stars, the creature was observing us in return. It existed as a shadow of a shadow, a monstrous relic from an ancient era long passed, and claiming that I truly saw it remains misleading, for the experience functioned more like a feeling; during the brief moment when I witnessed that blur slicing through the night, I realized everything was over. That night, they arrived.

Men clad in adaptable camouflage, armed with pulse rifles and lethal sabers, did not hesitate before cutting down the people in our village, and I remain lucky to have escaped with my life, an outcome I owe entirely to one artificial intelligence. He was a maintenance bot whom we had stolen from the federation, serving primarily to help us transport materials, yet on that day, he became a true hero. In the midst of the relentless gunfire and violent explosions, the mess hall collapsed, trapping me among the unfortunate souls inside; it happened in an instant, and before I possessed the time to react, I lay pinned beneath a pile of heavy rubble. Through the thick smoke and dancing flames, I glimpsed him, a grizzled maintenance bot bearing the serial number SR-71 upon his arm, his metallic silver eyes catching my gaze before he immediately rushed forward to facilitate my rescue.

As far as I know, we are the only ones who emerged alive, and we ran until I could no longer continue, eventually collapsing. As I lay there, clinging to the final threads of life, I kept stammering to myself, "Blackbird... Blackbird... Black..." SR-71 leaned in close, whispering into my ear: "There were a lot of things we couldn't do in an SR-71, but we were the fastest guys on the block and loved reminding our fellow aviators of this fact. People often asked us if, because of this fact, it was fun to fly the jet. Fun would not be the first word I would use to describe flying this plane. Intense, maybe, even cerebral. But there was one day in our Sled experience when we would have to say that it was pure fun to be the fastest guys out there, at least for a moment."
syntax_complex.writingprompts::30:
Although I initially harbored reservations regarding the first-person perspective, I ultimately elected to compose this piece nonetheless, as the provided prompt resonated deeply with my creative sensibilities.

Prisoner 778125-Sigma-8, you stand before this tribunal today, formally accused of egregious crimes against galactic civilization, which encompass murder, four distinct counts of xenocide, seventy counts of attempted xenocide, planetary dehabitation, total planetary destruction, and the treasonous attempt to overthrow the Pan-Galactic Alliance; how, therefore, do you choose to plead?

The man standing before Councilwoman Asaarha met the piercing gaze of both her and her fellow Arbiters with cold, unyielding blue eyes. Despite the one hundred and forty cycles of profound temporal isolation he had endured prior to this historic trial, Sacha Markes remained standing tall, entirely unbroken by his circumstances. He radiated an aura of inherent power and command, even now, when he had been stripped of his former rank, his vast fleet, and his mighty army. The last of the humans truly served as a living testament to his entire species.

The heavy silence that descended before he finally spoke seemed significantly louder to the Councilwoman than the rhythmic, crashing waves of her distant ocean home, and the duration it took for the human to respond seemed to stretch far longer than the vast span of the galaxy itself.

Guilty, he declared with a simple, chilling finality.

The Arbiters nodded their heads solemnly, acknowledging the admission, for none among them had truly expected that this one would ever plea for mercy.

Asaarha keyed the formal sentence into the terminal positioned before her, while the other six Arbiters followed suit in unison. The blue lights illuminating Markes’s uniform and his restraints shifted instantly to a warning red, and the screen mounted upon the psionic inhibitor encircling his head changed to display the word GUILTY in Galactic Standard.

Though the trial room remained empty save for the Tribunal and Markes, Asaarha could hear the phantom roars of vengeance that were surely reverberating throughout the galaxies, as each trial of the humans had been broadcast in its entirety, and each had concluded in a guilty verdict.

Sacha Markes, formerly the Admiral of the Seventh Human Expeditionary Fleet, High Captain of the Royal Guard, Commander-in-Chief of the Human Expeditionary Force, and Primarch of the Solar Empire, you are hereby sentenced to Psionic Stripping and immediate Execution by black hole; do you have any final words before the sentence is carried out?

The human threw his head back with defiance and turned his gaze directly upon the camera nearest him, where, addressing the billions of disparate life forms throughout the galaxy, he began the final soliloquy of the human race.

We brought you up out of the mud we found you in, offering you art, culture, and science. Our golden fleets created a civilization that will never be matched, not for one hundred thousand turns of the galaxy, and we are entirely responsible for all that you are. I remember clearly when the first of our race died after one hundred centuries of immortality, killed while trying to cure the sick of one of your backwater planets. I remember when we decided to take our retribution on our children, to punish you for your ignorance, and we burned that world. I watched our plasma cannons turn its surface to glass and its oceans to ash, for one world for one human life was a fair trade.

But you did not accept our judgment. Like Icarus chasing the sun, you rose up against us. Did you expect us to just let you? Did you think we would not defend ourselves? I was the commander of the fleet that met yours on the first day of battle, my ten cruisers against the most powerful battleships of three galaxies and a hundred races. Now, a hundred years later, you have finally defeated us. You have lost entire solar systems to us. You have sacrificed googles of lives and thousands of civilizations to bleed your gods dry and bind them in chains. Your worlds are shattered. Your cities are gone, wiped from history in an instant. Can you truly call that victory?

I am the last of my kind. I am Sacha Markes. Look upon my face, ye mighty, and despair. For when you kill me, you kill the last light left in this existence.
syntax_complex.writingprompts::32: War Journal of P1C Henry Whiticker, First Divine Armored. Entry:48. Having finally reached the rim of the first bolgia today, I find myself praying that heaven preserves me, for the scout reports, which I previously doubted, were certainly not lying; indeed, the chasm is more vast than anything I could have ever imagined. The reconnaissance photographs that we were given to prepare us for this descent are like a blind man attempting to describe a sunrise, and by God, the smell has actually, through some inexplicable process, gotten worse! Seeing the pit firsthand, I believe the enormity of our task has finally hit home for some of the crew, who look visibly rattled; I do not blame them for their hesitation, as I wonder, have we bitten off more than we can chew? I am not entirely sure, yet I maintain a steadfast faith in our mission and our commanders. The vastness of the pit really cannot be adequately put into words, but for the sake of this journal, I shall attempt to describe it. The rim extends further than the human eye should be able to see, and yet, despite the distance, I can make out tiny details on the far cliff face; it looks big enough that one could easily fit the whole Earth inside and knock it around like an ice cube in the bottom of a bourbon glass. Even while sitting in the cab of the rumbler, I get vertigo looking down onto the levels below, and if it were not for the special anti-psychotics the doctors provide us, I am certain that what I witness on the lower levels might have some lasting, horrific effect on my psyche. The crew and I wash down today’s dose with a bottle of sacramental wine, and why should we not, given that today was a good day after all? Today we reached the edge of Limbo. Entry:49. There is not much to record today, as there were only some minor skirmishes on the perimeter, consisting merely of some low-level demons taking a swipe at us, with otherwise nothing occurring but general camp maintenance. The engineers are working double time to ensure the security of Limbo Base, claiming it will be fully operational in two days, though I have my doubts. After their fiasco at the river, they have a lot of face to save, particularly considering the two rumblers, four squads of troops, and a Screacher that were lost because of their damned barges. Bastards. I hate just sitting around like this with nothing to distract me from the smell of rot and sulfur that somehow filters into the rumbler’s cab, despite the tech geeks’ assurances that the cab is perfectly, hermetically sealed; it feels as though the smell is inside my skull, rotting tiny holes into my brain. Entry:51. HOOAH! CONTACT BABY! Praise God, I have been waiting for this moment since the first days of the war for the surface. Hell finally saw fit to send us some worthy opponents, AND WE KICKED THEIR MUTHA-FUCKING TEETH IN!! HAHAHAHAHAHA. They came a few hours after my last entry, moving like a great black tornado. A swirling column of harpies, shrieks, and imps, beyond counting, rose up from the center of the pit and came crashing down, completely enveloping Limbo Base. The first few moments of engagement should have been chaos, but by the grace of God, we were ready. All the Screachers had been on high alert since we emerged from the maze of caves and onto the plains of Limbo proper eight days ago, and today that diligence paid off. The blitz of the winged demon assault crumbled before the wall of sound our blessed Screachers blasted out. The word of God is anathema to the denizens of Hell, and the word of God, pumped out through a mobile rig of high-powered speakers piloted by a devout member of the clergy, is downright debilitating. The shocked and paralyzed demons that twitched and writhed on the ground were easy targets, the rumblers’ blessed water cannons burning away swaths of the foul creatures as if the misted holy water were strong acid; huge piles of the creatures were reduced to ash in mere seconds. The larger demon harridans proved more resilient, and I saw more than a few grunts die on their talons, their sanctified body armor proving little better than cardboard. We repaid them in kind, and I am proud to say our rumblers’ javelin cannons sent a good lot of the giant buzzards screaming into oblivion, impaled on our gleaming silver spears. I should record this so it does not seem like I am diminishing the grunts’ efforts, their bravery and ferocity in battle being present in spades; despite the mortal danger, they collected their fair share of scalps, pinning the giant creatures with their silver pikes and finishing them off with their chain sickles. It was a glorious, bloody sight, like something out of a nature documentary. The greatest trial of the battle was yet to come, however. After a full day and a half of fighting, the black swarm began to thin out and we thought we might have finally broken their assault, but then they appeared. Three monstrous figures came into focus through the haze of ash and exhaustion. They were Hell Dragons, nothing like what we had seen in movies or our stories from childhood; these were great, pestilent, foul things that towered over us. They had snub-nosed heads, the size of a grand cathedral, covered in spines, and long armored bodies like insects, their faces and joints slick with thick black tar that bubbled and hissed as it fell from them and stained the plains of Limbo. Screachers focused their assault and prevented the titans from overrunning the base; the rumblers’ water tanks and javelin cannons ran dry just trying to keep them at bay, while our brave grunts held back the black swarm, fighting tirelessly, which allowed us time to retreat, resupply, and reenter the fray. And so it went for hours on end, and for all our efforts, the Hell Dragons seemed to be none the worse. Salvation finally came at the hands of the engineering corps—of all people! Through our efforts, we had given them enough time to secure and assemble Limbo Base’s major defenses, specifically the sanctified artillery and the holy rail gun. The rail gun punctured the dragons’ thick armor, spewing geysers of tar onto the battlefield, while the artillery smashed into the beasts’ vulnerable, exposed points, lodging shells etched with scripture deep in their bodies and wracking them with pain. The attack still went on for hours and we lost a great deal of our force, but after nearly two months since we first descended into this place, we finally have established a forward base to launch our attack on Hell. One bolgia down, eight to go. This is the first day here that the smell does not bother me.
syntax_complex.writingprompts::33: For ages, men have endured a fascination, disdain, fear, or general obsession with hell, yet it was the faithful who truly believed in its existence; some were caught up in the excitement of passing fervor, though most men never expected to have any contact with this hell, and certainly did not expect hell to come knocking. While I cannot at this time suppose a motive for the prince of lies to so suddenly mobilize the legions of the damned, I can, however, speak to its utter strangeness, and the devastation left in its wake. In hindsight, a company named Apollyon ought to have aroused some suspicion; alas, as few knew Greek, and the meaning of Apollyon—a medieval Greek translation for the destroyer attributed to Satan—a banking leviathan hiding behind less conspicuous shell corporations aroused no suspicion. While most of us were preoccupied with the myopic affairs of day-to-day life, Mr. Morning-Star stretched his hands to slowly throttle the cliché servants of the Lord of darkness, those being politicians, bankers, criminals, and any other disciplines traditionally associated with wickedness. Ironically, many who had been accused of consorting with the devil only now found themselves under his corrupting influence. So, long story short, the devil became a business tycoon, and it was the allure of cheap, mass-produced goods he invaded with, though I am sorry that I cannot write more, being sleepy as I am.
syntax_complex.writingprompts::34:
The planet Earth has undergone significant transformation recently, specifically since twenty-three years ago—almost to the very day—when the tempests that had been raging across the surface for roughly five thousand years finally ceased. After a few weeks elapsed while the dense cloud formations gradually disintegrated, we were granted our inaugural, unobstructed view of our ancestral home.

I, being merely five years old at that pivotal moment, found myself captivated primarily by the vibrant colors, as the breathtaking shades of blue and green were unlike anything I had ever witnessed aboard the Ark. While we certainly possessed water, we lacked pools sufficiently vast to manifest that specific, deep azure hue; similarly, though we cultivated plants, the suboptimal conditions aboard the station rendered them a drab, dirty green rather than the lush, thriving vegetation of Earth, fueling my intense desire to see the surface closer, to touch it, and to truly feel it.

That realization likely served as the catalyst for my decision to enlist in the recruitment process for the inaugural journey, which, as the moniker implies, was the very first expedition to return to the planet’s surface. Because numerous individuals clamored to descend immediately following the dissipation of the storms, leading to widespread protests and even violent riots, many fools demanded that the Ark return prematurely.

Although twenty-three years might have seemed an agonizingly long duration to wait, it remained imperative, for we were, after all, the remnants of humanity; had we landed prematurely only for unforeseen complications to arise, the risk would have been too great. Consequently, years of meticulous geological scans and low-atmosphere scouting provided us with an ideal landing site, offering minimal disturbance to the local environment, ample space for developing a new community, abundant food and water, and, crucially, significant natural protection provided by mountain ranges formed during the cataclysm and deep trenches filled with the darkest blue water.

Naturally, a vessel as gargantuan as the Ark could not simply land, which necessitated the first journey; we were the first cohort to descend planetside to live permanently in over seven generations. Our primary objective involved constructing the dock, a labor-intensive project projected to span five or six years, which would provide a much-needed foundation while enabling us to map the local geography, catalog indigenous flora, and study the fauna. The sobering reality remained that we were venturing into the unknown, as this safe-zone, so dubbed by the Corps, could easily devolve into a deathtrap, particularly because its isolated location ensured that, once we arrived, our shuttle would be incapable of departing.

Part of the persistent difficulty involved the storms; even now, twenty-three years after the primary weather systems ended, smaller, localized cells continued to circulate, though the mountain ranges, which were not quite powerful enough to crest the high peaks, protected our designated area. Even in the atmosphere above, vicious, relentless winds blew, threatening to tear any outgoing ship to pieces, meaning only a craft as massive as the Ark could survive, yet the Ark required a completed dock to perform a successful takeoff. Thus, that was our mission: descend, confront potential death, and construct a massive super-structure in less than six years, and I was damn excited.
syntax_complex.writingprompts::35:
Exterior, Jerusalem side street, day, where an area near a couple of large amphorae has been taped off while CSI techs are busy performing their forensic duties. Next to his car stands Moses, looking visibly tired and irritable, and after a few moments lingering on this scruffy patriarch leaning heavily on his walking stick, we pull back just as Jesus enters from the left, carrying takeout coffee.

Moses: Took you long enough, for it feels like we have been waiting for you forever!

Jesus: Sorry, there was a line, so tell me, what have we got here?

Moses: A dead body, which Uniform called in, and it looks like another dead hooker; hey, Hazdrubul, have you determined the cause of death yet?

We pan over to the masked and coveralled figure beside what we can now see as a corpse, and Hazdrubul steps away from the crime scene.

Hazdrubul: It is a little early to say, but if I were a betting man, I would go with blunt force trauma, as it looks like multiple contusions over the body and a really nasty one to the side of the head.

Jesus: When did she die?

Hazdrubul: It is hard to give a precise time of death right now, but I will go with some time last night and give you a better number when we get a liver temp.

Moses: Good enough.

Jesus moves to get closer to the crime scene, trying to get a better look, but he does not react well to the corpse and ducks behind an amphora to throw up.

Moses: Jesus! Well, at least you did not contaminate the crime scene.

Jesus re-emerges, wiping his mouth and looking pale.

Moses: OK, Uniform is going to canvas house to house, so let us go get you cleaned up and see if we can put a name to this poor girl.

Scene 23: Precinct House interior, interview room. Jesus and Moses are on opposite sides of the room with arms folded, obviously antagonistic.

Moses: Do not give me any of your holier than thou bullshit, because we needed results and I got them!

Jesus: And was it worth all the trouble it caused, Moses, or was it worth going down to their level?

Moses: I would do it again, I would do it again in a heartbeat, for forty years I have been in this job, and if there is one thing I know how to do, it is get a confession!

Jesus: You know, the first time I saw you with that stick, I thought it was a sign of age, and I thought it made you an elder, someone to be respected, but I guess I was wrong.

Moses: Maybe you are wrong about a lot of things.

Jesus: Maybe I am!

Moses: And maybe you want to think about how it looks out there to our brother cops when you, a snot nosed junior Levite, think you can tell me how to conduct myself!

Jesus: Look, let us just calm down here, as I respect you, sure I respect you, for you took down the Golden Calf gang and you were the guy who resolved the Dead Sea Hostage situation, but this is not the desert, this is Jerusalem, and we have to do things differently now!

Moses: The hell you say...

Jesus: Look, man, think what you like, but there is a girl down in the morgue on a slab and all she is doing is getting colder while we stand here throwing stones at each other... hhh, of course!

Moses: What?

Jesus: Of course, stone throwing, for don't you see it?

Moses: Jesus, slow down, will you, and see what?

Jesus: They thought they were better than her!

Scene 832: Jerusalem, exterior, night. Moses is leaning on a squad car as Jesus walks up with this week's bad guy in handcuffs, and Moses watches as Jesus hands the bad guy off to uniformed cops.

Moses: Good collar, kid.

Jesus: I could not have done it if you had not spotted the connection between the victims, but how did you know?

Moses: I have been on the job for longer than you have been alive, and after a while, you get a feel for this sort of thing.

Jesus: Do you think I will ever develop that kind of instinct?

Moses: Maybe, if you live long enough.

Jesus: You are full of encouragement, but I do not care, though, because we put a sinner behind bars and that is the kind of good news I want to share!
syntax_complex.writingprompts::36:
Hey, observe those chickadees currently occupying the birdbath, Kylo exclaimed, while he whooped and puffed out his chest with such excessive vigor that he nearly toppled off his precarious perch. 

Don't be a troglodyte, bro, Atticus groused, pecking rhythmically at his seeds, for you are merely a wren, and that species is not even within the same biological family. 

I do not care, Kylo replied, and I am going to go talk to them, whereupon he took off, swerving through the air like a fragile leaf trapped in a sudden gust. Atticus sighed and took off after him, knowing he would have to keep close tabs on Kylo or else they would surely get kicked out of the garden again. 

Kylo crashed into the water with a mighty splash, causing droplets to fly in every direction and drenching the startled occupants of the birdbath. They squawked with great indignation as Kylo emerged from beneath the surface, vigorously shaking the wetness from his head. He trotted up to a group of soaked finches and gave his wings a shake, declaring, Hey, birds, nice tits. 

We are not tits, a purple finch retorted, stepping forward from the group to launch into a tirade regarding how overused that particular pickup line was. Atticus alighted on the rim of the bath and began to walk around, apologizing to everyone for Kylo's boorish behavior while pleading with them not to call the bouncer over. 

Okay, sorry, Kylo interrupted, let me make it up to you, for how about you and I head over there—he motioned toward the bird feeder—and I share my seeds with you? If birds possessed lips, Kylo would undoubtedly be smirking right now. 

The finches began to flap their wings angrily, splashing Kylo with water as they cried, You are such a boor, so get out of here! Many of the onlookers chirped in agreement, and some of the larger birds began to puff their chests threateningly. Atticus shoved Kylo to the side and raised his own wings, stating, On behalf of my friend here, I apologize, as he has clearly had too much nectar, so we will just be going now. 

Oh, you think we are going to fall for that? The purple finch spat a nut shell at his feet, adding, He is just trying to play wingbird for you, is he not, so he can let you take the fall while he swoops in to look better by comparison? The other birds chorused in total agreement. 

I think these two need to be taught a lesson, a blue jay remarked, fluttering over to Atticus while towering a full inch above him. He spread his wings menacingly, effectively blocking Atticus from taking off, and asked, Why do you not peck on someone your own size? The onlookers broke into loud cheers, shouting for a fight. 

Well, you are kind of bigger than me, Atticus replied, taking a step back into the bath as he felt feathers ruffle against him while the crowd pressed around and urged him toward the jay, asking, That would not be my own size now, would it? 

Kylo staggered in front of him and began to hop around, insisting, Do not worry, Atticus, because we have got this. 

Hey, this is a one-on-one fight, the jay looked around and warned, so if you get back-up, then— 

Who on earth placed all this here? A door opened, and the birds began to scatter, screaming, Human! Atticus grabbed Kylo and urged him into the air, and the two lost themselves amongst the cloud of fleeing birds, while out of the corner of his eye, he saw the human scratching his head in front of the birdbath. 

Make sure to thank that human for bailing you out of yet another mess, Atticus said. 

Kylo scoffed, claiming, We could have totally taken that guy, and as the two flew over the Toyota in the driveway, he let loose a dropping that landed right in the center of the windshield.
syntax_complex.writingprompts::37: The man who was my father used to strike me with such relentless frequency that my body became a map of his rage. Although I had never even consumed a single drink, he beat cracked ribs, bruised kidneys, and loose teeth into my frame, claiming his violence was a twisted method to ensure I would never mirror his own debased existence. On the rare occasions when he remained sober, he would confess that his alcoholism stemmed from the trauma of his own upbringing, speaking as if he expected me to empathize with his plight or offer him some absolution. It was as if he were blind to the reality that my arm was fractured from his supposed protection against the bottle only a week prior, or that he could not perceive himself looming over my broken form, jeering while I wept blood, snot, and tears. He seemed unable to recall the very horrors of his childhood that necessitated his nightly intoxication, a desperate cycle intended to suppress the screaming terrors that haunted his sleep and the humiliating accidents that plagued his dreams. My father made me physically ill, leaving me with a breath that catches in my throat, a wrist that never healed correctly, rendering that hand perpetually crippled, and a set of eleven false teeth, all before I reached the age of twenty-three. Though I refused to attend his funeral, I celebrated his passing, yet I remained steadfast in my sobriety, for I could never bring myself to drink. I continue to weep myself to sleep, unable to suppress a scream if someone approaches me too suddenly, and lately, I have noticed blood emerging when I cough, yet I refuse to let him defeat me by granting him this final, hollow victory. When my son was born, it marked the happiest day of my life, as I felt truly needed for the first time, though his mother abandoned us shortly thereafter, claiming she desired an escape from a lifestyle she supposedly never chose, despite having carried our child for nine months without protest. After she departed, the weight became unbearable, leading me to leave my son with my mother for one night so I could finally have a drink. It felt perfect, providing the greatest sensation of my life, for during those few hours, I was finally free from fear, self-loathing, and constant anxiety. Feeling calm and capable of managing my burdens, I intend to continue drinking to maintain this relief, as sobriety now terrifies me, especially since I have discovered such a superior alternative. When I retrieved my son the following morning, my mother regarded me with suspicion, but I dismissed her concerns, rushing away because I was eager to sample whisky. Nevertheless, I will ensure my son never suffers as I did, teaching him that alcohol is inherently evil; I will guarantee he associates the substance with me, and since I am undeniably bad, he will inevitably break the cycle. I may lack the strength myself, but he will possess it, becoming calloused, cold, and hard enough to finally overcome the darkness that I cannot defeat.
syntax_complex.writingprompts::38:
While Craig was walking home from the shops, he unexpectedly encountered God, a meeting that he certainly was not anticipating, given that sane people rarely experience such divine interventions. In reality, he rarely contemplated the existence of God, for he neither strictly believed in a deity nor maintained a strong enough disbelief to dwell upon the non-existence of gods; religion, much like the concept of God itself, remained a topic that simply did not pique his interest.

A subject he cared about deeply, however, was that of Caramels, which, if you are unfamiliar with them, are rather delicious, chocolatey, biscuit-like confections composed of several layers of crisp wafer encased in smooth chocolate, and Craig was absolutely crazy about them. Although he might not have been a religious man, his fervent feelings regarding Caramels certainly approached the intensity of religious devotion. The primary reason behind his trip to the local shops had been to procure more Caramels, and his mind was brimming with sweet anticipation as he headed back toward his home.

He was approximately two minutes away from his residence, and the promise of Caramel satisfaction, when God first addressed him.

"Hey! Craig!"

His Caramel-centered contemplation having been interrupted, Craig turned around to identify the individual who had spoken to him. Standing behind him was a tall person clad in a loose-fitting suit; Craig, feeling uncertain regarding the person's gender, observed that they were quite androgynous, appearing not dissimilar to the Diamond Dogs era of David Bowie. They looked somewhat familiar to Craig, yet he could not quite put his finger on exactly where he might have seen them before. Realizing that he had been staring, he sought something appropriate to say.

"Hi," he began hesitantly. "Do I know you?"

"In a way," the Bowie lookalike replied. "I am God."

"Well, good for you. I must get going now. Bye," said Craig before starting back toward his house. Since he had Caramels in his bag, he did not want to be wasting precious time on some crazy person.

"Wait, do not go yet. Please," called out the person. "What would it take for you to believe me?"

Craig sighed and turned back, deciding that humouring the person would probably enable him to reach his Caramels much faster.

"I do not know," said Craig, visibly exasperated. "A miracle, or something similar. Some extraordinary thing which could not just be performed by any old person. Something more substantial than just claiming that you are God."

"Hmm. How about... this!" God pointed at a nearby bush, which suddenly burst into flames. The blaze rapidly shaped itself into the form of a dragon, which roared at the two of them. Then, with a mere snap of God's fingers, the blaze was extinguished, leaving the bush singed but entirely intact. God turned back to Craig with arms spread wide, as if to say, "Tada!"

Craig, looking only mildly impressed, turned back to God.

"Yeah, that was pretty good. It looked very impressive, I have to admit, although I have no idea how you did it. A hologram, perhaps? It worked for Tupac, so I can certainly see it working for a dragon."

God stared at him for a few seconds before responding.

"I did it by being God. You asked for a miracle, and I showed you one. What more do you want from me?"

"Do not get me wrong, it is very good. But the whole God thing probably is not going to fly. Maybe people would be more likely to believe you are a wizard."

"But I am not a damn wizard!" shouted God. "I am God. Why would I say I am a wizard?"

Craig backed off a few meters, holding his hands up in front of him in the international gesture of "I do not want any trouble, let us all just calm down."

"Hey, calm down, buddy. I am sorry if I came across as harsh, but it is just constructive criticism. This is for a T.V. show or a YouTube thing, right? You are not going to convince anyone with the whole 'God' thing."

God, visibly seething by this point, held Craig's gaze for a few more seconds before letting out an angry sigh and storming off. Craig watched them leave, then shook his head and returned to his journey. He considered checking out the bush to see if he could discover any clues as to how the trick had been performed, but he decided against it. Whoever had been recording the encounter was probably still watching, waiting for Craig to do exactly that. So, he pushed it out of his mind and set off home, for, after all, there were Caramels waiting for him.
syntax_complex.writingprompts::39:
Pass me the damn bottle, would you, Patsy, if you are not too busy to assist a dying man? Get it yourself, Ser Whyte, for I am certainly not your bloody squire anymore, having long since abandoned that subservient role. Right, well then, my liege, would you do me the honor of retrieving my wine so that I may finally die drunk and happy? As you wish, sir-knight, I shall provide this final service. I hate you, Patsy, the bedridden husk of a former knight bellowed with a harsh, rattling cough that shook his frail frame. His rusty suit of white armor, which had once gleamed in the sun, clinked and clanked loudly as he jerked up violently, while his greasy, gray hair shot up in an instant of agitation. Sputtering still, he downed the little glass bottle of wine clutched in his hand, and the subsequent belch was as loud as the lightning's thunder striking down on a dark, rainy night. 

Beside him, there sat a young man, upon whose short locks of brown rested a little silver crown, now chipped and beaten from the torn-away gemstones that once adorned it. Deep green eyes, far too young to experience what it truly means to rule a volatile kingdom, gazed down upon the Knight Whyte, who remained his knight despite the changing tides. Tell me, the knight's arm, weak and weary from years of strife, placed his bottle on the bedside table, how is Isabella faring, considering I haven't been able to receive a single letter from you for months? We have shut down the postal service, remember, and while the courier service still handles the delivery of packages, all official messages must go through that fancy, modern tele-ma-gram system. 

Hah, what an era your kingdom has come to, with bows that spew steel and fire and scribes who control entire townships, so that pretty soon, even my own kind will be entirely out of work. The king chuckled, though the sound was forced and awkward through his lips, for he had no need for knights anymore, nor did any neighboring kingdom, as they were now merely artifacts that talked and drank and fought. War in this time was determined solely by how much gold you could carry, how many people you could take, and how many flags you could successfully plant on some nameless hill. 

What is with that look, king, has that queen kicked you out of your castle again, because you are more than welcome to take some sleep in my castle here, provided you remember to clean the corpses out from their beds first? That is a terrible joke, Whyte, the king replied with a weary frown. So, we are dropping the titles, but I do not think we need another repeat of Georgie bringing about another revolution, given that the guillotines were only a little uncomfortable. A little, the king asked, and the knight replied, a little. 

The rain outside appeared to stop, the lightning-storm ceased in its steps, and the king moved to the windowsill to see that snow had started to fall. A snowfall, white and thick, had come just in time to shroud the world. Hmm, you see that, Whyte? The knight in rusting armor had gotten up out of his bed, placing his brownish-orange metal gauntlets on the young king's shoulder. A gust of wind came bellowing through, slapping its cold blanket of winter air against the faces of the two men, and the king's smile flashed warmly at the knight, who responded in kind. With wet eyes, the young man turned to the knight. How ironic that I said hello to you on a night as snowy as this. And you will say good-bye on a snowy night too. I am glad to have called you my knight. And you my king. 

The knight turned back to his dead, his legs suddenly shaking with a fury that sent him down to the hard wood floor. His king moved to help him up, stopped only by a raised gauntlet, still coppery-red and faded. With a great effort, the knight made it to his bed, taking his gauntlets off and throwing them right out the windowsill. I guess it is about time I have gotten rid of those, as they are too old for me. I have seen older, take a look at the man who wore them. You always were a cheeky little patsy, the knight murmured, his skin falling over his dry eyes, though drawing back before he could even blink. I grow tired, so would you tell me a story? What am I, your mother? Just tell me that story. That story, yes, after all, we only know that one story. Don't play cute with me, Patsy. Alright, alright, Whyte, but do you promise to go to sleep right after? 

The king sighed, taking a knee on the side of the bed, and the knight smiled, his eyelids finally drooping over his eyes as his hands clasped over his chest while the beating of his heart grew slow. The winter chill must be getting to him, for he too had felt the cold, and through hot tears, the king began, once upon a time, in a village far, far away...
syntax_complex.writingprompts::40: One metre high and as wide across, the blackened, dusty car roared down the desert road, pursued by the troupe who, while clutching their tank of helium, struggled in vain as the motorized unicycle blazed ahead of the fifteen clowns inside the vehicle, who now readied their weapons while closing fast upon their rivals. Boffo, Luffy, and Bobo, hearing Kinko grate that these fucking clowns had finally fucked with them for the last time, received orders to whitewash their asses so thoroughly that they would be forced to honk their noses from the inside, causing them to nod while gripping their slapsticks ever tighter. With a deafening roar, the car pulled ahead of the clowns, sliding to a sudden halt, at which point the doors opened in unison and the fifteen of them tumbled out, rolling to their feet. Two clowns grabbed the weaponized ladder from the roof, accidentally knocking over three others who were busy readying their semiautomatic pielaunchers, and then knocking those same three down again as they turned to see what they had hit, while two others collided, falling to the ground, outstretched and immobile. To one side, Bobo and Kinko hefted their pails of custard and started towards the unicycle. Bastards, screamed a whitefaced warrior as she fell from the shoulders of the topmost clown, rolling as she landed to spray a stream of water from the flower on her lapel, knocking Kinko to the ground with a highly amusing parp. Grabbing a rubber chicken from the driver, she waded into the fray, knocking Kinko's clowns over like bowling pins while yelling that the helium was theirs. The hell it is, roared Luffy, pulling the pin on his rubber nose before tossing it at the jesters falling from the unicycle seat, insisting that the helium was for their balloons, because balloon zoos belonged to them, and them alone. Grabbing the back of her pants, Bobo upended the bucket of custard into them before pushing her to the ground, and as she bounced up and started running in circles, he grabbed the cylinder from the unicycle and tossed it into the car. Our troupe, he cheered, as the rest of the clowns piled into the vehicle, one of whom cranked the front handle to life, and with a cheery melody, they drove off down the road toward their big top in the wasteland. As they disappeared over the horizon, the whitefaced warrior sadly blew her horn, watching the dust cloud fade in the distance.
syntax_complex.writingprompts::41: The air here remains remarkably cool, while thick fog rises steadily off the gardens, and the atmosphere becomes heavy, saturated with the pervasive, sweet perfume of blooming flowers. Suddenly, a sharp shout erupts from the high tower, announcing that a stranger is approaching from the distant south. In truth, there exists absolutely nothing to the south, save for vast stretches of sand and dry dust and, perhaps, if one chooses to believe the grim legends of the barbarians, the weathered, ancient bones of long-dead monsters. The traveler is a tattered, wretched man who, having lost his sandals along the grueling march, now displays the raw, bloodied bottoms of his feet, while filthy rags hang loosely off the protruding bones of his shoulders and hips, suggesting he remains alive only through the mysterious, lingering grace of the gods. Before he can be presented to the commander for questioning, he must be thoroughly cleaned, fed, and properly dressed, though he shall receive no reward as of yet, for it remains entirely unknown if he is a common deserter. When the servants attempt to wash him, the water almost kills the shivering man; he screams like a helpless babe, thrashing violently in the pool while sobbing piteously for his mother, his father, and his commander, even begging for the sweet release of death. That mercy is not granted to him, and soon he falls into a hollow silence, allowing the slaves to scrub him until his skin is clean, revealing that his various wounds are not truly grievous. As he is being dressed in fresh garments, a nearby sentry mutters that the boy is not yet a man, implying that the armor he wears must have been stolen from a corpse. When food is finally brought to him, he initially refuses to eat, though he eventually finds that the bread agrees with his stomach, yet he is strictly forbidden from gorging himself. The commander begins to ask about the others, specifically the hundred thousand strong, that whispered host of the strongest and most loyal warriors who were said to fear absolutely nothing. They are all dead, and the boy, appearing stunted and hollow, reveals that fear had stolen his nerve and his iron will, though not his underlying honor. They had walked for thousands of leagues, and upon entering a deep valley, the sun and the stars were entirely lost to them, replaced by monstrous things—half-men with sloping, misshapen torsos and sharp, jagged teeth, cats twice the size of a warhorse composed of fire and swirling smoke, and beasts with snakes for noses and tusks like a boar that roared with the deafening volume of a thousand trumpets. Deeper they must have marched, into a jungle that surely served as Pluto's own garden, where everything they encountered brought only swift death. They did not actually possess a hundred thousand men, but only five thousand, and by the time they finally discovered the thing of nightmares—a titan’s aborted, wretched fetus—they numbered merely in the hundreds. It came during the night, drawn inevitably by the warmth of their fires. It was precisely here that the boy stopped, trembling so violently that his teeth ground together with a force suggesting they might shatter within his mouth, yet he possessed enough honor to speak truthfully of the horrors he had witnessed. The creature must have been drawn by the fires, perhaps remembering the hell from which it originated, or perhaps it saw some flicker of strength within those flames. Its appearance was sudden, falling near the fire, stirring the embers and sending brilliant sparks into the air; it possessed small, hooked claws and was armored like a fish, and while it was not particularly large, the boy gestured to his waist to indicate it was roughly the size of a war dog, sporting leathery wings like a bat. It drank the fire, and the gods, in their cruelty, gave it power, allowing it to rise up and slaughter a hundred men during that first night. The host fled through the hellish garden, where some were felled by the predatory plants and the beasts; one man awoke screaming in the absolute darkness, for insects had eaten away at his flesh, swarming through his open mouth and nose and the empty, staring sockets of his eyes. After that night, no one slept. Was that how the boy lost his hand? No, that occurred on the fifth day. The men had begun to succumb to madness, as every tree, rock, puddle, and patch of dirt appeared identical in the gloom. They reached a cliff, and someone insisted they must climb it, so they did. The boy was quick, yet some men were quicker, standing along the top of the world to help the others climb; when the boy finally pulled himself over, he saw piles of bodies and called below, warning that death waited above, wearing the face of their own brothers. One of the men tried to kill him, but instead, the boy lost half of his hand to a jagged rock, which crushed and mangled his flesh, forcing him to haul himself up and scramble away in terror. He abandoned the men and headed north, for the host was scattered, and he could see the sky again, though his hand felt tight, hot, and swollen. His fingers turned white, then a deep red, and on the fifth day, he gnawed them off. On the seventh, he lost one sandal, threw the other away, and in a fit of absolute madness, stripped off his clothes, walking until the forest thinned and he was burnt by the sun. There was no water or food, though once he saw a golden eagle and followed it, only to realize there was no eagle. On the ninth day, he found a man hung from a tree, stripped the body of its clothes, and dressed himself in the garments of the dead. As he walked north, his hand leaked blood and his feet cramped, but one night he built a fire, which sparked a great fear in him; nevertheless, he was brave enough to put his hand inside the flames to stop the rot from spreading, after which he crawled away and cried until the sun rose again. As he walked, he left the grasslands, desperate to see water, desperate to die. On the tenth day, he saw the beast again, or perhaps a different one; it had the body of a dog, stood upright, had long claws, and chattered like a bird, being the size of a man's leg from the ground to his knee. A flock of them called to each other, and the boy followed until they took down a beast—the one with the snake for a nose—which had leather for skin and wailed as it died. After the dog-beasts left, the boy ate what he could. The boy stopped there, for there was nothing else to say; he had come to the sand and walked, his voice quiet and tired, his body telling the heavy toll that his voice could not. Could he die now? No, not yet, for more would surely want to hear of this.
syntax_complex.writingprompts::42:
The subway stopped with a sudden, bone-jarring jolt, causing Laurentius to awake with a sharp, involuntary gasp as he struggled to process the chilling environment that surrounded him. Having examined his strange armor, he noted that his hands were encased in gloves fashioned from what appeared to be cow hide, while his feet were tucked into warm, fur-lined black boots. Beneath a heavy, dark coat, he wore a soft white shirt secured by intricate clasps, complemented by a strip of red fabric that draped around his neck and extended past his midsection. Wondering if these were tokens of his own mortality, he asked himself how he had died, only to find his gaze meeting that of a rotund, darker-skinned woman who was preoccupied with a curious, layered-parchment device resting upon her lap. Observing a cross hanging about her neck, he looked at her with profound sympathy, concluding that perhaps this was indeed the custom of the dead.

Tubes of artificial light illuminated the metal chamber, which signaled its status with a smooth, resonant ding before the doors slid shut. To the astonishment of Laurentius, the chamber resumed its motion, prompting him to stand and seek out the man who appeared to be in command—a figure dressed in traditional attire for the era, distinguished by a large silver wig and glasses that bore the label "2015" across the front. When Laurentius offered a polite, archaic "Salve," the man merely returned a confused, vacant look before resuming his gaze out the window, smelling faintly of wine. Laurentius then inquired in his native tongue, "Aut ubi sum? Quis hic locus?", but the chamber shook once more, disrupting his balance as a garbled voice erupted from the loudspeaker. When the vessel halted again, Laurentius was caught off guard and tumbled onto the floor amidst a rushing wave of departing passengers. Rising to his feet, he followed the crowd through winding tunnels, struggling to comprehend the musicians lining the enclosed street and the sparse vendors he encountered before finally reaching a flight of stairs. Upon ascending, he was struck with overwhelming awe at the spectacle before him.

Bright lights flashed in every direction, transforming the steady hum of voices he had previously heard into an intense, chaotic onslaught of sound and movement. To his left and right, crowds of people surged toward a central location dominated by a massive spire that reached toward the heavens, topped by a mysterious, glowing sphere. Gazing upward at the sky, he found no stars, and as he pondered this absence, a sudden realization washed over him, bringing a profound sense of relief and happiness. Since he was clearly above the stars, he concluded that he must be traversing the beautiful, long-awaited plains of Asphodel.

Suddenly, a man dressed in a similar black coat, black pants, and white shirt hurried toward him, his eyes obscured by black metal, his breath forming frost in the air as he spoke. Grabbing Laurentius by the arm and exclaiming "Dick!", the man left the overwhelmed Laurentius with no room for protest, so he simply followed. As they moved, the man rambled about the crowd waiting and their growing impatience, noting that Kathy had tried her best to manage the situation. Realizing he must learn the language of this afterlife, Laurentius began to notice the crowd shifting their attention toward him, prompting him to offer the same greeting he had been given. Nodding at the passers-by while being led away, he repeated "Dick" once more to a young girl, whose mother immediately covered her ears and cast a scathing glare in his direction.

After navigating the bustling streets for several minutes, Laurentius was padded down by other gentlemen in similar attire before being ushered up steep metal stairs onto a platform that overlooked the massive, expectant crowd below. A red-haired woman holding a microphone greeted him with an urgent, "Dick! Where have you been? We're on in 2." Laurentius smiled and repeated the word "Dick," to which she replied, "Well, you know what I like." When someone handed him a plastic cord with a bud on the end, he followed the woman’s lead by placing it in his ear, assuming it was part of the welcoming ritual. He listened as she spoke to a man behind a large metal contraption featuring a folded glass mirror in the center, hearing her announce, "Live in 30." Looking directly at Laurentius, she asked if he was ready, and when he nodded, she handed him a metal stick tipped with fur. As she stared into the device, her lips curled into a smile, and Laurentius, mirroring her expression, felt his own face soften. A small red light illuminated the corner of the contraption, followed by a brief, heavy silence, until the woman nudged him expectantly. Taking a deep, steadying breath, Laurentius smiled and spoke the word "Dick" once more, looking toward his companion with an air of profound, hopeful anticipation.
syntax_complex.writingprompts::43: Finding a pizza company willing to deliver to my home proved remarkably difficult, primarily because the delivery boys invariably returned dazed, appearing notably paler and thinner, while clutching an untouched thin crust pizza still sealed within its box. After all, a vampire must eventually eat. I had considered myself quite clever thousands of years ago, choosing Rome—the home of every religion except the one that mattered—to escape those wretched crosses of cheap wood that had begun to rest against every doorway in Jerusalem. I truly believed I would make my home in Italy, naively assuming Christianity would never follow me to what had been the greatest nation the world had ever seen. How profoundly wrong I had been. Almost overnight, missionaries appeared, and within a century, a cross adorned every door while a church occupied every block, leaving me trapped, with certain death lurking just outside should I dare poke my head beyond my beautiful wooden door. Outside, I sensed three children giggling as they shoved one another upon my doorstep; finally, one jumped up to ring the bell before they all scampered away, thrilled by the prospect of ringing the recluse’s doorbell and living to tell the tale. How very riveting. I hate humans, I whispered to myself. Flipping through the seemingly eight-hundredth phone book crammed into my mail slot this past year, I desperately attempted to identify a restaurant that had not yet heard the local legend of the feared Pale Master of The Takeout. One could only hope for such a miracle.
syntax_complex.writingprompts::44:
The wizard, known as Marvolio IV, held the small garden slug within the palm of his hand, contemplating the absurdity of his recent ritual. Having previously summoned demons the size of sprawling castles, carved new rivers into the landscape, and devised a charm to prevent nose itches while one’s hands remained occupied, he found it impossible to believe that he would mistakenly summon a mere slug when his true intent had been to summon God himself. He carefully placed the creature down, reasoning that even if it obviously wasn't the Almighty, it might perhaps be God's favorite slug.

He spent hours meticulously scouring his notes, measuring the sacred summoning circles with precision, and teasing the element distillations for any lingering impurities, convinced that a mistake resided somewhere within his calculations. As the slug nibbled at the corner of his workbook, the moon began falling toward the ground and the sun started peeking over the horizon, at which point God finally decided to speak.

LETTUCE.

Wh-what, Marvolio whispered, his voice trembling; the sound had appeared directly inside his head, and although his mostly sane mind could barely tolerate the intrusion, he knew instinctively that this was the voice from which all existence sprang and by which all was sustained. He knew that this voice was older than time itself, and, most terrifyingly, he realized that this voice originated from the three-inch slug resting upon his workbench.

BRING ME LETTUCE. IT IS NOT WISE TO REFUSE ME.

Marvolio walked in a haze into his kitchens, where he discovered a basket of lettuce; he inspected it, noting that it appeared somewhat wilted and that a blue, fuzzy substance had begun creeping around the edges, for wizards rarely concerned themselves with vegetables. Although the slug remained on the opposite side of the house, its voice sprang again, unwelcome and intrusive, into Marvolio's brain.

YES THAT'LL DO NICELY.

Surely not, he stammered, I mean, for God? It is not—I mean, I could run to the market and procure some of that black Italian cabbage that—

NO, I LIKE IT LIKE THAT. NICE AND SOFT.

Marvolio gibbered quietly to himself as he brought the rotting vegetable back to the one true lord of life, who enjoyed the lettuce thoroughly while Marvolio sat and continued his frantic gibbering.

WELL.

Well what? I mean, um, yes—Lord.

YOU WANTED TO KNOW SOMETHING? YOU PUT A LOT OF EFFORT INTO BRINGING ME HERE SO YOU SHOULD PROBABLY ASK.

Oh, um, well, why did you create everything? I mean, there is so much suffering and—

LETTUCE.

I do not think I have any more.

NO, I CREATED THIS WORLD TO PRODUCE THE CORRECT KIND OF LETTUCE; THIS IS THE MOST LETTUCY OF ALL POSSIBLE WORLDS.

That actually explains a lot.

If God could shrug he would have; instead, he stared at Marvolio impassively with his divine stalks.

Should I try to send you back?

NO, JUST POP ME OUT IN THE BACK GARDEN; THAT IS A GOOD LAD.

Marvolio never spoke of his experience, nor did he practice wizardry again, but he did take up gardening, eventually becoming famous nationwide for his impressive variety of award-winning lettuce and cabbages.
syntax_complex.writingprompts::45:
I do not know, Sharon, for I am simply exhausted by it all, Markond remarked while leaning back into his throne, which was constructed from the bones of many a fallen hero. I sit within this dark lair throughout the day and the endless night, waiting for some poor, unsuspecting group of wide-eyed adventurers to stumble inside, yet I find myself feeling professionally unfulfilled.

Well honey, perhaps the time has arrived for a significant change, or maybe even a fresh start?

But we possess a stable financial situation, a beautiful cavern perfectly suited to raise some un-dead, and I enjoy absolute job security.

Marky, all of that means nothing if you are not truly happy, and you always dreamed of opening that inn, remember? She strolled over, lightly massaging his shoulders as she spoke, reminding him how we used to talk about it during those long, cold nights before you ascended, planning that we would buy an old barnhouse, fix it up, let out rooms, brew our own beer, cook hearty meals, and hire a bard or two.

Of course I remember, but that was nothing but a foolish dream, as there is no way a Lich could run a tavern; it is simply not the done thing.

Marky, baby, who cares what the done thing is? Let us do it! There is that nasty little tavern down the road where you send minions to spread rumors of your treasure, but that is our only competition, meaning we have the market cornered!

You know what, Sharon, you are right; you are always right. Let us do this, baby.

Six months later, Markond stood cleaning a mug with his favorite rag, a warm smile crossing his face. The tavern was bustling, the fire pit roared warmly in the center of the room, and the minstrel sang songs of heroes of old. Sharon served a group of rowdy dwarves, and she had never looked more beautiful to him, not even on the day he kidnapped her from her village, for everything was perfect.
syntax_complex.writingprompts::46:
Although I understood that I would not be able to perceive my surroundings immediately, having been warned that the process would necessitate significant exertion and might potentially leave me feeling utterly overwhelmed, I clung to vague, flickering memories of what sight had once been like before that catastrophic car accident rendered me blind in both eyes at the tender age of three. I firmly believe that this early experience proved beneficial, as the ability to process light and color for those initial three years likely enabled my brain to recall visual information rather than forcing me to learn how to interpret the world entirely anew.

Throughout this arduous transition, James provided invaluable support, often teasing me whenever I instinctively closed my eyes to navigate as I had done before; he would suddenly position himself directly in my path, and though it was never malicious, if I protested his interference, he would simply extend his arms to impede my movement until he finally drew me into a tight, reassuring embrace. He would whisper, insisting that he would not let go until I opened my eyes, and because no one had ever loved me with such profound intensity, I could hear that devotion resonating in his voice and feel it radiating from him every time he held me.

I practiced constantly, though frequent, painful headaches often resulted from my desperate attempts to observe everything at once; for instance, dark, irregular blotches smeared across the table while I ate breakfast, which James explained were merely shadows cast by the tree outside. That tree, which had never bothered me previously, now seemed to be actively interrupting my meal, making the simple act of eating a bowl of cereal remarkably difficult, and I still found myself reaching out to tactilely confirm the validity of my visual perceptions. It is impossible to describe how deeply strange it felt to witness my own hands before me, appearing as two misshapen, fumbling blurs that struggled to interact with objects I once touched with ease, despite the fact that I had always cherished those hands.

Eventually, those dark smears resolved into actual shadows, and James’s face finally became clear to me, marking what I consider the happiest moment of my life; upon waking one morning to find him turning toward me, I saw his eyes shining with a brilliance that suggested they contained their own internal light, revealing a level of beauty I had never truly comprehended. Once the confusing blotches no longer obscured his features and I could view him with absolute clarity, my internal struggle began as I realized my own face remained stubbornly unclear. The nasty, dark marks across my jawline were not mere tricks of light but were, in fact, acne scars that I had never perceived because my skin felt smooth to the touch, and while I had known about my wrinkles, the sickly green circles under my eyes contrasted so poorly with my dark irises that my eyes, unlike the radiant eyes of James, appeared profoundly dead and hollow.

I refrained from asking James about these revelations, as I had never known I was so ugly, and even if I were, I had previously assumed James must be equally unattractive; why else would a handsome man choose a blind girlfriend? I could finally observe how other women stared at him—a gaze never directed at me—transforming our once-fun trips to the grocery store into opportunities to witness every other woman, whom he could easily have, stealing furtive glances or smiling whenever he looked in their direction. I am entirely uncertain of what to think, especially since I occasionally suspect he smiles back; once, when I caught him looking at two women passing by at a restaurant, my stomach knotted, yet I merely stared at my pasta, forcing my pockmarked face into an amusement I did not feel when he asked if something was wrong, simply replying that I was fine, even as he smiled and told me he loved me, a sentiment I desperately wish I could believe.
syntax_complex.writingprompts::48:
I find myself unable to shake this persistent, gnawing feeling—that peculiar, insidious sensation creeping along my spine like some parasitic entity waiting to take up permanent residence at the base of my skull. It is an utterly indeterminable, unsettling feeling that I am being watched, and despite my most concerted efforts, I simply cannot shake it off. I am entirely certain that I know precisely what this signifies, yet I am far from ready to openly admit that I truly understand. Let us call him the author. He is watching, waiting, and perpetually building, and even as I formulate these very thoughts, he is scratching them down in his jagged, chicken-scratch scrawl, perhaps touching the tip of his pen against his teeth in deep, calculating thought. I can feel his presence; I can visualize him clearly within my mind’s eye, and he is undoubtedly attempting to determine the most effective manner in which to orchestrate my demise. 

I suppose, in retrospect, it is entirely my own fault. You see, I kept asking, for I desperately needed to understand; I had to discover if there existed some grand, directing hand behind the mechanics of life. If mankind possessed a definitive purpose, a reason for our existence, I needed to appreciate the specific goal toward which we all labored. There exists a moment, one of particular, crystalline realization, which caught me and held me fast, much like my growing apprehension regarding this unseen observer; only, this feeling was deeper, more primal. I knew—I mean I truly, deeply understood—that all of existence is merely a narrative. Life is a story, a conclusion which inevitably led me to the realization that there must necessarily be an architect, an author. 

The car narrowly missed me, and I experienced an inkling of pressure against my chest that verged on the absolute edge of panic. I did not cross the street when the green man displayed on the crossing signal; instead, I took a cautious step back. My instincts—my so-called spidey-sense—tingled violently. The taxi-cab driver never saw me, and I had not seen him either, until his drunken, sprawling vehicle slammed into the very same traffic signal post by which I had, until moments ago, been standing. Can I even begin to articulate how profoundly disturbing that is? I had this realization, followed immediately by a sudden, overwhelming sensation of cold fear. If I had not heeded my gutless compulsion to retreat, I might have been splattered between the cabbie's car and the hard, unyielding surface of the traffic signal pole. I turned my gaze upward, burning eyes and clenching jaw notwithstanding, and decried whoever worked at compiling this chaotic narrative. 

What the actual fuck was that? I shouted into the void. 

Okay, so I realize that my choice of words probably did not fall within the strict definition of circumspect, but hell, we are talking about some kind of god-figure who is actively deciding upon the precise moment of my death. 

Are you sure? my logical brain questioned. 

I pondered my position, both in the physical and the meta-physical sense, and finally answered myself internally. Yeah, I am fucking sure, I replied. How else could you possibly explain the sudden epiphany and my subsequent, almost immediate brush with death? There is an author, and he clearly does not want to be known. 

I am not entirely sure how I knew that the author did not wish to be acknowledged, or the fact that he was a man, but I figured it was something inherent in my general make-up that granted me this specific knowledge. Oh, do not get all high and mighty and begin to preach at me now; I am not talking about religion or spirituality, for I simply want to live, damnit. I stood there, still staring up at the darkening sky, attempting to impart my utter disgust and frustration when the signal pole creaked, doing so in a manner that felt entirely unnatural. I adjusted my head so that my eyes were perfectly level with the pole. 

The metal appeared strangely warped, and I suddenly realized that the car had burst into brilliant, violent flames. 

When had that even happened? I thought. Nevermind, run, you stupid fool. 

My internal dialog is not always the most kind; I am, by nature, a blunt sort. So, I ran. As to what I was running from, if Mr. Omniscient author was already ensconced within my head, he could follow me anywhere. Hell, I could suffer an inopportune flashback, and he could hit me with a mack truck. If this author had truly decided that I was going to die, why had he not already finished it? 

Fuck me, I thought. It is all about the drama; it is about the story. 

Sick fuck, I said aloud. I knew he would hear me, or at the very least, he would write that in his juvenile scrawl, fully aware that I intended it for him. 

What if I simply stop? 

I looked up again, and said, What are you going to do with a character who refuses to cooperate, huh? 

Naturally, he did not respond. It was not as if I expected a booming voice from the sky, but I figured he might strike me down with lightning or something; I mean, it is potentially within his ability, right? He might decide that my knowledge of the plan labeled me as a liability. 

What the hell is the plan anyway? 

I do not know, but I suppose the plan is for me to die. Perhaps he is not into the mundane. Maybe, just maybe, he wants my death to be something significant, something of a show. I bet that is it. I got the sense again; a gut punch to my stomach making my insides roil like they were leaking to the outside, and the rumbling in my stomach suggested I take a step back. I did. Something pierced the skin in my back. It was a fluid, smooth motion that parted the skin. I felt the warm blood mixing with my sweat as it soaked the back of my flannel shirt. 

A quiet voice whispered in my ear. Hello protagonist, she said. I am your antagonist; the author says hello. 

That was all she said. She did not have a scent, like one would normally expect. She was a ghost from the shadows. I do not know who she was, or why she was chosen, but she had made it clear... I was right. Take that, you fucker. I did not have the strength to say it, but I know he heard me.
syntax_complex.writingprompts::49: Will life ever improve, or must I perpetually wonder about the nature of tomorrow’s weather, especially while that girl, who is currently staring directly at me with what I suspect is profound hatred, causes me to sweat profusely as I stand in this agonizing coffee line? These people are all watching me, and as my hands drip with nervous perspiration, I realize that I am finally next in line. I accidentally screamed, "I-I'll have 20!" and immediately questioned why I would do that, feeling that I should simply walk out while everyone watched my horrible mistake. Wishing I had remained in bed, I stammered, "S-Sorry, I'll have a Venti Matcha Green," noticing that the barista, who was shaking as much as I was, clearly felt nervous because of my outburst. Recognizing that I had to own my behavior, I apologized for shouting, claiming I was distracted, to which she replied that it was her first day. Muttering an acknowledgment while avoiding eye contact as my heart raced, I noted her cute voice before paying and fleeing to the curb. What a relief it was to escape those people, whose judging eyes had nearly caused a heart attack, although I could not help but think about how cute that girl was. When was the last time I had actually spoken to a female—perhaps in the first grade—and did it even matter, given that she likely perceived me as a freak? After shouting at her, I buried my face in my hands, listening to the ambient sounds of the suburbs, where birds chirped, distant horns beeped, and trees swished, until the door behind me opened. I turned to find the girl sitting down next to me, covered in green tea, as she handed me my order. When I asked what had happened, she explained that while making my drink, she had realized she added too much cream and mistakenly included coffee in the tea. I laughed, which only made her more nervous, so I tried to calm her by saying it was funny while sipping the drink, which tasted terrible. When she abruptly asked if I wanted to come over, I felt nervous, yet seeing her own visible shaking, I agreed.
